title: திருமுருகாற்றுப்படை
theme: Thirumurugatruppadai is a guide poem in which one who has received the god's grace directs another seeker to Murugan: after a 66-line opening sentence that ends in the promise that the seeker will have what he wants, it describes the god at six places (Parankunram, Alaivay, Avinankudi, Eragam, every hill, and Pazhamudircholai with all the places of his worship), each with its own worshippers, and closes by scripting the seeker's praise, the god's appearance and his gift, and the waterfall of his hill.
structure_note: Six sections, each closing on a refrain of right (உரியன், அதாஅன்று; நின்றதன் பண்பே). Twelve of the 21 core units were moved to sentence breaks inside the sections, giving 18 units.
source_issues: Throughout the text the comitative ending -ஒடு after ய and some other letters is printed -அடு (தெய்வ வுத்தியடு 23, ஓடையடு 79, கூகையடு 49, வள்ளியடு 102, மடந்தையடு 175, குளவியடு 191, கொடியடு 219, 227, தொகுதியடு 212, அருவியடு 240, மஞ்சளடு 235): this looks like an encoding loss of the vowel sign ொ, like the TSCII repairs flagged at lines 39, 285 and 291. Karu forms are copied as printed.
Line 173 மருங்கிந்தம் looks like a misprint for மருங்கில் தம்.
Line 188 பெரிந்துஉவந்து looks like a misprint for பெரிது உவந்து.

Line 295 prints நல்கும்;அதி, which reads more naturally as one word with the particle -மதி (நல்குமதி); the semicolon may be an editorial or encoding error. The sentence break used for the units (after பரிசில் நல்கும்) does not depend on it.
Line 314 கருந்கோட்டு has an irregular nasal (expected கருங்கோட்டு).

reading: The god's far-reaching brightness is first likened to the sun that the world praises, rising out of the sea; then he is named by his works, feet that bore up those who came to him and a great hand that wore down his foes, as the husband of a bright-browed woman of spotless chastity, wearing on his chest a cool rolling garland from the kadamba of a forest freshly soaked by the first rains.
nuance: Lines 4 and 5 are built as a pair (உறுநர்த் தாங்கிய ... நோன்றாள், செறுநர்த் தேய்த்த ... தடக்கை): the same god is shelter to those who come and ruin to those who oppose, which is the whole promise the guide will make. The consort of line 6 is not named.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 1-16: the opening description of the god closes at மார்பினன் in line 11, and line 12 turns to his hill and its women.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the great hand that wore down his enemies

reading: On the god's high hill, women with anklets on small red feet, cloth as red as the cochineal insect and girdles strung with coins dress their parted hair with vetchi and kuvalai petals, set a tilakam on the brow, tuck in champak and marutham clusters, hang pindi shoots in their ears, smear their young breasts with sandal paste and vengai pollen, and pluck and toss the tender leaves of the vila tree.
nuance: The women are not named until line 41 (சூரர மகளிர், the fearsome maidens of the hill), so this long toilet scene is a description of goddesses of the slope, not of mortal girls; the flowers they wear are of every land, and the poem does not comment on it.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 1-16, 17-32 and 33-48: lines 12 to 44 are one description of the hill's women and the god's garland. This unit takes the women's adornment to line 37, where they toss the vila shoots, before the song they sing in line 38.

thinai_evidence.note: a description of the god's hill and its women inside the praise; no love situation is stated

comparisons.tenor: the scent of the sandal paste

reading: The women sing 'long live the victorious cock banner' and dance in a grove on a slope so dense even the female monkey does not know it; the god wears on his head a cool garland of kaanthal that bees do not swarm, and with his long bright spear entered the cold old sea and cut down Sur at the root, while a dread demoness with dry hair and rolling eyes, owl and snake hanging from her ears, held up a skull and danced the thunangai of the battlefield; this red-speared god of flawless victory is the one, the guide says, that you will reach at once if your heart desires to go to his red feet.
nuance: The poem's first sentence runs 66 lines before its main verb: the sunrise, the hill, the women and the war on Sur all lead to the promise இன்னே பெறுதி நீ முன்னிய வினையே (66), so the whole description serves as the guide's grounds for that promise. Lines 57 and 58 (இருபே ருருவின் ஒருபே ரியாக்கை / அறுவேறு வகையின்) are hard: whether the great body of two forms is Sur's or the god's, and what the six ways are, I cannot settle from the words alone.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 33-48 and 49-66: begins with the women's song in line 38 and ends at line 66, where முன்னிய வினையே closes the poem's first sentence.

thinai_evidence.note: the god's victory over Sur, praised; the battle is the god's deed, so the thinai stays paadaan

reading: He also has a right to dwell on the hill west of Koodal, the city of crowded mansion streets whose gate, hung with tall war banners, ball and doll, has worn down its enemies; there bees sleep in the thorny-stemmed lotus of the wide muddy fields, hum on the honeyed neythal at dawn, and when the sun is up swarm humming round the pool flowers that open like eyes on the hill.
nuance: The bees' day, from field lotus to dawn neythal to the hill pool, joins the city's farmland to the god's hill: the shrine is placed by walking the eye from the walled city out to the slope, and the war-scarred gate of Koodal is the first thing the seeker passes.

thinai_evidence.note: the first of the god's dwelling places, praised; the refrain உரியன் names his right to each

comparisons.tenor: the pool flowers opening at sunrise

reading: At Alaivay he rides an elephant fast as the wind and irresistible as Death, its scarred, striped brow carrying an unfading garland and frontlet and bells ringing at its sides; gems of five kinds flash like lightning in his crown, gold earrings shine like stars clasping the moon, and each of his six faces does a work: one spreads rays so the dark world shines, one gladly grants boons to those who praise, one watches over the sacrifices of brahmins who keep the mantra rule, one lights the directions like the moon as it searches out the meanings left over, one crushes enemies in battle with a wrathful heart, and one smiles with Valli, the young kuravar girl with a waist like a creeper.
nuance: The six faces are a list of offices (light, boon, sacrifice, knowledge, war, love) rather than a portrait; only the last face is turned toward one person, Valli, and she is placed among the kuravar of the hill, not among the gods.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 78-90 and 91-108: the six faces (91 to 102) belong with the faces introduced in line 90, and line 103 (ஆங்குஅம் மூவிருமுகனும்) sums them up and turns to the twelve hands.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the flashing of the crown's gems
the gold earrings shining around the face
the face that lights the directions

reading: As the six faces keep their order, each of the twelve hands does its part: one raised for the sages who travel the sky, one at the waist, one on the thigh, one driving the goad, two whirling shield and spear, one at the chest, one with the garland, one swinging the bangle aloft, one ringing the bell, one pouring rain from the blue sky, one crowning the heavenly women with the wedding garland; and with the sky's instruments, horns, white conches and thunder-voiced drums sounding and the peacock crying on his victory banner, he goes swiftly by the sky road to Alaivay, which the world praises: dwelling there is his settled nature.
nuance: Where the faces were given offices in the world, the hands are given gestures, and two of them (rain, line 116; the wedding garland, line 117) reach out to the sky and its women. The god reaches his sea shrine by the sky road (விசும்பு ஆறாக), not over land.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 91-108 and 109-125: begins at line 103, which sums up the six faces and turns to the twelve hands, and ends at the Alaivay refrain in line 125.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

reading: At Avinankudi the sages go first: clothed in bark, hair white as the valampuri conch, bodies shining, deerskin on chests where the flesh has wasted, bones showing, fasting for many days, minds rid of hostility and hatred, knowing what the learned do not and themselves the limit of the learned, having cast out lust and fierce anger and knowing no distress; after them come musicians in spotless clothes like smoke, their gentle hearts trained to the lute, plucking its sweet strings, with flawless women whose bodies glow like mango shoots and whose skin is spotted like gold on a touchstone.
nuance: The sages are described almost wholly by what they have removed (flesh, food, hostility, lust, anger, distress), and that list is what gives them the right to walk in first, ahead of the gods of the next lines.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 126-142 and 143-159: the sages (126 to 137) and the musicians with their women (138 to 147) are one procession that closes at விளங்க in line 147; line 148 begins the first of the three great gods.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the ascetic's excellence in his own calling, the தாபதப் பக்கம் of vaakai (porul 2.16)

comparisons.tenor: the spots on the women's skin

reading: Then come three lords, each known by banner, mount and deed: the rich one whose long banner bears the many-striped bird that strikes down the snake with venomous fangs and fire-hot breath; the one with the white bull raised on his banner, Uma beside him, three unwinking eyes, who destroyed the three walled cities; and the one with a thousand eyes, who completed a hundred sacrifices, mounted on the neck of the four-tusked elephant.
nuance: None of the three gods is named; they are identified by emblem and deed, and all three come as visitors to the younger god's shrine.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 143-159: begins at line 148, where the three great gods begin, after the sages' procession closes at 147; ends at line 159 with the third god (செல்வனும்).

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

reading: With those three famed lords, who guard the world from their good cities, at their head, and with the four-faced one born of the lotus in mind, the thirty-three gods of four kinds and the eighteen companies, bright as stars in bloom, swift as rising wind, strong as fire in wind and loud as thunder, whirl through the sky and come together to see him and win what they need; and with his flawless consort he rests some days at Avinankudi.
nuance: Lines 160 to 168 are hard: why the four-faced one is 'pointed to' (நான்முக ஒருவற் சுட்டி) and what high state the gods seek (உயர்நிலை பெறீஇயர்) are not said. One later reading takes it as the gods coming to ask for Brahma's release; the words here say only that they come with a need (உறுகுறை).

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

reading: At Eragam, the twice-born of many ancient families, never failing in the six duties, who spent forty-eight years of youth in study, devoted to dharma and rich in the three fires, chant at the proper hours; wearing the fine thread of three strands of nine, their wet cloth drying on them, hands joined above their heads, they praise him, recite with their tongues the rare hidden mantra of six letters, and holding fragrant flowers rejoice; and there he dwells.
nuance: Every number in the passage (six duties, 'the two', forty-eight years, three fires, nine threads, six letters) marks the brahmins' order, and the six-letter mantra (ஆறெழுத்து, line 186) is the only place the idyll names a mantra. இருவர்ச் சுட்டிய (178) is obscure to me: it may mean families traced from both parents.

thinai_evidence.note: the brahmin's six duties praised: the பார்ப்பனப் பக்கம் of vaakai (porul 2.16)

reading: On the hills the velan wears a garland of green naRai pods with wild jasmine and white koothaalam, his chest smeared with fragrant sandal; the hunters with their cruel bows, drinking with their kin in the small hill village the toddy matured in long bamboo, dance the kuravai to the small thondagam drum; and the women, their hair bound with flowers from deep pools, kulai leaves and the white clusters of red-stemmed kadamba, wearing skirts of cool leaves strung for the bees, walk with the soft gait of peacocks.
nuance: This is the only section of the idyll where the worshippers are the people of the land itself, the velan, the hunters and their women, drinking and dancing, rather than sages, gods or brahmins.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill people's festival for the god, inside the praise

reading: The god himself is red, in red clothes, with tender seyalai shoots swaying at his ears, wearing waistband, anklets and a garland of red ixora, with flute, horn and many small instruments, the ram and the peacock, and the flawless cock on his banner; tall, with bangled shoulders, among women whose voices are sweet as plucked strings, wearing a fine cloth that reaches the ground, he takes the many soft-shouldered does in his drum-like arms and leads them: dancing on every hill is his settled nature.
nuance: The god is described in the same list form as the hill people of the previous lines, with the same red garland, instruments and women: on the hills he is one of the dancers, leading the kuravai, not a figure carried through the sky as at Alaivay.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the women he leads in the dance

reading: He is found wherever he is worshipped: at the festivals each town holds, where small millet is mixed with flowers, a kid is cut and the cock banner is set up; wherever devotees praise him; at the veri ground the velan prepares; in forests, groves and lovely river islets, at rivers and tanks and many other places, at crossroads and junctions and under fresh-flowered kadamba, in the common ground, the hall and at the sacred post.
nuance: The list moves from the town's festival to the open country, the crossroads and a single kadamba tree: the god's places are not only the named shrines but any spot where he is called, which is why the guide will say 'whatever the place may be' (ஆண்டாண்டு ஆயினும் ஆக, line 250).
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 218-233: lines 218 to 226 list the places of his worship, ending at கந்துடை நிலையினும்; line 227 begins the rite itself, which runs to line 249.

thinai_evidence.note: the places of the god's worship listed, inside the praise

reading: There the rite is performed: the place is washed with a fine banner raised, smeared with ghee and white mustard, words murmured and bows made, rich flowers scattered, two clothes of contrasting colour worn, a red thread tied, white puffed rice strewn, pure white rice mixed with the blood of a strong fat ram set out in small offerings in many baskets, turmeric and fragrant water sprinkled, cool oleander garlands cut in pairs and hung, the hill town praised, incense raised and the kurinji tune sung; with waterfall and instruments sounding, flowers scattered so that all fear, and red millet spread with blood, the kuramagal sets up Murugu's music in the dread great house where the god is brought, horns are blown and curved bells rung, the unyielding elephant is praised, and those who seek obtain what they sought; so it is known that he dwells in each place.
nuance: முருகாற்றுப் படுத்த (244), 'where Murugu is guided in', uses the same verb as the poem's own title: the priestess guides the god to the worshippers just as the poem guides the worshipper to the god. The rite is presented as effective without qualification (வேண்டுநர் வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தினர், 248).
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 218-233 and 234-249: begins at line 227, where the rite begins after the list of places, and ends at line 249, which closes places and rites with அறிந்த வாறே.

thinai_evidence.note: the worship rite that brings the god, inside the praise

reading: Whatever the place, when you first see him, praise him with a glad face, worship with joined hands, bow to touch his feet, and say: lord of six dwellings, born of the six, whom one of the five took into his palm at the blue pool on the high peak; son of the god of the banyan; son of the mountain's daughter; Death to enemies; child of victorious Kotravai; infant of the jewelled ancient one; leader of the army of the gods; garlanded chest; poet who knows the texts; unmatched in war; warrior of peerless strength; wealth of the brahmins; mountain of the words of the wise; husband of the women; bull among men; great lord with the spear in your hand.
nuance: The guide gives the seeker the very words to say: the poem turns from description to a script of address. The epithets of birth name three mothers in a row (the mountain's daughter, Kotravai, the ancient one), and the six of his birth and the six of his dwelling are set side by side (அறுவர் பயந்த ஆறமர் செல்வ).

thinai_evidence.note: praise and supplication (பரவல், புகழ்ச்சி), paadaan (porul 2.22)

comparisons.tenor: the god as destroyer of his enemies
the god's store of the words of the wise

reading: ...of undiminished victory, who killed the mountain; lord of kurinji with its sky-touching peaks; bull among poets of praised good speech; Muruga, of great name and rare lineage; famed one who satisfies those who long; red one of gold ornament who gives to the afflicted; tall Vel who shelters suppliants on your fearsome chest that won great wars; god of great name whom the great praise; mighty one whose strength cut down Sur; warrior great in battle; chief!
nuance: The god is praised in the words a bard uses of a patron: one who satisfies those who long (நசையுநர்க்கு ஆர்த்தும்), gives to the afflicted, and shelters suppliants (பரிசிலர்த் தாங்கும்). The puram patron's praise is carried over whole to a god, and he is also made a poet himself (புலவர் ஏறே).
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 266-275 and 276-291: the string of epithets ends at குரிசில் in line 276, closed by எனப்பல; line 277 turns to the seeker's own words.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god as warrior and as giver to suppliants, paadaan

reading: Praising him tirelessly as far as you know, say: 'Since it is hard for living beings to know you to your measure, I have come thinking of your feet, wise one who has no equal'; and before you finish what you meant, his many small attendants of many forms will appear at the festival ground and say, 'Great one, a poor old-mouthed suppliant has come, longing for your generous fame,' praising many sweet and good things; and he, coming in a sky-high form full of divine power, will take his awesome high place, show the young beauty of his fragrant ancient godhead, say 'Fear not; I knew of your coming,' speak kind words lovingly, and give you the rare gift that makes you stand alone in the dark-sea-girt world.
nuance: The scene follows the bard's arrival at a king's court step by step: the suppliant (இரவலன்) is announced by attendants, praised to the patron, reassured, and given a gift; only the gift is different, since it makes him unique in the world rather than rich. நின்னளந்து அறிதல் மன்னுயிர்க்கு அருமையின் (278) gives the reason for coming to the feet at all: the god cannot be known, only approached.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 276-291 and 292-307: the god's reply that begins in line 291 (அஞ்சல் ஓம்புமதி) runs to the gift in line 295 (பரிசில் நல்குமதி); the waterfall's sentence begins with பலவுடன் at the end of line 295 and is taken whole into the next unit.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide's promise of the patron's gift, the core of the ஆற்றுப்படை, paadaan

reading: The poem closes on the god's waterfall: swaying like many different cloths, carrying agil, rolling whole sandal trunks, tearing up bamboo with its flowered branches, breaking the cool fragrant honeycombs that hang like the sun's disc from the sky-touching peak, mixing in old jackfruit segments, shedding fragrant naga flowers, chilling langur and monkey, drenching the great she-elephant, sweeping along the pearl-bearing tusk of the great tusker so that gold and gems gleam, felling banana trunks and coconut clusters, bending pepper vines, scattering peacocks and the jungle hen, driving the boar and the bear with fur like palmyra fibre into the rock clefts and making the wild bull bellow, it roars down from afar: he is the lord of the hill of Pazhamudircholai.
nuance: The last sentence (296 to 317) is a single torrent through every native thing of the hill, trees, fruit, beasts and birds, and only its last line names the god as lord of the hill: the poem ends by showing the seeker the god's land in motion rather than the god.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 292-307 and 308-317: begins at line 296, where the waterfall's sentence starts after பரிசில் நல்குமதி in line 295, and runs to the end of the poem, since lines 296 to 317 are one sentence ending in மலைகிழவோனே.

comparisons.tenor: the round honeycombs on the peak

title: பொருநராற்றுப்படை
theme: Porunaratruppadai: a bard who has been rewarded by Karikal Valavan guides another bard to him, describing the lute and its singer, his own reception, feast and parting gifts, the king's birth and victory at Venni, and the Chola land where the five landscapes mingle and the Kaveri does not fail.
structure_note: The idyll is one long address. Lines 1-59 hail the bard and describe the lute and the paadini; 60-129 tell the guide's own reception; 130-148 praise the king; 149-177 promise the gifts; 178-248 describe the land. Fourteen of the sixteen core units were re-cut at sense breaks into thirteen adjusted units (fifteen units in all); 189-207 and 208-217 are unchanged.
source_issues: Line 168 prints முறையுழிக்; tamilvu reads முறையுளிக் (flag r11). The sense (in due order) is the same; our reading kept.
Line 73 prints ஓன்றியான் with a long initial vowel; ஒன்றியான் (or ஒன்று யான்) is expected.
Line 97 prints கண்டோட்; கண்டோர் (those who see) is the expected form.
Line 123 prints அகறி ரொவெம், which reads as அகறிரோ எம்; the short ொ for ோ looks like a misprint.
Line 145 prints ஒங்கிருஞ் with a short initial vowel; ஓங்கிருஞ் is expected (as line 206 was repaired, flag r7).
Lines 129 and 177 each end with the first word of the next sentence (வென்வேல், நொல்லென); units cannot split a line, so these words stay in the earlier unit.
Line 228 is printed ஒரு குடையா னென்று கூற; the sense (they say: one umbrella) takes it as ஒரு குடையான் என்று.

reading: The guide hails a skilled porunan who, once the festival of a great town of unfailing plenty is over, cares nothing for its leftover food and sets out for another land, and describes his lute part by part: a bowl forked like a hoofprint, a covering skin the colour of lamp flame stitched with a seam like the line of down on a young pregnant woman's belly, pegs like the eyes of a crab in its hole, a mouth shaped like the eighth-day moon, a stem rising like a snake's raised hood, bands like the bangles on a dark woman's forearm, strings fine as pounded millet, the whole like a bathed and fragrant bride, a paalai lute so sweet that it makes the robbers who waylay travellers drop their weapons and turn back.
nuance: Almost every part of the lute is likened to a woman's body or ornament (the down on a pregnant woman's belly, a dark woman's bangles, a bathed bride), so the instrument is already a body before the singing woman of the next unit is described. The power of the paalai tune over robbers (lines 21 and 22) is the first proof that this bard's art protects him on the road.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 1-14 and 15-29: the description of the lute runs from line 4 to பாலை in line 22, and line 23 turns to how it is played and to the singing woman.

thinai_evidence.note: a performer addresses a fellow bard to direct him to a patron: the guide poem (ஆற்றுப்படை) under paadaan

reading: Playing the lute in all its ways and scattering fine words with the music, the bard is accompanied by his paadini, described from head to foot: hair like rippled sand, brow like the crescent, brows like a killing bow, mouth red as the silk-cotton petal, teeth like pearls, ears hung with swinging earrings, neck bent with modesty, shoulders like swaying bamboo, fingers like the kaanthal of the high hills, nails like a parrot's beak, breasts so close a split rib cannot pass between, navel like an eddy, a waist one hardly knows is there, a girdle of strands like rows of bees, thighs like a she-elephant's trunk, and small feet like a panting dog's tongue, blistered like ripe marul fruit from walking on ground red as melted lac, so that at midday she stops on the road, like a peahen.
nuance: The head-to-foot description ends not on beauty but on injury: the feet like a panting dog's tongue are soft because they are hurt, and the blisters are the road's mark on her. The ideal body and the poverty of the journey are drawn in one sentence, which is the guide poem's whole case for going to the patron.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 15-29 and 30-48: the playing begins at line 23, and the description of the paadini closes at பெருந்தகு பாடினி in line 47.

thinai_evidence.note: the companion of the bard on the guide's road; the description belongs to the guide poem under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the many strands of her girdle

reading: Singing to the beat day after day, halting in forest tracks where tuskers roam, bearing the hardship of thin, net-like shade under the leafless maraa, and making the due offering to the god who dwells in the forest, the leader of the performers with his lute, which looks like the three drum-thundering kings seated together in council, is told that having strayed from the way he did not know, meeting the guide on the road is the fruit of his past penance.
nuance: What the simile of the three kings in council (lines 53 to 55) describes is not fixed by the words: it may be the lute, held up as a court in itself, or the gathered company of performers. 'நோற்றதன் பயனே' (line 59) makes the chance meeting a reward for past austerity, the first of the poem's comparisons between the bard's luck and the fruit of tapas (see lines 91 and 92).
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 30-48 and 49-59: line 48 (the singing to the beat) begins the clause that closes at நோற்றதன் பயனே in line 59.

reading: Listen well, the guide says, you who excel in fame: if you want to end the long hunger of your large kin, worn by wasting hunger, rise without delay, master of the seven strings; for I too, like a bird that thinks of a fruiting tree, entered unannounced the wide humming palace whose great gate stops no one who comes in need, weary in body, to end my distress, and beat my wide drum, its face stained by the hand like the spots on a cobra's spread hood, to a double beat in the depth of night as Venus rose.
nuance: The open gate 'that does not bar those who come in need' (line 66) is what makes the fruit-tree simile work: a fruiting tree in the open is free to every bird. The guide's argument is his own story, told in the first person, so the promise rests on testimony rather than on the patron's reputation.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 60-75: the bard's arrival and playing end with the time of day in line 72; from line 73 the patron's welcome begins.

reading: Before I could say what I wanted, the patron, wishing to take me as kin, spoke words of welcome, seated me close where his eyes could reach me, looked at me without tiring as if drinking me in, so that my bones cooled as if melting, had my rags, sweat-soaked, patched with other threads and full of lice and nits, stripped off and gave me cloth fine as a snake's slough that the eye cannot see through, and had jewelled, smiling women pour drink again and again into golden cups in his cloud-high mansion until my weariness ended; so I stayed in a corner of his palace like ascetics who gain the fruit of their penance without leaving the body, and rose free of every care except the drowsy tremor of drink.
nuance: The patron gives before he is asked (line 73), and the comparison in lines 91 and 92 makes the bard's ease the reward that ascetics get only after death, here received in the living body. The removal of the patched rags is the first act, before food: the bard is re-dressed as a guest of rank.

comparisons.vehicle: தவஞ்செய் மாக்கள் தம்முடம் பிடாஅ ததன்பய மெய்திய வளவை மான

reading: Waking to find his former misery gone like dusk and his state now one of bee-ringed garlands that amazes all who see it, the bard wonders whether it is a dream, until untaught young servants tell him; the patron calls him at once, and after the rites serves boiled meat of sheep fed on grass and fat roasted on spits, urging him to eat, then many kinds of sweets when he tires of meat, with drum and small lute and bright-browed dancing women keeping time; after many days of drinking he begs him to take rice, unbroken, husked, the grains straight as fingers, with fried relish floating in sour gruel, until the guests' teeth, blunted by meat day and night, are like the ploughshare that has ploughed a dry field.
nuance: The comedy of lines 117 and 118 answers the hunger of line 61: the poor bard's teeth wear down from too much meat, like a share on dry ground. Rice is begged on him (இரப்ப, line 112), so the host now does the asking that the bard did before. Line 96's 'misery like dusk' is uncertain in its construction, and line 97 prints கண்டோட், which reads best as கண்டோர்.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 95-117 and 118-127: the morning begins at line 96, and the image of the blunted teeth closes with மழுங்கி in line 118.

reading: Sated with meat and with no room left to breathe, one day the bard softly tells the lord to whom angry enemies bring tribute that he will go back to his old town; the lord, looking at him angrily like one wronged, asks 'will you leave our company?', and then, saying 'take what you like', gives elephants with their mates and calves whose slow gait is like the beat of the thudi drum, giving and giving by the measure he knows, while the bard takes what he needs by the measure he knows and comes away with his poverty ended.
nuance: The king's anger at being left is the form his affection takes. Lines 127 and 128 set two measures side by side, தன் அறி அளவையின் and என் அறி அளவையின்: the giver gives to the limit of what he knows to give, and the taker takes to the limit of what he knows to need, so that the gift is bounded by the receiver's restraint as much as by the giver's wealth.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 118-127 and 128-144: the leave-taking begins at line 119 and the bard's story ends at இன்மை தீர வந்தனென் in line 129; the last word of line 129, வென்வேல், opens the next sentence but cannot be split from its line.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's parting gifts to the bard

reading: The patron is the son of Ilaiyon of many fine chariots, a lord fierce with Murugan's anger, who received his inheritance while still in the womb, made unknowing foes obey, threw enemy lands into turmoil, and grew from the day he learned to crawl, bearing his land on his shoulder, like the sun that spreads its rays over the sea and climbs the sky; like the fierce cub of the yaali, which before it leaves the breast kills a tusker in its first hunt, Karikal Valavan with his eye-filling chaplet struck at Venni so that the two great kings, who wore the palmyra frond and the neem's tender leaf on their heads, fell together on one field.
nuance: The whole stretch answers one charge, youth: the king inherited in the womb, ruled from the crawling age, and won at Venni like a cub still at the breast. The two defeated kings are named only by their flowers, the Chera palmyra and the Pandya neem, so the victory is told as heraldry.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 128-144 and 145-160: the description of the patron begins at line 130 (after வந்தனென் in line 129) and his name closes it in line 148.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's birth and his victory at Venni

comparisons.vehicle: பவ்வ மீமிசைப் பகற்கதிர் பரப்பி வெல்வெஞ் செல்வன் விசும்புபடர்ந் தாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: the king's rise and growth from childhood

comparisons.vehicle: ஆளி நன்மான் அணங்குடைக் குருளை மீளி மொய்ம்பின் மிகுவலி செருக்கி முலைக்கோள் விடாஅ மாத்திரை ஞெரேரெனத் தலைக்கோள் வேட்டங் களிறட் டாஅங்கு
comparisons.tenor: the young king's victory at Venni

reading: If you go near the shade of his feet and stand before him in worship, he will look on you with the unfailing love of a cow that has calved and, before you even ask, strip off your stitched rags, worn and dirty like the roots of moss, and give you silk cloth with knotted borders, pour flower-scented toddy into precious cups day after day until you cover the cup with your hand, set on your curly hair a lotus of gold, petalless, bright as flame, and adorn your paadini with a fine chain that no thread strings and with bright pearls.
nuance: The promised gifts repeat in order what the guide himself received (lines 79 to 88: the rags removed, cloth given, drink poured), so the guide poem works by turning one man's experience into a forecast. The lotus is 'without petals' (ஏடில்) because it is gold: a flower that will not fade.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 145-160 and 161-176: the guide's promise begins at line 149 and the first gifts close with பாடினி அணிய in line 162; line 163 turns to the chariot.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide promises the bard the gifts he will receive

comparisons.tenor: the patron's love for the bard

reading: He will yoke four milk-white horses with swaying dyed plumes to a tall chariot whose rail is of ivory, walk seven steps behind it on foot, take away the goad and bid you mount, send you off in due order with your great lute, and give you a land of many good villages in cool fields and many fierce elephants at whom the warning drum is beaten; he does not stop giving, and if, feeding others with what you received on the way, you hurry to leave, he will grieve, and weighing the nature of this unstable world, will not be the one to send you off saying 'go'.
nuance: Walking seven steps behind the departing guest's chariot is the king's humility in giving. The syntax of lines 173 to 177 is not certain: the participle ஆர்த்தி most naturally has the bard as subject (you feed others with what you got), and பல புலந்து and நிலைமை தூக்கி may belong to the king, who will not dismiss a guest because he knows how little in the world stays.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 161-176 and 177-188: the chariot begins at line 163, and the sentence closes at செல்கென விடுக்குவன் அல்லன் in line 177; the last word of line 177, நொல்லென, opens the description of his land.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide's promise of the patron's gifts and farewell

reading: His land lies wide within the shore of the great wave-tossed sea, with dark mango trees, paddy here and there, low-hanging coconut palms and cool groves; in homes with granaries the black crow, when it tires of the red rice offerings it has eaten, leaves the tortoise that has laid its eggs to guard its young in the shade of the house's nochchi, the young play at building sand houses, and the old, entering the assembly, speak their quarrels there.
nuance: The crow is sated by the offerings (கவவு முனையின்), so the nesting tortoise is safe: in this land even the predator is fed. The quarrels of the old are carried to the assembly, not settled by force, which is the only sign of conflict in the picture.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 177-188: the description of the land begins after the farewell sentence that closes in line 177, so the unit starts at line 178.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's land

reading: Gentle-eyed peacocks dance on crooked kaanji and red marutham trees, feed on the clustered fruit of the green bitter gourd and red-segmented fruit amid the noise of labourers at the cut sugarcane and the reaped paddy, and, when they tire of that place with its beach creepers, pakanrai, budding punku, low groves and njaazhal, move to the good woodland with its thalavam, thondri, smiling mullai, golden konrai and sapphire kaayaa; and when that walk too wearies them, the herons that have fed on prawns of the shark-haunted sea, frightened from the flowering punnai by the roar of high waves, rest on the fronds of the sweet palmyra.
nuance: The creatures move between the landscapes not from want but from surfeit: the repeated முனையின் (198, 202, and 184 before it) makes boredom with plenty the motive for crossing from field to woodland to shore, the reverse of the hungry bard's crossing that opened the poem. Who moves in lines 198 to 202, the peacocks or the field folk, is not fixed by the syntax.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's land as a place every landscape shares

reading: Where tall coconuts, banana bunches, lush kaanthal and flowering naagam trees grow, in hamlets where the owl calls like a thudi drum, the gentle peacock spreads its plumes to the tune of bees humming like a lute and wanders over sand dunes white as moonlight; those who bartered honey and tubers go home with fish oil and toddy, and those who gave sweet sugarcane and flattened rice go home with venison and liquor.
nuance: The barter of lines 214 to 217 pairs the hill's honey and tubers with the shore's fish oil, and the field's cane and flattened rice with the forest's venison: the five lands are joined by trade as well as by the wandering creatures of the previous unit.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's land through the exchange of its products

reading: There the fishermen sing the kurinji tune and the hill people wear chaplets of fragrant neythal flowers, the forest people sing the marutham tune and the bards tell of the mullai and the other landscapes, the jungle fowl pecks the ears of paddy and the house fowl takes the millet, hill monkeys dive in the backwaters and backwater herons perch on the hills: in the cool settlements the lands gather without blemish, and the people say there is one umbrella; such is the lord who has ruled greatly with great kinship and a just sceptre joined to virtue and knowing the right ways; long live that lord of the victorious spear.
nuance: Each people sings another land's tune, wears another land's flower, and each land's creature eats or rests in another's place: the poet takes the poetics of karu, in which each landscape has its own people, birds, food and music, and inverts it point by point to show a realm where the borders of the five lands no longer hold under one umbrella.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 218-234: the description of the mingled lands and the blessing of the king close at அன்னோன் வாழி வென்வேற் குருசில் in line 231; line 232 begins the description of drought.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's rule as one umbrella over all the lands

reading: Even in a bad season of great drought, when the sun appears so that kings tremble and spreads its many rays, scorching the kullai and setting branches aflame, when the falls of the great hills dwindle and the clustered clouds forget to draw water from the sea, the Kaveri, carrying nari, naratham, agil and sandal, sets down its load at every ford and flows on, its foaming, roaring flood entering every enclosure where bathing women plunge in, and the paddy cut with bent sickles is piled in sheaves day after day in unfailing heaps like hills, packed into sacks that crowd the space, in hedged fields of saali paddy that yield a thousandfold: he is the lord of the land the Kaveri nourishes.
nuance: The drought is granted in full, sun, dried falls and clouds that forget the sea, and the river is set against it: the land's wealth is made independent of the rain, and so of the cosmic signs that might be read against a king. The sun that makes kings tremble here is the same image the poem used for the king himself (lines 135 and 136), now turned against the land and answered by the Kaveri.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's land, whose river does not fail

title: சிறுபாணாற்றுப்படை
theme: Sirupanatruppadai: a bard who has been enriched by Nalliyakkodan, chief of Oymanadu, directs a hungry fellow bard and his troupe to him, first measuring the patron against the three crowned cities and the seven famous givers, then promising the food of each land on the road to his town and the gifts he gives before he is asked.
structure_note: The poem moves from the road and the troupe (1-40) to the address to the suppliant, the three crowned cities set down as empty (41-83), the seven givers (84-113) and the patron who bore their yoke alone (114-129); then the speaker's own former poverty (130-145), three roads through neythal, mullai and marutham each ending in a meal (146-195), the patron's town (196-202), his virtues as four audiences praise them (203-220), the praise song (221-234), the gifts (235-260) and the patron's kurinji hill (261-269).
source_issues: Line 49 prints குட்டுவண் for the king's name, elsewhere குட்டுவன் (a ண/ன confusion); the entity copies the printed form.
Line 116 prints நாககு, which reads as a misprint for நாகமும் (the list நாகமும் அகிலும் ஆரமும்); the karu form copies the printed text.
Line 52 prints தறைவாய்த் குறுந்துணி: a த் before கு is irregular; expected அறைவாய்க் (or the like).
Lines 50 and 83 print யதாஅன்று but line 67 prints யுதாஅன்று for the same connective (அதாஅன்று).
Line 131 prints கறவாக் பால்முலை, where sandhi expects கறவாப் பால்முலை.
Line 139 prints இருக்பே ரொக்கலொ, which reads as a misprint for இரும்பேர் ஒக்கலொடு (as at line 144, இரும்பே ரொக்கற்).
Line 145 prints செம்ம லூள்ளமொடு with ஊ, where உள்ளம் expects லுள்ளமொடு.
Line 152 prints மணிநீர்ப் வைப்பு: a ப் before வ is irregular.
Line 245 prints றனின் றூட்டி; தான் நின்று ஊட்டி expects றானின் றூட்டி.
Line 242 சூழ்த்த may be a misprint for சூழ்ந்த.

reading: The poem opens on the summer road the suppliants are walking: a forest river that once wound like the necklace swaying on the breast of the earth, a woman whose broad shoulders are gem-bearing hills, has left on its bank flowers the koels shook down and fine dark sand rippled like spread hair, and that sand has grown hot as heated iron, so that the travellers, stepping lightly over pebbles that tear their feet in the late days of summer under the driving morning sun, rest in the striped shade of a maraa tree on the long paalai road.
nuance: Line 11 says பாலை நின்ற பாலை: the paalai tree standing on the paalai road, or the paalai season standing over it; the pun is the poem's own. The bard will play the paalai mode on this same road at line 36, so land, season and music are tuned to one another. The river is dry here only by implication: its sand is described, not its water.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 1-16, which ended inside the word சாஅய் (lines 16-17). Lines 1 to 12 are the road and the rest in the shade; line 12 ends with அசைஇ, and line 13 begins the description of the women who rest there.

reading: The women dancers of the troupe are described feature by feature, each surpassing a thing of the land: their oiled dark hair outdoes the train that peacocks spread in the thin rain, so that the peacocks hide before their grace; their small feet are lovely as a tired dog's tongue; their thighs are closer and smoother than a she-elephant's trunk; the knot of their hair shines like the plantain's flower; bees drawn to the vengai's fresh blossom buzz at the spots on their skin; their breasts mock the kongu bud; their teeth drip sweetness like the palmyra's young fruit; and they are gentle, deer-eyed and bright-browed, with a chastity full as the mullai that opens in the kullai woodland.
nuance: The figure repeated through the passage (கதுப்பிற் கதுப்பு, குறங்கிற் குறங்கு, எயிற்றின் எயிறு, முலை முலை) sets each feature against a thing of the land that it surpasses, so the women are praised by making the forest yield to them; the frame returns at lines 263 and 264, where the peacocks of the patron's hill spread their trains like women's hair. The comparison of the feet to a tired dog's tongue is one of the poem's boldest: softness and redness, taken from the road's own weariness.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 1-16, 17-26 and 27-42, whose cuts at 16 and 26 fall inside the description (16 splits சாஅய், 26 ends one item of a list). Lines 13 to 31 are one catalogue of the women's beauty, closed by the noun விறலியர் in line 31.

thinai_evidence.note: a description of the troupe's dancing women inside the praise poem; no love situation

comparisons.tenor: the knot of the women's hair (ஓதி)
the spots on the women's skin (சுணங்கு)

reading: While untaught young men gently stroke the small soft feet of the women, worn out by walking, the skilled bard holds on his left side the small sweet-voiced lute with strings tight-twisted like drawn gold and plays the paalai mode as its rule requires; and the guide turns to the addressee: old-mouthed suppliant, who has put weariness behind you though grief and longing for the generous in an unmoving world drive you along the road.
nuance: Line 38 இயங்கா வையத்து is hard: either a world that does not move to help, or a world in which the generous do not go about; both make the suppliant's search the cause of his grief. The address முதுவாய் இரவல, the suppliant of seasoned speech, is the same phrase the god's attendants use of the devotee in Thirumurugatruppadai line 284.

reading: In the western land, a wide-mouthed buffalo that has grazed the broad-petalled blue lilies, making the fat fish scatter, lies chewing on a bed of wild jasmine in the shade of jackfruit trees climbed by green pepper vines, with soft turmeric leaves stroking its hairy back and the scent of young toddy about it; yet even Vanji, with flood-water at its gate, the city of Kuttuvan of the well-made chariot, the descendant of the western guardians whose bar-like shoulders carved the curved bow on the northern Himalaya, is set down as empty.
nuance: வறிதே can mean that Vanji is small beside the patron the poem will name, or that it was barren for suppliants like these; the three cities are dismissed in the same words (lines 50, 67, 83) before the poem says what they are measured against, so the comparison is held back for more than seventy lines. The Chera's mark on the Himalaya is the boast that the Chera bow was carved there.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 27-42 and 43-58: lines 41 to 50 are the Chera land and its city, closed by வஞ்சியும் வறிதே in line 50.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a crowned king's land used as a foil inside the guide poem

comparisons.tenor: the patron's giving, to which the poem builds

reading: Young female monkeys, decked like children with carved chest-pieces of old honey-dripping nunavu wood and made flower chaplets set at the ear, come with the strong-oxen carts of the salt merchants and play rattle, with pearls from the sea like teeth taken from the bellies of sharp-edged shells, together with the ornamented sons born to the salt women whose loose five-part hair hides their shoulders: such is the wave-bounded Korkai of the Pandya Seliyan, descendant of the southern guardians, of the swift chariot, eye-filling chaplet and garlanded white umbrella that took the enemies' land; yet even Madurai, of his unbearable lineage in which Tamil found its standing, its streets soaked in revelry, is set down as empty.
nuance: Monkeys playing with pearls beside the salt carts makes the pearl a toy: the wealth of Korkai is shown by how carelessly it is handled. தமிழ்நிலை பெற்ற in line 66 ties the standing of Tamil to the Pandya lineage and its city, though the poem says it only in passing, as an epithet.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 43-58 and 59-79: lines 51 to 67 are the Pandya land and its city, closed by மதுரையும் வறிதே in line 67.

reading: On the bank of a fragrant pond beside a ford lovely as a painting, where kadamba garlands rise from the thick water, the divine lotus opens its face, its rich bud like a young breast, its pollen-covered outer petals red as the cochineal insect, and its golden seed-head wrapped in red petals like a flawless palm dipped in lac, while a bee, ruffling its wings and clasping its sweet mate, sings the kaamaram tune: such is the cool field country of the Chola Sembiyan, descendant of the eastern guardians, of the good chariot and fame that need not be sought, whose bangled hand destroyed the hanging fort whose high gates the thunder scrapes; yet even Uranthai, of his unretreating resolve, is set down as empty.
nuance: Each of the three cities is entered through one small scene of its land (the buffalo of the west, the monkeys of the south, the lotus and bee of the east) and each king through his ancestors and one deed; the pattern makes the three crowned dynasties a single formula that the patron, a minor chief, is then said to exceed.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 59-79 and 80-98: lines 68 to 83 are the Chola land and its city, closed by உறந்தையும் வறிதே in line 83.

reading: The seven givers of old are named by their gifts: Pekan, chief of the Aviyar of the hill land guarded by a fearsome goddess, who gave a cloak to the forest peacock; Pari of Parambu, where white falls drop, who gave his great chariot to the small-flowered mullai on the long road; Kaari of the flashing spear, who gave suppliants horses with ringing bells and white manes and kind words that amazed the world; Aay, of loving speech and bow-bearing shoulders, who gave the god under the banyan the cloth the shining blue serpent had given him; Athikan of the roaring army, who gave Avvai the sweet nectar-yielding nelli fruit of the fragrant slope; Nalli of the dense hill, who gave his friends without stint the means to live; and Ori of the horse Ori, who fought Kaari of the horse Kaari and gave the performers a good land of hillocks: these seven together wore the red yoke of giving.
nuance: Several of the gifts are useless to the receiver (a cloak to a peacock, a chariot to a creeper, a god's cloth to a god): the list praises giving that does not weigh the receiver's need. Two of the seven, Kaari and Ori, are named as having fought each other (line 110), yet they share one yoke; the rivalry of chiefs is set aside in the canon of givers. The next unit says the patron bore alone the yoke the seven bore together.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 80-98, 99-112 and 113-128: the list of the seven runs from line 84 to ஈகைச் செந்நுகம் in line 113, the noun that sums it up; the cuts at 98 and 112 fall inside it.

reading: He who alone, with strong legs and strength, bore that yoke so that the sea-fenced wide world shone is the great chief of the Oviyar, best among the kings of good Mavilangai (named after ancient Ilangai, where the dashing river brings fragrant naagam, agil and sandal that serve the bathing women as floats), with a true sword without blemish, the strength of a pouncing tiger, anklets on feet scarred by the elephant, and a hand that pours like rain and scatters herds of she-elephants as gifts: Nalliyakkodan, the famed patron of the many-instrumented performers; desiring him, we sang him, his father of unbearable lineage and the wealth of his sky-touching hill, and went to him the other day.
nuance: Here the comparison held back since line 50 is completed: the yoke seven wore together, this one bore alone (ஒருதான் தாங்கிய), and the three crowned cities were 'empty' beside it. The town is said to carry the name of ancient Ilangai, a claim about the name and not about the place.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 113-128 and 129-148: line 113 ends the list of the seven, and the sentence about the patron runs to சென்றனமாக in line 129; the rest of line 129 (இந்நாள்) begins the next unit's scene.

reading: In our dreary kitchen a new-whelped bitch, unable to bear her blind, droop-eared puppies tugging at her milkless teats, barked; under old walls with rotting rafters eaten by swarms of termites a hollow-stemmed mushroom grew in the dust; and the kinai-drummer's wife, her waist shrunk by settled hunger, nipped with her nails rubbish-heap velai greens, boiled them without salt and, ashamed before the gaze of the ignorant, shut the door to eat them with all her large family; so that this ruinous hunger might end, we got small-eyed elephants with streaming temples and bells at their sides and great chariots, and are coming from there; you too, with the large family that waits here in hope, if you go with a lifted heart . . .
nuance: The poverty is shown by what is missing in the kitchen (milk, salt, fire) and by the shame that makes the woman shut the door: hunger is also a public disgrace. The gift (elephants and chariots) is out of all proportion to the need for food, which is the point of the comparison with the seven givers.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 129-148 and 149-164: the poverty scene and the gift run from line 130 to the conditional செல்குவிராயின் in line 145, which opens the road to the patron's country (lines 146 onward).

reading: On the long neythal road worthy of song, where the screwpine on the waves blooms white as swans, the first-day serunthi mimics gold, the full-swollen mundagam sheds bright gems, the tall punnai sets out pearls and the sea roams over the white sand of the shore grove, if you go to the port town of cool pools, named for its wall, the fishermen will light a red fire with black smoke from fragrant driftwood the waves brought in, lying like tall camels asleep, and pour you old clear toddy strained by a fisher-girl with a faultless face that makes the moon pine and spear-tip eyes; singing the noble lord of Kidangil with his bud-opened garland, and dancing to the beat with your women of sand-dark hair, you will get roast dried fish at every halt.
nuance: The town is named only by a riddle (named with the word for wall, மதிலொடு பெயரிய), which the reader is expected to solve as Eyil-pattinam. The camel, a beast of no Tamil landscape, is used as the image for logs on the beach. The patron is first named here as lord of Kidangil, the town the three roads lead to.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 129-148 and 149-164: the neythal road and its welcome run from line 146 to பெறுகுவிர் in line 163, the first of the poem's three 'you will get' promises.

comparisons.tenor: the driftwood logs on the shore

reading: In the mullai woodland full of mullai, where the green-budded avarai strings corals, the dark-budded kaayaa opens like a flock of peacocks, the rich musundai creeper spreads, the clustered kaanthal blooms like fingers and cochineal insects crawl on the long field road, if, watching for the hour when the hill, bathed by falls from its clefts, has lost the sun's heat, you reach victorious Velur with its well that flowered at a spear's tip, you will get, in huts bright and shrivelled by the fierce sun, hot rice soured with sweet tamarind cooked by the hunter women, with roast wild cow, shared with your company of few bangles and mango-coloured skin.
nuance: Line 172, the well that 'flowered at the tip of a mighty spear', points to a story of a well opened with a spear, which the poem does not tell. The flowers listed (kaayaa, kaanthal, the cochineal after rain) are signs of the rains, so the road has passed from the summer of the opening to the wet season without saying so.

reading: In the cool marutham fields full of marutham, where a blue kingfisher with a golden beak, having sat long on a bough of the short-stemmed kaanji whose fresh branch looks like a strung garland, watching the deep pool, snatches a stinking kayal fish, its sharp claws scarring the green lotus leaf, and a dark red-eyed male bee taking pollen on the opening lotus looks like the serpent seizing the moon, if you reach his Amur, the great guarded town of the brahmins with its lovely cool moat, the ploughmen's sister, her braid hanging on her small back like a she-elephant's trunk, will stop you as kin and give you heaps of white rice, well pounded by a black pestle with a worn iron mouth, with a mixture of forked-legged crab.
nuance: The three roads go through neythal, mullai and marutham in turn, each called 'full of' its own name (நெய்தல் 151, முல்லை சான்ற 169, மருதஞ் சான்ற 186), and each ends in a meal of its land; the patron's hill (kurinji) is reached last, at line 267, so his country holds all the lands. Which creature is the red-eyed male of line 184 is not certain; a bee fits the image of a dark thing on a bright flower.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 165-180 and 181-202: the marutham road and its welcome run from line 178 to பெறுகுவிர் in line 195; line 196 begins a new sentence about the patron's own town.

comparisons.tenor: the dark bee on the bright lotus

reading: His festive old town, whose streets have their dust laid by the streams from his great war elephants, their broad feet with huge nails reddened by trampling corpses like the look of a ghoul-woman laughing after eating fat, with a tongue like overturned fire, gleaming teeth, ears like black kids' and forked feet, is not far: it is quite near.
nuance: The ghoul feeding on the battlefield, a figure of the war poems, is used here to measure the redness of an elephant's feet in a town at festival: the patron's violence abroad is the guarantee of the peace in which suppliants are fed. The streams that lay the dust (அருவி) may be the elephants' ichor or water they spray; the line does not decide.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 181-202: lines 196 to 202 are one sentence, the patron's own town, which ends with நணியதுவே in line 202.

reading: Approaching the hard threshold of his gate, which is never shut to war-bards, poets or brahmins with the rare Veda on their tongues, open like the eye of a god's great hill, you will find him seated among his smiling company like the full moon among many stars: the wise praise him for knowing a favour done, keeping no low company, a glad face and a sweet manner; warriors of sword-sharp speech praise him for shielding those in fear, freedom from fierce anger, entering the enemy's array and holding a breaking army; women with lovely kohled eyes praise him for finishing what he purposes, being loved, not leaning to one side and understanding what has passed; and suppliants who live by gifts praise him for seeming simple in his knowledge while knowing well, knowing each one's due and giving without limit.
nuance: The virtues come in four sets of four, each set closed by the people who praise it (அறிந்தோர் ஏத்த, வயவர் ஏத்த, அரிவையர் ஏத்த, பரிசிலர் ஏத்த): the poem divides one man's character among the audiences who know it best. The suppliants praise last and praise two things about judgement (knowing each one's due) before the limitless giving that concerns them most. அறிவுமடம் படுதல் in line 216, knowledge that consents to seem simple, is a rare phrase.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 203-217 and 218-233: the approach and the four praises run from line 203 to இருந்தோற் குறுகி in line 220, where the hearer reaches the patron; the cut at 217 falls in the middle of the fourth praise.

comparisons.tenor: the gate that is never shut

reading: Holding your lute, whose stem with its bands is tight like a green-eyed langur gripping a snake, its mouth set with beauty like a row of gems, its bowl smoothly joined and covered with famed leather the colour of the forest kumizh fruit, its strings tight-twisted and oozing nectar, tune it by the rule of the treatise, voice answering voice, with the learning of one who has mastered the modes, and sing without tiring: 'you have a hand folded before elders, a chest open to the young, a sceptre that shades the ploughmen and a spear that burns the chariot warriors.'
nuance: The four praises are two pairs of opposites (folded and open; shade and fire), each pair setting a gentle gesture toward one's own people against a fierce one toward others; the poem gives the bard the words of his praise, so the guide also teaches what to say.

reading: Before you have said those few words, he will dress you in flawless cloth like the peeled skin of bamboo, give you toddy fierce as an angry snake, stand and feed you himself with endless care, from shining gold vessels set round like planets about the young sun and mocking it, the many foods of the subtle treatise written by the snow-hill-chested elder brother of the famed one with the flowered girdle whose forked arrows fed fire to the grove; and after ending the distress of connoisseurs and bards with the treasure his warriors brought from driving out enemies and razing kings' forts, he will give you a chariot whose wheel, its hub scarred by the sharp chisel and its spokes ringed by an iron rim, is like the full moon with its halo spreading milk-white rays in the seasonal sky, its covering of poured lac like the crowded buds of the tall murukku opening, finished by the iron-smiths' craft, with famed drivers of fine gait, draught beasts strong enough to outrun horses, and a charioteer.
nuance: The gift comes before the request (நீ சில மொழியா அளவை): the patron does not wait to be asked, which is the virtue the suppliants praised (வரையாது கொடுத்தல்). The cook-book author of lines 238 to 241 is described, not named, as the elder brother of a famed archer whose arrows fed fire to a grove; read as Bhima and Arjuna, it is a Mahabharata allusion inside a Tamil guide poem, and the food is said to follow that treatise to the letter.

reading: He sends you off that very day with his gift: go, if you desire Nalliyakkodan, lord of the kurinji with a chaplet of plucked shoots and a nature in which far-going fame has settled, whose peaks of swaying bamboo, where clear clouds creep and blue peacocks spread their trains in the mist like the soft lovely hair that women with swaying gait and fine-clothed hips spread to take agil smoke, rise to a summit hard to climb where the thunder strikes and passes.
nuance: The poem ends where it began: in lines 13 to 16 the women's hair outdid the peacock's train, and here the peacocks spread their trains like the women's hair, so the comparison is turned round at the patron's hill. The last line closes the conditional opened at line 145 (செல்குவிராயின் . . . செலினே): the whole road and every gift hang on the hearer's going.

title: பெரும்பாணாற்றுப்படை (1/2)
theme: The first half of Perumpanatruppadai: a bard rewarded by Thondaiman Ilanthiraiyan tells a hungry bard of the patron's lineage, just rule and safe roads, and then describes the way to him land by land (salt caravans and armed traders, the hunters of the dry tract, cattle-raiding warriors, herders, dry-land farmers, the wet paddy country with its rich town, sugar presses and fishers' huts), promising at each settlement the meal its people will give.
structure_note: The units are moved to sentence breaks. After the address (1-22) and the praise of the patron (23-45), each stage of the road is one long sentence that ends by naming the food the bard will receive (பெறுகுவிர் 105, 133, 168, 256; பெறுவிர் 196; மிசைமின் 262), and the passage from one land to the next is marked by பின்றை (147, 206). The chapter ends at line 270 in the middle of the sentence about the fishers' huts.
source_issues: The text as printed by show carries the repairs flagged at lines 4, 17, 27, 71, 102, 112, 120, 123, 153, 176, 188 (the vowel sign ொ lost or misread), 214 (கட்கனழ் for கட்கமழ்), 251 (செவிவிஅம் for செவிலியம்) and 260 (துங்சாக் for துஞ்சாக்); all were read as repaired, and karu forms are copied from the repaired lines.

The core unit break at 91/92 falls inside a word (விழுக்கோ / லுளிவாய்), and several other core breaks fall mid-sentence (34/35, 50/51, 66/67, 119/120, 135/136, 151/152, 167/168); units were moved accordingly.
Lines 141 (நாள்ஆ), 148 (குளகுஅரை) and 243 (பகட்டுஆ) print a vowel-initial word without sandhi, unlike the rest of the text, which joins words in sandhi; this may be editorial spacing.
Line 61 (முடலை யாக்கை முழுவலி மாக்கள்) is repeated as line 32 of Nedunalvadai; it reads as a shared formula, not an error.
The sentence of lines 263-270 continues into the next chapter (line 271 onwards).

reading: As the many-rayed sun rises, having drunk the darkness of the wide sky, in a summer whose fierce heat has stripped the pathiri of its leaves, the poet describes the bard's lute part by part (a belly like the inside of the pathiri flower, a cover fitted like molten wax, an empty mouth dark as a dried spring, a forked end like the new crescent, frets like a girl's small bangles, a neck like drawn sapphire, strings like drawn gold) and hails the lean bard with the meat-smelling mouth who, finding no supporter anywhere in the sea-bounded world, wanders with his noisy kin like birds searching for fruiting trees on a smoky hill the rain has abandoned.
nuance: Fourteen lines go to the lute and one to its owner (புல்லென் யாக்கை): the opening sets a finely made instrument against the poverty of the man who carries it. The bard finds no supporter in the whole world that sun and moon circle (lines 17, 18), so the patron's rarity is put on a cosmic scale before he is even named.

reading: The speaker says that, like a cloud pouring rain on a parched forest, the patron gave him and his large kin, long hungry, a wealth that spending does not exhaust, and that they come from there with white-maned horses and strong elephants; if the bard too goes to Thiraiyan of many spears, heir of the sea-coloured one whose chest bears the mark of Sri, scion of the mighty line the waves brought, who among the three drum-sounding kings is praised above them as the valampuri is above other conches, whose just sceptre has banished all that is not dharma, then let him hear how it is: may his sorrow end, for in that guarded wide land there are no cruel men who live by the plough of theft, robbing travellers on the road, thunder does not strike, snakes do not bite and wild beasts do no harm, so he may rest where he likes, stay where he wishes and go on, his heart glad.
nuance: The patron's protection reaches beyond men: thunder, snakes and beasts also do no harm in his land (lines 42, 43), which is the just sceptre of line 36 made into a law of nature. The speaker's credential is the gift itself (horses and elephants), and the old hunger of line 25 (பழம்பசி) is the starting point that the whole road will answer.

reading: On the long road from town to town go the salt merchants with their many oxen: their roofed carts have spokes set in a fat hub, wheels of whole timber like drums, axle-beams like joined bolts, a hood like a rain-laden hill, a hen-coop at the door like an elephant-watcher's hut, a small mortar hung up like a cow elephant's knee and ropes bound like the stretched drum on a dancers' stage; a woman with her child drives the oxen from behind while men with neem garlands and massive shoulders guard the long train of yoked carts, proclaiming the rate of their goods against grain.
nuance: The cart is a moving house, with a coop for the hen and a mortar for the grain, and the whole family travels: a mother with her child drives from behind while armed men walk beside. The phrase கொள்ளை சாற்றி (line 64), proclaiming the exchange rate, is the same formula an Akananuru poet uses for the salt carts.

reading: As a safeguard for those who pass by day, armed travellers who carry the rare goods of hills and seas (feet shod, coats on, chests healed of arrow wounds, bright white-hilted swords hanging at their sides like snakes climbing a hill, daggers thrust in their belts, heroes like the tall Vel who loves the kadamba, spear in hand, never turning back) go along with caravans of long-eared donkeys whose scarred backs bear sacks of pepper like the great fruit of the jackfruit tree, along the great toll road whose forks the bowmen's posts guard in the wide forest.
nuance: The safety promised in lines 39 to 43 is shown here as an institution, not a miracle: armed traders guard their own goods and bowmen's posts hold the road's junctions where the toll (உல்கு) is taken. Who is the subject of lines 67 and 68 (the traders who bring the goods of hill and sea, or the escort who makes it possible) is not fixed by the syntax, and the reading takes the first.

reading: In the huts of the bowmen's forest, thatched with date-palm leaves whose spined fronds are like spear-heads and whose backs ripple like river sand, where the striped squirrel and the rat do not play, the mother lies curled with her newborn on a deerskin bed while the white-toothed hunting women go out with iron-tipped digging sticks, heave the hard ground until they are covered with dust, gather the fine grass seed, pound it in the ground-mortar in the shade of the vila tree where the decoy is tied, draw brackish water from a deep well and cook it with dried meat in an old broken-rimmed pot on a broken hearth; if the bard says he belongs to the lord of the red hills, chief of warriors with unfading thumbai, he and his kin will get that food heaped on teak leaves like a god's offering.
nuance: This is the poorest meal of the road, grass seed dug from hard ground and boiled with dried meat in a broken pot, yet it is served like a god's offering, and the hosts give it because the bard names his patron: Thiraiyan's name works as a passport across his land. The sense of சென்னியம் (line 103) as a claim to belong to the lord's following is the reading taken here; the word is rare.

reading: Along paths confused with deer tracks, the fierce-eyed hunters hide in pits dug round dried water-holes at the time the sky withholds rain, waiting by night for the boar whose curved tusks are like the vaakai flower, and when that hunt fails, by day they beat the green bushes with wide-mouthed dogs, string chain-nets on a fence and ring in the long-eared hare whose ears are like the coarse petals of the thorny lotus, and eat together on the slope; in the hard wasteland the curved-bow eyinar keep fortified homes, spears blunted from striking foes and laid with shields, bows leaning, arrows asleep under a roof of ooga grass, quivers like honeycomb and the tudi drum hung on the pandal posts, chained dogs, thorn fences, a guarded wood and gates set with sharp stakes; there the bard will receive in every house red rice of upland paddy like the seeds of the eenthu palm, with fried iguana the dogs have caught.
nuance: The hunters' settlement is a small fort (thorn fence, guarded gate, stakes, chained dogs) because it holds the frontier of the dry tract; the men whose spear-tips are blunt from killing foes are the bard's hosts, which is the guide poem's point: under this patron the violence of the frontier faces outward. The hill hunt for boar and hare is set in the waste (அருஞ்சுரம்), so the land is mixed.

reading: Born of a sword-wielding clan whose food is taken by force and whose life of valour even a pregnant woman will not give up though an elephant charges, a snake crawls over her or thunder roars in the blue sky, the thin-bearded youth like a tiger cub goes with kin whose bows are like wild dogs into the guarded land of hostile kings, drives cattle home by daylight, trades them for toddy, drinks the thick home-brewed liquor, slaughters a rutting bull in the rich common ground and, as the drum sounds in their midst, raises his bow-trained arm and dances in a ring: such is the never-sleeping settlement that revels by day.
nuance: The raid, the sale of the stolen cattle for toddy and the day-long drinking are told as marks of a valour that even the pregnant women keep, and the poem passes no judgement: the warrior settlement is one stage of the bard's road. Its epithet துஞ்சா/தூங்கா இருக்கை recurs for each settlement (146, 242 தளரா, 253 துளங்கா), a refrain of the patron's land. The matter of the unit is vetchi, the colophon's thinai is that of the whole idyll.

reading: Beyond that hostile ground lie the herders' huts with short legs bound with fodder leaves, brushwood doorways and doors of close-set sticks, where lambs are tied to short stakes with long ropes and the curved-faced ram and the white goat sleep inside a dung-heaped thorn fence; at dawn, when the birds rise from the thick dark, the herd girl, dark and fine, small earrings swaying, hair gathered in short curls, churns the sweet set curd whose top is closed like the white bud of a mushroom with a churning rod that growls like a tiger, lifts out the butter, carries the pot on a flower-pad on her head and sells the day's buttermilk, feeds her kin with food bought by buttermilk and will not take gold nuggets for her ghee but takes good buffalo and black heifers; at those herders' homes the bard will get green millet rice, like the small young of the crab, with milk.
nuance: The herd girl's trade is exact: buttermilk buys food for her kin, but ghee she exchanges only for livestock, never for gold, so the household turns its best product back into the herd. The idyll records a barter economy in which cattle, not metal, are wealth.

reading: The herdsman, his feet scarred by his sandals, his hand hard from leaning on his staff, his shoulder worn bare by the sling of pots, wearing a garland of many forest flowers from trees and creepers and living on gruel, camps in the forest with his calf-loving herd, twirls a fire-drill till the smoke smells sweet, burns the holes of his black flute, and when he tires of the sweet paalai tune on it plays the kurinji mode on a bow-lute strung with twisted marul fibre on a hollow kumizh stick, so that the many-legged bees listen, taking it for the hum of their kin.
nuance: The herdsman makes his own instruments (he burns the flute's holes with a fire-drill and strings a bow-lute with fibre) and plays the paalai and kurinji modes far from those lands: the bard on his way to a patron is shown his own art in its plainest form. Paalai and kurinji here name melodies, not landscapes.

reading: Past that grassy wide land, in the farmers' small village fenced by tall thorn forest, with cattle pens, granaries like a herd of cow elephants in the yards, pandals on posts like the legs of tuskers, small cart wheels and ploughs leaning against them, smoke-filled sheds with weathered long walls and thatch of karuvai grass like the spread clouds of the rainy sky, the bard will get sweet rice of short-stalked varagu like the flowers of the long-spiked poolai, mixed with white-boiled avarai beans like a spotted cluster of vengai blossom.
nuance: The dry-land farmers' wealth is measured with elephants (granaries like a herd of cows, posts like tuskers' legs), and the food is not paddy but millet and beans: plenty in this land is the plenty of rain-fed fields.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 184-205: lines 184 to 196 describe the dry-land village and close with மூரற் பெறுவிர் in line 196; ஞாங்கர், at the end of line 196, opens the ploughing scene.

comparisons.tenor: the karuvai thatch of the houses

reading: Nearby, ploughmen of the red furrow, whose grain fills their households, yoke their great trained oxen at the gate and drive the curved plough, its mouth like a cow elephant's, deep into the earth, ploughing the field again and again till it crumbles, and when the reapers enter at harvest the short-legged, dark-throated quail flees and settles in the brush, holding close its growing chick that looks like a fragrant kadamba flower.
nuance: The quail that flees the reapers with its chick is the only creature of the chapter shown protecting its young; in a love poem it might carry a sense of its own, but here, in praise, it is part of the harvest scene.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 184-205: the ploughing scene begins with ஞாங்கர் at the end of line 196 and runs to line 205, which describes the dry land the bard then leaves (வன்புலம் இறந்த பின்றை, line 206).

thinai_evidence.note: the ploughmen of the patron's dry land

reading: After the dry land come the wide wet fields: there a black bull, its horns muddied from goring the green sedge, has fought and broken the mud-holes of the crab whose forked legs are like a smith's broken tongs, workers have levelled the soft mud and pressed in seedlings from the bundles, and the dark-handed workers, skin taut like hammered iron, chests smeared with sedge pollen as gold is rubbed on a touchstone, tire of the neythal flowers the weeders bring, pluck the mulli's curved-stalked flowers, chew sedge into fibre to tie garlands for their wet heads, while their dear children, bored with lumps of old rice, pound flattened rice outside the new-thatched huts on the ridges so loudly that the curved-beaked parrot fears it as an enemy, in fields of bending ears whose fresh yield never ends.
nuance: The field labourers, dark-skinned like hammered iron, are given a toilet scene of their own (flowers chosen and rejected, garlands woven from sedge fibre, pollen on the chest), the kind of scene the court poems give to nobles; and their children are bored with old rice, the poem's quick sign of a land that has more than enough.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 206-229: line 228 (வாங்குகதிர்க் கழனி) closes the description of the fields; the simile of line 229 (கடுப்புடைப் பறவைச் சாதி அன்ன) belongs to the paddy of line 230.
