comparisons.tenor: the workers' chests smeared with pollen

reading: The workers cut the round hollow stalks of the great red paddy, ripe like a swarm of stinging insects, heap them on the wide threshing floor that receives offerings in the shade of the tall-branched marutham where snakes live, the stacks wrapped in white spider-web like the spirits of the thunangai dance dressed in cloth, dancing hand in hand with their troop; then they pull down the stacks, drive oxen over them, sift out dust and straw, winnow in the west wind, and the heap of grain shines like the red-gold mountain of the north.
nuance: The threshing floor receives offerings (பலிபெறு) and the stacks are seen as dancing spirits; the harvest is a sacred scene before it is a store of wealth, and the heap is measured against the golden mountain of the north.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 206-229 and 230-245: the unit begins at line 229 with the simile for the paddy of line 230 and ends at line 241, where the winnowed heap shines like the golden mountain; line 242 begins the settlement that the harvest belongs to.

thinai_evidence.note: the harvest of the patron's wet land

comparisons.tenor: the stacks of sheaves wrapped in spider-web

reading: In the unfailing settlement set among cool fields, in good houses where the crooked-gaited calf of the buffalo cow is tied to a stake with a forked rope, whose tall granaries, beyond the reach of a ladder, have grown old unopened and are cut at the top to pour out old grain, where the boys, tired of toddling after pulling the toy chariot the carpenter's lads made for them, cling to their full-breasted nurses, drink milk and sleep in their beds, in the great rich town that has never known hunger, whose workers do not idle when others idle, the bard will get white rice that the workers bring with fried domestic fowl.
nuance: The granaries have 'grown old as maidens' (குமரி மூத்த), never needing to be opened, and the town has never known hunger from of old (தொல்பசி அறியா, line 253): the phrase answers the bard's old hunger (பழம்பசி) of line 25, so the road ends its first stage where his want began.

reading: At every smoky shed where sugar is boiled, where the cane press roars with a never-sleeping din like a great herd of elephants stampeding together when a dread yali attacks on the bamboo slopes where the clouds play, the bard may drink the sweet juice of the cane as much as he likes.
nuance: The terror of the hill (a herd of elephants fleeing the yali) is borrowed to measure the noise of the press, so a kurinji scene of danger becomes the sound of the wet land's plenty; the bard is not promised this but told to help himself (மிசைமின்).

reading: In the courtyards of low-eaved huts built of rows of reed bound with white stems and screwpine and thatched with darbha grass, with fishing baskets lying about, under pandals of spread sand made from cut branches of the curved punnai where green fruit hangs, young and old crowd together with their kin, and the red-striped kayal and the green prawns leap like arrows with flesh-smelling tips and like bows.

title: பெரும்பாணாற்றுப்படை (2/2)
theme: The second half of Perumpanatruppadai finishes the road to Kanchi, through the fisherfolk's settlement, the Brahmin village, the port of Neerpeyarru, the toddy-sellers' houses, the lighthouse, the grove farmers and the shrine of the god on the serpent bed, then praises Thondaiman Ilanthiraiyan's city, victory and court, scripts the bard's praise, and lists the gifts the king gives the same day before closing on his peaceful hill.
structure_note: Thirteen units against the core's fourteen; every boundary was moved to a sentence end, mostly the guide's verbs of promise and command (பெறுகுவிர், கழிமின், ஆர்குவிர், குறுகி). The first unit opens mid-sentence: the sentence starts at line 263 in chapter 4.
source_issues: Line 481: our text reads அழல்தவிர் தாமரை; the tamilvu text reads அழலவிர் (bright as flame). Either is an epithet of the golden lotus; the reading is kept and the karu form is copied from our text.

The comitative -ஒடு lost its vowel sign after ய/ள in lines 293, 299, 320, 345, 434 and 492 (repaired in the core as flagged by show); karu forms such as குவளையொடு, கோழியொடு and புரவியொடு are copied as repaired.
Line 467 lost its first letter in the 2021 e-text (repaired from the 2000 version as யந்நிலை).
Line 308 prints யளை இப் with a space inside அளைஇ; it reads as one word.
Line 388 (பெறற்கருந் தொல்சீர்த் துறக்க மேய்க்கும்) is the same line as Pattinappalai line 104; it is a shared formula, not a copying error.
Line 271 begins in the middle of a sentence that starts at line 263 in chapter 4; the unit could not be moved across the chapter boundary.

reading: At the settlement of the net-fishers who guard the banks of a deep tank that never dwindles even in a long summer, moving with their children through its dark pool, the guide promises the bards a toddy made from unpounded rice mash cooled in wide-mouthed baskets, mixed with malt whose flowered crust looks like the grubs in a snake's anthill, left two turns of day and night, matured in strong-mouthed jars, strained hot and squeezed by hand, served with roasted fish, until they stagger.
nuance: The brew is given step by step (mash, cool, mix in malt, ferment, mature in jars, strain, squeeze), so the guide's knowledge of how the poorest folk of the road make their drink is itself part of the promise that the road will feed the bard. இருமறை கழிப்பி (279) I take as two turns of day and night; it could also mean two coverings of the jar.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 271-286: ends at line 282, where பெறுகுவிர் closes the promise of toddy and fish. The sentence itself begins at line 263 in chapter 4 (the fishers' huts), a chapter boundary that cannot be moved, so the unit opens mid-sentence.

comparisons.tenor: the flowered crust of the malt

reading: A fisher-bard skilled at catching ties his line to a long bamboo rod with a green hide bag of raw-meat bait, and the split-mouthed vaalai that has seized the bait on the bent iron hook shies from the trembling shadow of the cane by the water; in the old deep pond thick with red-petalled kuvalai and blue lilies, where the god's bright flower that has bloomed like fire is left unplucked and the whole is like the wide sky at its fullness after the rain, the guide tells the bards to wear the many opened flowers the pluckers have thrown down, on the great festival day, and pass on.
nuance: The lotus is called the god's bright flower (கடவுள் ஒண்பூ) and is not taken (அடைதல் ஓம்பி), while the bards are told to wear the flowers that others have dropped: even flowers on the road follow a rule of what may be taken. Lines 291 and 292 compare something to the wide sky 'without lack' after the rain has stopped; I read the pond at its fullest, but the tenor is not fixed by the words, and the angler's and the fish's parts in 283 to 288 may belong to one image of the pond rather than to an act of fishing.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 271-286 and 287-300: begins with பச்சூன் (283), after பெறுகுவிர் ends the previous sentence at line 282, and ends at கழிமின் (296), the command to wear flowers and pass on.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide's direction along the road, the matter of the guide poem under paadaan

reading: In the good houses of those who keep the vows, with a low pandal where the fat calf is tied and floors smeared with fresh dung, which the house fowl and the dog do not approach, where the hook-beaked parrot is taught the secret recitation, if the bards stay in the village of the guardians of the Veda, the bangled wife of fragrant brow, chaste like the small star that shines in the north, will knowingly cook for them the rice named after a bird and serve it with the fragrant buttermilk and butter of the red cow, slices of young pomegranate fried with pepper and mixed with fragrant leaves, and pieces of tender mango from the tall tree in fine pickle.
nuance: The street is marked by what keeps away as much as by what is there: the fowl and the dog do not come near, and even the parrot repeats the recitation (மறைவிளி), so the Veda is heard from the birds. 'The rice named after a bird' (பறவைப் பெயர்ப்படு வத்தம்) is given only as a riddle; I take it as the swan-named rice. The cook is the wife herself, praised for chastity in the same breath as for knowing what to cook (வயினறிந்து அட்ட).

reading: When girls bathing with their playmates at the drinking ford let fall a golden earring, the jewel-coloured kingfisher hunting prey strikes it for a fish, cannot carry it to the lonely frond of the bird-filled palmyra and rests on the sacrificial pillar set up by Brahmins of learning who paid their hard debt of sacrifice, showing slowly like the dawn star above the Yavanas' swan lamp; past the bounds of Neerpeyarru, by the watered gardens crowded with ships that bring milk-white horses and northern wealth, in sandy streets of high mansions filled with traders and guarded by servants, in rich houses where the plough-ox and the milch cow do not come but rams and swans wander, girls with curved jewels, their fine cloth swaying like dew creeping along the soft kondrai branch, move like peacocks dancing on a great hill, gold anklets ringing, and after the striped ball play golden kazhangu on the pearl sand of their sky-touching terraces.
nuance: The port is marked by what does not belong to the farm: the plough-ox and the milch cow keep away from its houses while rams and swans walk there, and ships bring horses from the north. One sentence carries the earring from a bathing girl through a kingfisher and a palmyra to a Brahmin sacrificial post beside a Yavana lamp, so the poem's single image joins the port's peoples: women at play, priests at sacrifice, foreign craftsmen.

This unit runs from the bathing girls (311) to line 335, where the description of the port's houses and the girls' game ends in the participle ஆடும், which qualifies பட்டினம் in line 336; the next unit begins there.

reading: Near the port, at the toddy-sellers' houses whose green flags sway over doorways many enter and whose swept courtyards are strewn with red flowers, the guide promises the bards strong toddy with chunks of fat from the short-legged boar that, once a dark piglet wallowing in the mud made by the little water the brewing women spilled washing their bowls, was kept many days in a pit, fed on rice flour and not let go to its hairy sow.
nuance: The boar's whole life is told in three lines, from piglet in the brewers' runoff to a pit where it is fed rice flour and kept from its sow (பாயம் போகாது), so the guests' meat is shown as raised for them. கள்ளடு (339) is a genuine அடு, to brew, not the comitative.

reading: Passing the harbour where at night a bright torch hung on an unroofed tower, rising to fight the sky like a pillar propping it, its hard top reached by ladders, calls the ships sailing the rough sea, the bards come to the lone houses of the grove farmers, roofed with withering fronds of coconut whose trunk is like the flank of a hill-like elephant, with yellow courtyards and fragrant gardens; there they will eat the big jackfruit of clustered segments from the low branch, the sweet water of tender coconut, the curved white fruit of ripe banana bunches like the cheek-tusks of a dark she-elephant, palmyra nungu and other sweet things, and when tired of these, the full tubers of the chembu.
nuance: The torch calls the ships (ஓடுகலம் கரையும்), with the verb used for a crow that calls guests, so the port too has a way of inviting strangers. The elephant is the measure twice, for the coconut trunk and for the curve of the banana: the farmers' grove is described in the terms of the hill.

comparisons.tenor: the unroofed tower that carries the torch

reading: Through the long way of many trees in never-failing rich villages where tall areca palms stand like streaks of daytime rain among coconuts whose three-sided nuts fall and break the pots cooking rice for hungry travellers, and past many lands of good towns whose sky-touching walls are clothed with unfading painted creepers, the bards come to where the one on the serpent bed lies like a bull elephant lying on a kaanthal slope; there, in groves no sunlight enters but the cuckoo does, where kuruku creepers wound on kaanji trees drop striped flowers like the round sweets that cake-makers shape with treacle and dip in milk onto the shaded sand at the water's edge, they may empty blue pots of toddy shaped like the areca's swelling spathe, sit in great joy, play by day with young women whose foreheads carry the shark-mouth ornament like the young crescent and whose eyes are drowsy with drink, rest at the great flowered ford of unfailing custom, like heaven itself, with those who wait for the hour, then praise the god of great strength, play a little on their black-horned instruments, and pass on.
nuance: The god's town is not named; the serpent bed and the bull elephant lying on the slope identify him, and the bards' worship is brief: praise him, play a little, go on. The groves' pleasures (toddy, play with women) and the shrine sit in one sentence, likened as a whole to heaven (துறக்கம் ஏய்க்கும், 388), a line the Pattinappalai repeats at its line 104. In line 378 போல் stands as போ before னிழல் by sandhi.

reading: Kanchi: groves where a big-bellied female monkey snatches the ghee-trodden rice ball of the long-trunked elephant while its keepers look away, posts where tuskers' rage is tamed, deep long streets cut by strong chariots, many families of great fame whose strength never knew defeat, gates never shut, crowded with those who give and take, gardens ringed with thorn, a city of tall brick mansions that rises beautiful like the pericarp of the many-petalled lotus that bore the four-faced one from the navel of the tall blue god; as the jackfruit is praised for its fruit among the rich-branched trees that bear without flowering where flocks of birds gather, so among the cities of this wide world, clothed in the smelling sea and crowned by the sky, this old town of ancient valour, worshipped by many, excels in festivals.
nuance: The lotus from Vishnu's navel is a picture of the city's plan: the walled town is the flower and its great houses rise in it like the pericarp (பொகுட்டு); the Paripadal fragment on Madurai uses the same lotus, with petals for streets and the pericarp for the palace. The jackfruit 'praised for its fruit' among trees that fruit without flowering (கோளி) gives the town a rank among cities rather than a picture.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 389-407 and 408-417: begins at காழோர் (393), after கழிமின் ends the previous sentence at line 392, and ends with மூதூர் at the turn of lines 411 and 412, which closes the description of Kanchi before the comparison with the Five begins.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's city, part of the praise of the patron (paadaan)

comparisons.tenor: the tall-housed town within its walls
the old town among the cities of the world

reading: Like the Five whose banner-crowned tall chariot crossed the great war that never ended, when all the hundred fell fighting on a field where the bodies of white-tusked elephants dragged blood like the dancing clouds of a red evening sky crowned with the waxing crescent, he roared at the place where the hostile foes who came against him with countless armies were destroyed: he is the lord of Kachchi, open-handed, a refuge to those who come in want; because his grace and his wrath are both ready, the lands of those who fought him become ruined commons and the lands of those who love him bloom with gold, and kings who want his friendship and kings without allies who want his help, bowing in many ways like waterfalls running to the sea, crowd with unfailing wealth, like people waiting at the hard-to-cross Ganges ford for the boat that cleaves its white waves, watching for their hour in the courtyard of his rich city.
nuance: Lines 422 to 424 state the king's double face in one balanced pair, அளியும் தெறலும் எளிய: the same readiness that makes him a refuge makes him dangerous, and the poem shows the result in land, ruined commons for foes and gold-blooming country for friends. The Five (ஐவர்) and the hundred (ஈரைம் பதின்மர்) are the Bharata war, used as a measure of victory.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 408-417, 418-433 and 434-451: begins at அவ்வாய் வளர்பிறை (412), after மூதூர் closes the description of the city, and ends at செழுநகர் முற்றத்து (435), where the kings who wait for his audience are placed; the core cut at 433 fell between the simile of the Ganges ford and its tenor in line 434.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's victory and liberality (paadaan)

comparisons.tenor: the blood-dragging bodies of the elephants
the king roaring at the field of his victory
the kings bowing to him in many ways
the kings waiting with their tribute for his hour

reading: In his great city where the red-legged cock-dove nesting in the eaves of the mansion starts from its sweet sleep, afraid of the hard ringing of the smithy where the dark-handed smith hammers the curved rings for the great-trunked elephants' tusks, he sits among his flawless kin like the sun spreading its disc over the middle of the eastern sea, granting to those who seek justice and to those who seek their needs whatever they ask, with a clear sight that discerns between them and a heart that never closes in the debt of giving: approach him.
nuance: முறைவேண்டுநர் and குறைவேண்டுநர் (443) are those who come for a judgment and those who come for a need; the king answers both, and the clear sight that discerns between them (இடைத்தெரிந்து உணரும் இருள்தீர் காட்சி) is what makes the giving just. The frightened dove in the eaves lets the smithy's war-work be heard inside the king's house.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 434-451: begins at பெருங்கை யானை (436), after செழுநகர் முற்றத்து (435) ends the sentence of the waiting kings, and ends at குறுகி (447), where the bards are told to approach him; the tiger simile that follows opens the bard's address.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's justice and giving (paadaan)

comparisons.tenor: the king granting to all who ask

reading: Like the striped tiger cub that longs to seize the spotted-faced elephant its mother has struck, you pay the debt owed to poets and break your enemies' guarded walls to take their crowns; your strong sword-hand will not agree to any work but victory; descendant of the Tondaiyar who live on plunder, warrior of warriors, hero of heroes, lord of the wealthy, foremost in battle: as spirits snap their fingers before the goddess of the thunangai dance, the big-bellied mother of the red one with green jewels who killed fierce Sur in the white-waved sea, so praising your great name of unceasing giving I have come, lord; may you live long: so the guide tells the bard to say.
nuance: The guide gives the bard the very words of his praise (மள்ளர் மள்ள, மறவர் மறவ, செல்வர் செல்வ) and the formula of arrival (வந்தேன் பெரும வாழிய நெடிது). கொண்டி உண்டித் தொண்டையோர் (454) says the Tondaiyar live on plunder, so what the king gives the bard is drawn from what he takes in war. Lines 457 to 459 are hard: I read அணங்கு நொடித்தாங்கு as spirits snapping their fingers before Murugan's mother, the goddess of the thunangai, but who snaps and for whom is not fixed by the words, and the tiger simile may belong to the line before.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 434-451 and 452-475: begins at பொறிவரி (448), the tiger simile that opens the bard's address, and ends at நெடிதென (461), where the scripted praise closes.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's valour and giving, scripted for the bard (paadaan)

comparisons.tenor: the king's eagerness to take his enemies' forts and crowns
the bard praising the king's name

reading: When you have played the roomy great yaazh in due order and praised him with joined hands as custom knows, before you have finished telling your state he weighs the condition of this unlasting world and, wishing his own state to shine without end in the cool land of the naaval tree, strips from your waist the rag like moss and dresses you and your great family together in cloth bright as vapour, and with a glad face, looking on you again and again as on his children, stands and feeds you himself without tiring, spreading white bowls like flowering stars with rich pieces of many meats cooked by a skilled cook whose strong hand is scarred by the curved knife, long boiled grains of choice rice of the great red paddy, and sweet dishes guarded like nectar.
nuance: The king acts before the bard has finished asking (நின்னிலை தெரியா அளவை), and the poem gives his reason as a reckoning: he weighs the unlasting world (நில்லா உலகத்து நிலைமை தூக்கி) and wants the state of undying fame. He feeds the bard himself, standing (தான் நின்று ஊட்டி), looking at him as at his own children (மகமுறை); the order of the gift (rags off, new cloth on, food) is the order of other gift poems.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 452-475 and 476-500: begins at இடனுடைப் பேரியாழ் (462), after the scripted praise ends at line 461, and ends at ஊட்டி (479), where the feeding closes and the gifts of ornament begin.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's giving to the bard, the gift the guide promises (paadaan)

comparisons.tenor: the white bowls spread for the meal

reading: He crowns your thick hair with a golden lotus like the moon in the misty sky, round which no bee hums, and has the viraliyar wear golden garlands that shine in their dark hair like lightning darting through the daytime rain of a season sky that has drunk from the rough sea; not content with giving a striped chariot yoked with four mated horses whose white manes look like the conches of the great sea, praised by the horse books, he adds the sky-going steeds and green trappings he took from the foes he routed in war, and sends you off that very day with his gift: he is the lord of the hill of shining falls, where kinnaras hum on haunted slopes, peacocks dance in the thickets, flowers shaken down by leaping stags lie in the glades, the female monkey sweeps the yards where the beasts sleep, and the sages who tend the red fire sacrifice with firewood that white-tusked elephants bring.
nuance: The poem ends naming the patron only as lord of the hill (மலைகிழவோனே), and the hill is described by its peace: beasts sleep in yards a monkey sweeps, and elephants carry firewood for the sages' fire, so the last picture of the war-king's land is of wild things serving a sacrifice. அன்றே விடுக்கும் (493) makes speed part of the gift. Line 481's அழல்தவிர் (our reading) against அழலவிர் (bright as flame) changes only the epithet of the golden lotus.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 476-500: begins at மங்குல் வானத்து (480), after the feeding ends at ஊட்டி in line 479; the poem ends at line 500.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's gifts and his hill, the close of the guide poem (paadaan)

comparisons.tenor: the gold garlands in the viraliyar's dark hair

title: முல்லைப்பாட்டு
theme: Mullaippattu is the waiting of mullai told in three places at one rainy night: a wife at home who will not be comforted by the old women's omen, a king in his war camp kept awake by what the battle cost, and the road on which his chariot returns through the flowering forest; the poem joins the two vigils only through sound, ending when his horses fill her ears.
structure_note: The text runs as a few long sentences, so the five core units were all moved to breaks of description: the omen and the wife's tears (1-23), the camp's layout (24-44), the guard of the king's tent (45-66), the king's sleepless thought (67-79), and the wife's vigil with the return (80-103). The colophon gives only the thinai; the camp units are puram matter (vanji) inside an akam frame.
source_issues: Line 92 prints வயிறும் (belly) beside வளை (conch); in a list of instruments sounding as the army returns it reads only as வயிரும், the horn trumpet, so ற looks like a misprint for ர. The line-final வயிர, before செறியிலைக் காயா in line 93, is unclear in our text.

Lines 71 and 78 both carry கண்ணி நல்வலந் திருத்தி (தேம்பாய் கண்ணி, நகைதாழ் கண்ணி). Both are printed as part of the text and show does not flag a repeat; whether line 71 describes the fallen warriors and line 78 the king, as read here, is not settled by the text alone.
Line 97 prints கான நந் திய, splitting the word நந்திய across a space; line 84 prints மேவுறு for -ம் ஏவுறு across a word boundary (உயிர்த்தும் ஏவுறு). Karu forms and words are copied as printed.
The colophon gives the thinai (முல்லை) but no thurai, so there is no speech situation to copy; the speech of the old women in lines 17 to 21 is recorded from the poem, with occasion words left null.

reading: As a cloud that has drunk the roaring cold sea rises to the right like Mal standing tall as the water was poured, with conch and discus in his hand, and rains heavily in the small, sad evening, old women go out to the edge of the guarded old town, scatter paddy and fresh mullai buds, join their hands and stand listening for a chance word; they hear a herd-girl, her hands on her shivering shoulders, tell a calf tied with a short rope and looking about in distress that its mothers will come soon, driven by the cowherds, and they tell the wife that the good word means her lord will surely return with tribute, his work done, so she should put away her grief; but however often they show her, she will not see it, and her flower-like eyes, overflowing, drop the pearls of loneliness.
nuance: The calf is a near miss for ullurai and iraicchi: tied, distressed and promised its mothers' return, it matches the wife at several points, but the old women state the match themselves (அதனால் ... வருதல் தலைவர் வாய்வது), so condition 2 fails and the calf stays scene; the herd-girl's words matter as overheard speech, the omen, not as an image. The poem's first sentence is itself a sign, since the cloud rises on the right (வலனேர்பு), so the sky's omen comes before the street's.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 1-16 and 17-38: the core break at line 16 falls inside the old women's speech (என்போள் / நன்னர் நன்மொழி). This unit runs to line 23, where the wife's weeping (புலம்புமுத் துறைப்ப) closes the scene at home before the war camp begins in line 24.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife waits for a husband away at war in the rainy evening and is told he will come: waiting, the uri of mullai

thurai_akam.speaker: pira
thurai_akam.note: the old women (பெருமுது பெண்டிர்) who sought the omen speak to the wife; the colophon has no thurai

comparisons.tenor: the dark rain cloud rising after drinking the sea
the hum of the swarming bees

reading: In the wide, long woodland that a forest river embraces, the soldiers clear the far-scented pidavam and green bushes, set up the hunters' huts, ring the camp with a fence of laid thorns, and spread it out like the sea; in its leaf-thatched streets, at the crossings, stands a small-eyed elephant with musth on its cheeks that will not eat the sweet fodder of sugarcane and paddy ears bound together, but wipes its brow and holds it on its tusks, while unlettered young men speak to it in the northern tongue with forked goads and press the balls of food on it; bows that never run from battle, with quivers hung on them like the triple staff of a vowed brahmin in ochre cloth, are planted, posts driven and ropes drawn, spears set up and shields ranged, bows made into a wall, and in the middle of the many armies a separate tall-poled tent of cloth is raised for the king.
nuance: The elephant's keepers are கல்லா இளைஞர், young men without learning, who drive it in வடமொழி: the northern speech is the language of elephant handling, not of learning. The fodder the elephant refuses, sugarcane and paddy from the fields, comes from the watered country, so marutham things sit in the forest camp.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 17-38 and 39-54: the core break at line 38 falls inside the simile of the brahmin's triple staff (கடுப்ப நற்போ / ரோடா வல்விற் றூணி). This unit takes the laying out of the camp from line 24 to line 44, where the king's separate tent (வேறோர் நெடுங்காழ்க் கண்டங் கோலி) completes the plan, before the women of his tent begin in line 45.

thinai_evidence.note: the camp of an army on campaign in another's land, described for itself, with no love situation in the unit

comparisons.tenor: the planted bows with quivers hung on them

reading: Inside, women with short bangles and hair falling on small backs, who make night into day, wear bright swords in striped belts and, holding oil-filled lamps with long wicks, relight them whenever they dim; at midnight, when the long-tongued bells are silenced, old guards wrapped in cloth sway as they doze, like the flowering athiral creeper on a padar bush stirred by a drizzling wind; men who measure the hours without error stand with joined hands, hail the king who goes out to conquer the wave-girt world and tell him how much water the little clock has let through; strong-bodied Yavanas of fearsome look, in tight coats with whips at their waists, set up a gem lamp in the fine chamber hung with tiger chains and screened by curtains on strong ropes, and Mlecchas who speak only by signs stand close by in their mantles.
nuance: The guard of the king's sleep is a list of strangers to the Tamil household: armed women, Yavanas and Mlecchas who cannot speak the language (உடம்பின் உரைக்கும் உரையா நாவின்). The hour-keepers' formula addresses the king as the one who goes to conquer the world, so even the telling of time is praise.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 39-54 and 55-70: those breaks fall inside one description of the king's tent (சூழப் / பொழுதளந் தறியும்; பரூஉக்கை துமியத் / தேம்பாய்). This unit holds the guard of the king's tent from the women lamp-bearers (line 45) to the Mlecchas at his side (உழைய ராக, line 66), before the king himself appears in line 67.

thinai_evidence.note: the night watch round a king who has gone out to conquer the world

comparisons.tenor: the old guards nodding in sleep

reading: The king, eager for close battle, cannot sleep: he thinks of the tusker that forgot its herd of cow elephants when thrown spears pierced it and its thick trunk, writhing like a snake, was cut off; he remembers the men in honey-dripping garlands who fought well and fell, having made good the rice they ate; he thinks of the horses that, deep-pierced by sharp arrows, droop their ears and stand suffering without eating; one hand pressed on the bed, the other, with its bracelet, raised to his crown, he thinks long, his strong finger that grips the weapon pointing at the enemy, in the camp where the drum roars and kings tremble.
nuance: His sleeplessness begins as desire for battle (மண்டமர் நசையொடு) and turns, line by line, into memory of what the battle cost, the elephant, the men, the horses; the camp is then called the place of the drum before which kings shiver, so the reckoning of loss sits inside the boast. The next line calls him இன்துயில் வதியுநன், one who lies in sweet sleep, which may say he has slept at last or name him as the husband the wife cannot see.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 55-70 and 71-88: the core break at line 70 falls between a phrase and its verb (பரூஉக்கை துமியத் / தேம்பாய் கண்ணி), and the break at 88 inside the wife's scene. This unit takes the king's sleepless thought from line 67 to the camp it ends on (முரசுமுழங்கு பாசறை, line 79); line 80 turns to the wife.

thinai_evidence.note: a king on campaign, awake in his camp, thinking of his wounded and his foes

reading: Not seeing him, the wife suffers, her loneliness breaking the self-command with which she held her heart; she thinks long and steadies herself, straightens her slipping bangles, falls into a daze and sighs deeply, trembles like a peacock struck by an arrow, her ornaments loosening, and lies in the seven-storeyed mansion, the lamp in the statuette's hands burning with a thick flame, listening to the sweet many-voiced music of the streams falling from the curved eaves; then her ears are filled by the sound of his horses: with the great gathered army that has seized the lands others wanted, the victory banner raised, rising to the right while horns and conches blare, along the great red road that the forest has enriched, where the kaayaa flowers collyrium, the konrai spills good gold, the kodal's closed buds open like palms and the thondri blooms blood, past the rain-fed millet where the twisted-horned stag leaps with the young doe, leaving behind the forest of ripe fruit in the month of white rain, the horses yoked to the tall chariot famed for its deeds race, urged on.
nuance: The return is told through her hearing (அஞ்செவி நிறைய ஆலின): she lies listening to the rain on the eaves, and the next sound to fill her ears is his horses, so the poem ends before anyone meets. The road home is lined with the mullai flowers of the season he would have promised, each set as a jewel or as blood, the colours of victory.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 71-88 and 89-103: the core break at line 88 falls inside a single phrase (ஓர்ப்பனள் கிடந்தோ / ளஞ்செவி நிறைய), since the sound of the returning horses fills the ears of the wife who lay listening. This unit takes her from line 80 (காணா டுயருழந்து) to the end of the poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife endures the waiting until the sound of the returning chariot reaches her, in a mullai forest of the rains

comparisons.tenor: the dark blossoms of the kaayaa
the opening buds of the kodal
the red flowers of the thondri

iraicchi.act: the twisted-horned stag leaps about together with the young doe in the rain-fed millet
iraicchi.sense: the beasts of the season are already together, as the husband and wife will be when the chariot that passes them arrives

title: மதுரைக்காஞ்சி (1/2)
theme: The first half of Maduraikkanchi, Mangudi Maruthanar's counsel to the Pandya who won at Thalaiyalanganam: a long address that praises the king's lineage, battles, sieges, port wealth and giving, ravages his enemies' land, blesses him, and then sets against all this the countless kings who ruled as he does and passed away; with அதனால், 'therefore', it turns to a description of his realm in its five lands (marutham, mullai, kurinji, paalai, neythal) and approaches Madurai through the Vaiyai's banks, the refugees and defeated kings at its edge, its walls, its festival flags and its streets.
structure_note: The core cut placed most units in the middle of the poem's long participial sentences (break scores 0 and 1). Seventeen units were moved to the vocatives that close each address (lines 23, 42, 63, 74, 88, 105, 151, 176), to the start of the counsel (line 210), and to the 'ஒருசார்' and '... சான்ற' lines that close each of the five lands (270, 285, 301, 314, 326). The chapter ends at line 393 inside the description of the city, which continues in chapter 8.
source_issues: The idyll's colophon has no thurai (the record gives only the thinai காஞ்சி); puram_thurai is therefore empty for every unit.
Line 112 கறவுக் is obscure; சுறவுக் (shark) would fit புலவு நீர் வியன் பெளவத்து in the next line and may be the intended reading.
Line 187 நா டழியக் எயில் has an irregular doubled க் before a vowel (expected நாடழிய எயில்).
Line 214 ends inside a word: தின் றானா இன வைக / னிலனெடுக் (lines 214, 215) splits வைகல் and நிலன் across the line break as printed.
Line 308 கமழ்சூழ் is flagged against the tamilvu reading கமஞ்சூழ் (full, laden); our reading is kept, and the karu and mutal of that unit do not depend on it.

Line 323 புரவிய டனைத்தும் looks like the same loss of the vowel sign ொ that was repaired at lines 172, 180, 269, 276, 281, 299, 369 and 372 (புரவியொடு அனைத்தும்); it is not flagged and the karu form is copied as printed.

reading: The poem opens on an ordered world, bounded by the roaring sea and standing on honey-hung mountains, where the winds keep their direction, the stars their course, sun and moon shine clear, the rain does its work, one seed yields a thousand and men are free of disease, and it names the king as descendant of the exalted ones who ruled that world among truthful, famous men, so that a good age followed in their steps.
nuance: The order of the cosmos is described before any king is named and is credited to the rule of the ancestors (lines 21 to 23); truthful speech (பொய் யறியா வாய்மொழி, line 19) is counted among the goods of that world alongside rain and harvest.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 1-16 and 17-32: the opening sentence runs through the description of the ordered world (line 16 கட்கின் பத்து continues into line 17) to the vocative உயர்ந்தோர் மருக in line 23; line 24 begins the battlefield.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron through the ordered world his ancestors ruled

reading: On a dreadful field where elephants carry corpses on their tusks and demon women with fat in their mouths dance the tunangai in pairs, the blood of strong kings boils in the fire of wrath and, with a bangled arm for a ladle, the cook who knows the rite serves the flesh-rice to the soldiers who never stepped back; the king is hailed as lord of the hill of falling streams where the ancient god named after the southern king dwells.
nuance: The food of the rite goes to படை யோர் ... பிற் பெயரா, the soldiers who did not step back (lines 37, 38): the grisly sacrifice is also the army's reward. Lines 40 to 42 (தென்னவற் பெயரிய ... தொல்முது கடவுள்) are hard: the hill may be one where an ancient god bearing the Pandya's name dwells, or the king may be said to dwell after that god; the reading is not fixed.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 17-32 and 33-42: the battlefield passage begins at பிணக் கோட்ட in line 24 and closes with the vocative பொருப்பிற் பொருந in line 42.

thinai_evidence.note: the battlefield sacrifice after victory, a deed of vaakai

comparisons.tenor: the wrath of the strong kings, as the fire on which their own blood boils

reading: While the great war-trained elephant, mountain-like, its head wet with fragrant musth, tramples the field in fury, the dust the horses raise hides the sun, the swift chariots whirl like wind and sword-bearing warriors fight shoulder to shoulder, the king defeats the two great kings together with the Velir, crosses falling hills and splits the wilderness, and, descendant of the golden-garlanded Nediyon who gave the land, is like the white thunderbolt that eats trees and shatters mountains.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 43-56 and 57-72: the sentence of the battle and the lineage closes at ஏற னையை, 'you are like the thunderbolt', in line 63; line 64 begins the forts.

thinai_evidence.note: victory over the two crowned kings and the Velir

comparisons.tenor: the speed of the chariots wheeling on the field

reading: Going on without pause he took, and left, forts with guard forests, deep moats, rows of tall gates, long walls with lines of battlements and arrow-spitting towers, so that from southern Kumari to the great northern mountain and between the eastern and western seas the kings who lived in victory speak their old allegiance and obey, and he will be king over them all.
nuance: The bounds of rule in lines 70 and 71 (Kumari, the northern mountain, the two seas) are the formula Purananuru 6 and 17 also use; here they come as the result of a run of sieges, not as an inheritance.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 57-72 and 73-82: the sieges begin at அருங் குழுமிளை in line 64 and the sentence ends in கோனா குவை, 'you will be king of kings', line 74.

thinai_evidence.note: the taking of fortified strongholds, a deed of uzhinai

reading: On the dread, sky-touching sea, ships with sails raised on tall masts cut the curling waves before a strong wind and come to shore to the sound of drums, unloading gold and precious goods that fill the land, great rocking ships like cloud-capped mountains crowding the harbour; the king is hailed as the lofty victor who took that town of tall paddy with the clear sea for its moat.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 73-82 and 83-105: the sea passage that begins at வானி யைந்த in line 75 closes with the vocative உயர் கொற்றவ in line 88.

thinai_evidence.note: the capture of a sea-moated town, whose port wealth is the praise

comparisons.tenor: the great ships crowding the harbour

reading: Everywhere sound the songs of the water-lifters at their rows of lifts, the clear bells of the threshers' oxen that scare off the great birds, and the kuravai of the fisherwomen on the sandy shore of blue-flowered mundakam, while on one side, in the wide festival ground, the king gives the drum-shouldered bards bright-tusked elephants, crowns them with golden lotuses and scatters fine ornaments: he is the victorious king of the many Kuttuvar.
nuance: The giving is set among the sounds of field and shore (இசையே என்றும், line 95): the bards' gift belongs to the same abundance as the threshing and the fisherwomen's dance. Line 92 கய னகைய and line 101 இரு பெயர்ப் பேரா யம் are obscure.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 83-105: the sounds of the fields and the shore begin at நீர்த் தெவ்வும் in line 89 and lead to the gifts and the vocative வெல் கோவே, line 105.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's giving to the bards amid the sounds of his land

reading: Even when summer scorches the stones, the sky hides its rain and the stars of the coming days go astray, the king's land never lacks flood or harvest: the din of paddy and reapers and the cries of birds never cease, and on the shore the fishermen landing their boats and the sellers of white salt keep up the noise of Muthuvellil's wealth; with the farmers of the small hamlets and the people of the four lands obeying him, he swept on like wind, spread fire till the land was ruined, camped fearsomely at Alankanam, crushed the kings, took their drums and made the battlefield his sacrifice.
nuance: Lines 106 to 109 claim that the land yields even when rain fails and the stars go wrong, the reverse of the rule that rain follows the king; the land's plenty is offered as given, and the counsel that comes later has to work on a king who has it.

thinai_evidence.note: the victory at Alankanam closes the unit

comparisons.tenor: the screwpine with its drum-like fruit

reading: He raises the houses of his friends and unseats the kingdoms of his foes; desired by the people of good Korkai with its ripe pearls and conch-bangled quarters, he is the war-bull of the southern fisherfolk who eat rich meat; taking everything hard with ease and throwing away all that is his without keeping it, he will not say 'let us stay' but rises, goes through the forests of the snowy peaks, enters the inner lands, seizes what they prize and camps for many years in the land he wants.

reading: Spreading fierce tall-tusked elephants and an army wide as the sea, going against his foes like Murugan, arrows falling like rain, horses raising dust and conches and horns sounding, he broke their pride, took their forts and rooted them out with their kin, so that his enemies walk his way; he has ringed the old wide world, shown the path of dharma without failing in statecraft or straying from the steps of the great, and the poet wishes his victory to grow like the waxing crescent seen in the west and his foes' fortune to wane like the moon rising in the east; even for heaven with its nectar he would not leave his true friendship for a lie.

title: மதுரைக்காஞ்சி (2/2)
theme: The second half of Maduraikkanchi walks through one day and night of Madurai, from the day market, the shrines, the sages, the court and the crafts to the evening market, the lovers and courtesans, the festivals, the guarded watches and the dawn, then turns to the king: the spoils that feed the city, his waking among women, his honouring of warriors by merit and his open-gated giving, and ends by bidding him rejoice daily in the good time he has been given within its bound.
structure_note: The poem runs as one long chain of clauses, each description closing on a noun in -உம் (பள்ளியும், அவையமும், பகர்நரும்) or on a subject held back after a predicate in -ஏ (lines 428 to 430, 543 to 544). The core cut fell inside these descriptions in most places, so 19 of the 21 units are adjusted to the description breaks; 747-763 and 764-782 are the core units. The unit at 394 begins inside a sentence from chapter 7 and was not moved across the chapter.
source_issues: Line 662: our text reads களிதொடை (the toddy sellers' 'intoxicating strings'?), the flagged tvu reading is களிநொடை, 'selling' (நொடை, as at line 622 நொடைநவில்); the tvu reading fits the toddy sellers' calling out better. Our reading is kept in the marks.

Lines 753 to 761 print the short lines with word-internal spaces (கள் ளரிப்ப, மை வீழ்ப்ப, தொல் லாணை நல் லாசிரியர்); line 761 is the same as Pattinappalai 170 (தொல்லாணை நல்லாசிரியர்), where it is printed without the spaces. Karu forms are taken from the spaced text.

Lines 776 and 777 split one word across the line break (மன்ன / ரவரும், for மன்னர் அவரும்), and பிறகும் in line 777 looks like a misprint for பிறரும் ('and others'), matching பிறரும் in lines 518, 577 and 746.
Line 682 (பொன்சுடு நெருப்பி னிலமுக் கென்ன) is unclear to us; நிலமுக்கு may be a corrupt or rare word.
Line 394 begins inside a sentence that started in chapter 7 (the crowd of elephants, chariots and horses, lines 380 to 393); the chapter boundary was not moved.

What the drum-head simile of lines 395 and 396 is compared to is not fixed by the text.

reading: Young women glowing like a golden doll in the tender light of the setting sun, with wounding glances, dark skin, slipping armlets, painted young breasts and hair thick as spilled kohl, some with a peacock's gait and some with soft speech, walk gently, clap and laugh and play with unlettered men, and carry their wares in decorated caskets with fragrant flowers from house to house; and the din of the wide day market of Koodal, never lessened by what is taken nor swollen by what is brought, like the sea that clouds drink from and rivers pour into, rose like a land in festival on the evening of the seventh day.
nuance: The sea simile (lines 424 to 426) is built as a double balance: the sea keeps its level because what the clouds take and what the rivers bring cancel out, and the market keeps its plenty because taking and bringing go on together. reading: With the axe-bearing tall one, who made water, earth, fire, wind and the great sky together, at their head, the gods of spotless shining bodies, unfading flowers, unblinking eyes and food of fragrance receive high offerings of unchanging custom at the evening festival with drums; and mature women holding little boys in bright pendants, as one holds a pollen-filled lotus bud, shining together with them, worship with flowers and incense at the gods' shrine that guards the city from outside.

reading: Next the Brahmins' dwelling, like a hill carved out, where great ones of loving heart live at ease, singing the Veda, keeping a conduct of high merit, unique in this world and reaching the higher world from here without straying from the path of right; and the fragrant flowered dwelling of the sages, praised with flowers and incense by the lay followers (சாவகர்), where knowers who understand past and coming time and the present and know sky and earth whole, of unbending body and restrained, crowd in to keep their fasts, with water pots hung in slings of twisted cord, high red walls like copper rising beyond sight, the place shining like many hills gathered together.
nuance: Two religious houses are set side by side: the Brahmins, marked by Veda and rite but also by a loving heart (அன்புடை நெஞ்சு, line 472), and a community of ascetics whose lay followers are called சாவகர் and who know past, present and future. The text names their practices (fasting, water pots in slings) but not their sect; that they are Jain or Buddhist is an inference.

reading: Then the court that speaks right, which puts away fear, grief and desire, and keeps from both hatred and delight, being straight like the beam of a balance; the kaviti officers with sandal on their chests, who like the great ones who move in the sky examine good and evil and restrain them, keep love and right, shun blame and are full of fame; and the merchants who never stray from right, in many-roomed houses like a cluster of hills where kites perch and fly, rich with goods and food, selling things of hill, land and water and gems, pearls and gold from excellent countries.
nuance: Lines 489 and 490 list exactly what the judges must set aside: three feelings that bend a judgment by weakness (fear, grief, desire) and two that bend it by partisanship (hatred, delight). The balance word ஞெமன் is the one Purananuru 6 uses for the same image.

reading: Like the four-tongued Kosar appearing at the assembly of Pazhaiyan's Mohur, a town of rain that never fails and harvests that never fail, the four great groups appear; and shell cutters, gem borers, goldsmiths, gold assayers, cloth sellers, weighers of copper, bundle tiers, those who choose flowers and incense, and painters of keen sight who can show any work in images, small and great craftsmen together, spread their goods short and long like the ripples of a clear wave and stand in all four streets, with a clamour like the eager din of the great day's assembly of the cool-sea lord, whom drum-beating kodiyar bless with their families.
nuance: The poet measures Madurai's assembly against another lord's: the four-tongued Kosar at Pazhaiyan's Mohur, a vassal court. Which the four groups are is not said. The trades of lines 511 to 518 are a catalogue of the city's crafts, ending with the painter, whose work is to 'show every work by likeness' (எவ்வகைச் செய்தியும் உவமங் காட்டி).

reading: Fragrant sap, jackfruit segments, sweet mangoes of rare beauty, vegetables and fruits of many shapes, tender greens with their buds loosed, grown by the east wind's rain, pieces of sweet cane like nectar, famous rice with meat, tubers that grow downward and the rest are eaten everywhere from those who serve sweet rice; and, like the roar of the port where wind-driven ships with white sails unload many goods, or the cries of many birds that rise at midnight when the flood of the great sea pours into the backwaters, there spills the clamour of the evening market.
nuance: As at line 430, the subject (the din of the evening market) comes after the predicate, so the two markets of Madurai, the day market (நாளங்காடி) and the evening market (அல்லங்காடி), each end a long period on the word கம்பலை. reading: The sun, its burning light dimmed and its anger cooled, takes the good day with it to the western hill; from the east the full moon rises and night comes wearing the look of day; women who long to join their dear partners string cool water-lilies, put on jewels, perfume their long hair, grind narantham, stir sandal and smoke their soft clothes; doe-eyed women glad in their womanhood light tall lamps; love-sickness enters every part of the great city as the noisy evening departs; and, tuning the seven-stringed small lute to a changed mode, they embrace the partners they desire, so that the wide sky is fragrant.
nuance: This is akam matter (lovers making ready for union at nightfall) carried inside a puram poem's tour of the city, so the love-sickness (நோய், line 557) is not one woman's but the whole city's. Line 549 makes the moonlit night 'take on the form of day', which is why the city can keep moving. The vehicle of the simile in line 560 (தாழ்பயல்) is not clear to us.

reading: The courtesans throw off garlands bright as gathered water, swing their bright bangles, fill the street with the scent of fresh flowers, deck themselves like a flowering bush in the rains, embrace until their ornaments scar the chest, weave many deceiving lies and hide their true embrace, and draw in the many rich young men who came from far and near for their beauty until their wealth is spent, then leave them as soft-winged bees drink the pollen and abandon the empty flower; and like fruit-seeking birds the wealthy householders and others come to their fine houses, where women in bright bangles crowd under lamps like celestial women dancing in the blue sky, kondi women who make onlookers' hearts tremble, dance to the drum amid the midnight lute, and, tired of the sand of the cold ford, pluck tender sprays, put on long-stalked water-lilies and play at poythal in every fragrant house.
nuance: The poet names the deceit outright (மாயப் பொய்பல, line 570) and the draining of wealth (வளந்தப வாங்கி, line 572), and gives the men two images that are not flattering, the bee at an empty flower and the bird that lives by seeking fruit; but the scene stays inside the praise of the city. கொண்டி (line 583) elsewhere means plunder, so these may be women brought in from conquered lands.

reading: On the good day of Onam, the feast of Mayon of the golden garland who overcame the hosts of asuras, warriors of the fighting quarter, faces and foreheads scarred from unyielding battle, hands that bear the fight, wearing garlands full of bees, eager for combat, drive fierce elephants at each other in mock battle so that the cloths the watchers spread are strewn on the ground, and roam drunk on strong toddy; and women of rich houses who have borne sons to their husbands' joy, milk flowing from their young breasts, the smell of childbirth gone, bathe in the tank with their shining kin.
nuance: Lines 592 to 598 are hard: what scarred the warriors' faces (கோணம், சாணம்) and what the watchers threw on the shore (காழகம்) we read only tentatively. The festival joins two kinds of strength the city honours, the scarred warrior and the mother newly risen from childbirth.

reading: Setting the frets and tuning the sevvazhi mode, the lute joined with the drum and the small aguli beating, lamps going ahead with the offerings, pregnant women moving gently like peacocks worship with joined hands while the broad-shouldered priestess gives them the offering; on one side the velan of strict rites surrounds them with Murugan's presence to the sound of sweet instruments, and wearing kurinji flowers of the rainy season and kadamba they honour the tall Vel and dance the kuravai hand in hand in every square; in every quarter speech, song and dance mingle, many separate clamours whirl in frenzy, like the roar of the street festival in the land of Nannan of great fame.
nuance: The hill god's rite has come into the city: the kurinji flower (a thing of another land, line 613) is worn in Madurai's squares. The priestess (சாலினி) and the velan serve women at a life crisis, pregnancy, which suggests what the Murugan rite was used for in town.

reading: When the first watch of night has gone, the conch's noise dies down, the traders lower their bars and shut their long shop doors, young women bright in jewels go to bed, the sweet-makers who sell soft cakes like fine-lined honeycomb, sugar shaped like fine sand and carefully folded modakam doze and sleep, the dancers of the festival lie still, and, like the cold sea when its roar has ceased, those on their beds sleep sweetly in the depth of midnight.
nuance: The city that roared like the sea by day (lines 424 to 426, 536 to 543) is now the sea with its roar ceased; the poet keeps one image for Madurai across the whole day.

reading: In that midnight, ghosts and spirits take on forms and roam with Death of the killing chariot and the demons, and in darkness thick as the hide of a black she-elephant, thieves go about seeking jewels, with swords that cut stone and wood, leather on their feet, short daggers at the thigh, blue belts, rope ladders of soft thread and chisels that dig through earth; but the town's guards, who track the hiding places of these men, sleepless like a strong tiger watching a strong elephant, fearless, praised for their manhood, never straying from the treatise and keen in judgment, with arrows none can escape, rise tirelessly and walk the streets through the half night of rain, when water runs in the chariot streets and the gods themselves walk, so that the last watch passes safe and without fear until day.
nuance: The thieves' kit is listed as closely as the craftsmen's tools by day (lines 511 to 518): night too has its trades. The guards are praised as men who keep to the treatise (நூல்வழிப் பிழையா, line 646), so watch-keeping is a learned craft, not only courage.

reading: At dawn, like the bee that drinks pollen humming at the bud in a fragrant pond whose flowers have loosed their bonds, the Brahmins who recite chant the Veda; lute players tune the strings sweetly and play the marutham mode; mahouts feed balls of food to the fierce elephants; the stabled horses of the tall chariots are sated with grass; the shops of many wares are washed with dung; the toddy sellers call out their drink; and wives who slept in their loving husbands' arms, wanting the spreading dawn, walk with their bright gold jewels ringing, like streaks of lightning that dazzle the eye, and the doors of the strong-walled houses creak open.
nuance: The lute players' mode is marutham, the mode of the landscape whose hour, by porul 1.9, is dawn; the music keeps the time-scheme of akam even in a city poem.

reading: Old warriors whose tongues lisp with drink raise their roaring voices; the sootar praise, the magadhar recite and the vaitalikar announce the hours; the sounding drum resounds and bulls bellow in answer; the spotted cock crows at daybreak; the heron with its mate and the lovely swan cry, the peacock calls, the great tusker with its cow trumpets, the caged beast roars with the tiger; and women of fine jewels, like lightning leaping in a sky cleared of cloud, who sulked over their wine and tore their thick necklaces, have the scattered pearls, the fallen young fruits and the soft faded flowers swept from the sanded courtyards where bees hum, at the safe dawn when night departs.
nuance: The dawn is told entirely by sound: men (warriors, bards, heralds), then drum and bull, then birds, then beasts. The women's sulking over wine (புலந்தனர், line 680) is akam's oodal, glimpsed only by its litter. Lines 682 and 683 (the 'fire that melts gold' simile and the young fruits) we cannot fix.

reading: Tuskers left behind in the middle ground when the dark-shouldered mazhavar were routed, leaping horses seized in enemy country, herds that the fierce kooliyar, cutting men down with the spear as their goad, brought back by the light of burning towns, and all the precious things that came from every land, worshipped daily at the guarded gate of the good fort, pour into Madurai of great name with immeasurable wealth, like the great Ganges spreading into the sea, so that it shines like the gods' world and has surpassing fame.
nuance: The wealth of the markets has a source, and this unit names it: elephants left on the field, horses taken, herds driven home by the light of burning towns. The 'burning towns' (ஊர்சுடு) are what the Purananuru's raid poems celebrate; here they are the start of a flow that ends in the city's splendour. What the அணங்குடைத் தோட்டி of line 693 is (a guarded gate, a goad hung as an emblem) we read tentatively.

reading: In a grove where the ashoka's bright flowers, red as fire and humming with bees, have opened on every branch, you embraced the fragrant shoulders of women whose gold jewels shine like the young sunlight of the rising sun, with a peacock's gentle grace, skin like mango shoots, freckles on their backs, bright earrings in their ears and faces like the great pollen-laden lotus of the god's pond, and slept on a bed bright with garlands; then, rising sweetly when good sleep left you, you rubbed sandal on your chest hung with bright pearl strings, the bee-swarmed garland hanging to your neck, gold armlets shining on your strong hands, starched cloth wrapped as your dress, and stood in a form like Murugan's, like a painted figure made by a master.
nuance: Here the poem turns from the city to the king and from the third person to 'you' (நின், line 727, and the second-person உருவினை யாகி, line 724). His waking repeats the city's: Madurai woke to sounds and opened doors, the king wakes from his women's arms and is dressed, so the ruler's day is told as one more part of the city's day.

reading: Warriors eager for battle, who cut through and routed the enemy like a stone dam that stops a flood, praise the victory of your feet joined with the sword's wealth; and the strong-armed warriors whose chests took arrows round the bow, the lords who strove at strong forts with stone-cut moats, the chiefs who fell nobly where great elephants fell in battle amid an army like rising flame and drums of unscraped bull hide sounded ceaselessly, and those of worn chests like a strong hub, armour split by spears and arrows, who did not slacken in high service, and the men of great deeds who captured herds of tall elephants: on the worthy you set the golden thumbai, not asking who they are but weighing their order of merit.
nuance: Line 738 is the hinge: the king crowns the worthy 'without saying who are you' (நீர்யார் என்னாது) and 'considering order' (முறைகருதுபு). Honour goes by the order of deeds just listed (arrows taken, forts stormed, elephants captured), not by birth.

reading: 'Let all come, and bring the others too,' you say, sitting without anger at a gate that is never barred, 'let the bards come, let the women singers come, let the new poets come with the dancers', and to all the suppliants who support large families you give tall chariots with kodinji and elephants; in every yard toddy is strained, at every tree post rams are felled, fat meat roasts and melts, ghee boils and frying sizzles, and the smoke of seasoning spreads like rain mist so the wide city cannot be seen; like the Tall One of land-giving fortune who, with the good teachers of ancient command trained in the sacrificial rites of Mudukudumi of many halls, ate the shared feast.
nuance: The king is measured against the dynasty's past: the feast is like that of a Tall One (நெடியோன்) who ate with the teachers of Mudukudumi's sacrifices. Whether this நெடியோன் is an earlier Pandya or the god is not settled by the line. Line 761 (தொல்லாணை நல்லாசிரியர்) recurs in Pattinappalai 170, a shared formula for the Vedic teachers.

reading: Worthy in wonder, nobility and rectitude, flawless in the praise of many mouths, bringing rare things and widening your people, learning great things and spreading fame, shining sweetly with flourishing kin like the sun amid the sea and the moon amid many stars, while the young Kosar of victorious true swords, with Maran of great name and unfailing fame at their head, listen to your true word of ordered custom, and the chieftains of great valour, the five of golden ornaments among them, crowd in and praise you in your assembly of shining fame, and bright-jewelled women pour fragrant wine from golden vessels: rejoice and live sweetly every day, great one, in the good span of time you have been given within its bound.
nuance: The poem's last word sets the whole description in its kaanchi frame: the good time is one 'you got within a bound' (வரைந்து நீ பெற்ற, line 782), so the closing 'rejoice every day' is counsel given in view of its end, not only a blessing. The formula 'with X at the head' (மாறன் தலைவனாக, line 772) also opens the list of praising chiefs, as in Purananuru 72.

title: நெடுநல்வாடை
theme: Nedunalvadai describes the long cold season, first in the world and the town, then inside a king's palace, where the queen lies unadorned and unconsoled on a bed made for two; it ends with the poet's wish that the war end now, and with the king at midnight walking his winter camp to see his wounded, so that a poem the colophon files as vaakai spends most of its lines on a wife's waiting.
structure_note: The idyll is one sentence. Its ten units here follow its movements: the season outside (1-72), the palace and its inner chamber (73-114), the bed (115-135), the queen (136-166), and the prayer and the camp (167-188). All twelve core units were moved to sense breaks.
source_issues: Line 17 நாரைய டெவ்வாயுங் is நாரையொடு எவ்வாயும் with the vowel sign ொ lost, the same loss show flags at lines 46, 82, 84, 142, 169 and 178 but not flagged here; the karu form is copied as printed.
Line 35 இருகோட்ட டறுவையர் has a doubled ட (expected இருகோட் டறுவையர், two-ended cloth); probably a typing error.
Line 110 விளங்குஞ் கதையுரீஇ: ஞ் before க is not regular sandhi, and கதை makes no sense here; the expected reading is விளங்கும் சுதையுரீஇ (plastered with lime). The reading follows சுதை.
Line 72 has போதே where the same formula in Akananuru 264 line 10 has பொழுதே; both are read as the season (time) having set in.
The colophon gives no patron, though the neem tied to the spear (வேம்புதலை, line 176) marks the king as a Pandya; the poem names no one.

reading: When the unfailing clouds wheel to the right and pour new rain till the earth shivers, cowherds with crooked staffs drive their herds and bulls to other ground and, their kodal garlands sodden, shiver with firebrands held to their cheeks; beasts forget to graze, monkeys huddle, birds drop from their perches and cows kick away their calves; in the cold-season midnight that would chill a hill, musundai and gold-like peerkkai bloom on every bush, herons and storks pick fish on the wet white sand, and the emptied white clouds drift in drizzle across the sky.
nuance: The cold is shown entirely through what it does to bodies, the herders' chattering jaws, the monkeys' huddle, the birds that fall: a reader of the whole idyll will later meet a queen who shivers for another reason, but this unit names no lover at all.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 1-16 and 17-32: the description of the first rains and of the creatures on the wet sand runs to line 20, where the spent clouds scatter drizzle; the fields and the town begin at line 21.

thinai_evidence.note: the cold season and midnight are kurinji's time (porul 1.7, 1.8), though no love situation is stated in the unit

reading: In the wide fields the paddy, grown thick in the rains, bows its coming ears; the clusters of the tall areca swell and their green nuts firm; the cold branches of the dense flowering groves drip; and in the rich old town of high mansions, along streets as broad as a river lying there, strong men in leaf garlands, drunk on bee-swarmed toddy, ignore the drizzle and wander past midday in cloth hanging on both sides as they please.
nuance: The men who ignore the rain are the only people in the season's prelude who enjoy it, and they enjoy it in company and drink; the contrast with the shut chambers to come is the poet's arrangement, not stated.

reading: At evening young women with silver bangles on bamboo-smooth arms, soft gait, pearl smiles and cool eyes reaching to their flower earrings, knowing the hour by the scent of jasmine buds opening in their baskets, light the wet wicks of iron lamps, scatter paddy and flowers, join their hands and keep the evening rite in the rich market; while the red-legged male dove that lives in the house will not go out with his loving hen to feed in the common ground, but, unable to tell night from day, sits helpless on the rafter perch, shifting.
nuance: The dove that stays on the rafter with his mate in the cold is the first pair in the poem kept together by the season; it passes iraicchi's conditions 1 and 2 (one pair, an act) but the unit itself states no love situation for its sense to bear on, so it is left as scene.
