thinai_evidence.note: evening is mullai's hour (porul 1.6), and the hour is known here by the opening of the jasmine

reading: In the guarded mansion the servants grind fragrant stone for many blends, the round stone the northerners brought lies unused with the southern sandal, the women wear no garlands and put only a few flowers in their dense hair, dried over fires of tagaram stems with dark aloe and white resin; spider webs hang on the folded fans; the summer chambers of the high upper storey that let in the south wind are shut with bolted doors; for the spray, no one drinks cold water from the jars but all sit by the braziers; the dancing women warm against their breasts the lute strings gone slack in the cold before they tune the small lute; and so, while the rains thicken and those parted from their lovers lament, the cold season has set in.
nuance: Twenty-two lines of a household's defences against the cold (fires, shut doors, no cold water, warmed strings) end in a single clause naming the people the season hurts, the parted lovers; the line's formula is shared with Akananuru 264, where பொழுதே stands for this போதே. The sense of கொள்ளுறழ் நறுங்கல் in line 50 is not secure.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 49-64 and 65-80: the season's description is one sentence that closes at line 72 with கூதிர்நின் றன்றாற் போதே; the palace building begins with மாதிரம் at the end of that line, which is kept with this unit.

thinai_evidence.note: the only love situation in the unit is the lament of those whose lovers are away, the waiting of mullai

reading: At midday, when the spreading sun throws no slant from the two marker poles, builders who know the treatise stretch their cord, take the directions, worship the gods and lay out a house fit for great kings; inside its high encircling wall stands a gateway tall as a cut hill, with paired doors bound in iron, posts of a fine tree named for a star, a lintel carved with a newly opened water-lily, smeared with white mustard and ghee, high enough for an elephant with its victory flag to pass; in the courtyard of spread sand male swans with long feathers play with short-legged hens, maned horses tired of the stall chew their grass with lonely cries, rain-water pours from the gaping makara spouts, and peacocks call like horns from a palace that rings like a mountain slope.
nuance: The courtyard's swans play in pairs and its horse cries alone (புலம்புவிடு குரல்), so even the description of masonry carries the poem's two states, together and parted.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 65-80, 81-96 and 97-112: the building of the palace runs from மாதிரம் at the end of line 72 (kept with the previous unit) to கோயில், line 100, where the sentence on the outer palace ends.

thinai_evidence.note: the unit praises the excellence of the builders and the king's house; no love situation is stated

reading: In the palace, lamp-figures made by Yavanas hold bowls brimming with ghee whose thick wicks raise upright flames, trimmed whenever they burn low, so that the spreading dark leaves every chamber; within the hard-guarded precinct that no man but the great lord may approach stand rooms like hills, creepers like bows, walls plastered bright as silver, pillars dark and thick as gems, walls red as wrought copper painted round with a single creeper of many flowers, and among them the fine chamber named for the womb.
nuance: That only the great lord (பெருந்தகை) may enter the precinct makes the chamber's emptiness the king's absence; the unit is architecture, but it locks the door that the poem will not open again.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 97-112 and 113-128: the inner palace is one description from the Yavana lamps (line 101) to the chamber named for the womb (கருவொடு பெயரிய காண்பி னல்லில், line 114); the couch begins at line 115.

thinai_evidence.note: craft and splendour of the king's inner palace, with no love situation stated

reading: In that chamber stands a full-sized couch on strong legs, swelling like drums, cut from the tusks of a forty-year elephant fallen in battle and shaped with a sharp chisel by a master, the legs rounded like the breasts of women heavy with child and narrowing at the middle, set on garlic-shaped feet; it is strung with fine work and hung with a lattice of pearls, its board covered with a tiger-spotted spread whose dyed cushions picture a hunt of strong beasts in a wide forest among flowers set like mullai buds; on it a soft bed, paired pillows filled with the white down of swans that had mated, and a washed, starched white sheet over all.
nuance: The down is from swans that had mated (துணைபுணர்) and the pillows are a pair (இணையணை): the bed is made for two in every detail before the next unit lays one woman on it. Lines 115 to 117, on the elephant's age and how its tusk was taken, are hard to construe.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 113-128 and 129-144: the couch and bedding are one description from line 115 to the spread sheet (சேக்கை, line 135); the queen on it begins at line 136.

thinai_evidence.note: the bed is described for the absent pair, and its patterned flowers are likened to mullai

comparisons.tenor: the flowers set on the spread

reading: On it lies the queen: on her breast, where the necklace lay, only a long plait hangs; her few soft locks lie dry over her fair brow; her ears, the long earrings removed, keep only small rings; her wrists, bared of gold bangles, carry only the right-whorled conch bangle and a protective thread, her finger a red ring bent like a vaalai fish's mouth, and her waist a soiled cloth, so that she looks like a picture left uncoloured; soft-limbed maids rub her feet, and grey-haired, red-faced foster mothers crowd round her, telling tales short and long and saying her dear one will come at once, all to please her; but she will not take comfort and weeps.
nuance: Each ornament is named with the token kept in its place (the plait for the necklace, the small ring for the earring, the conch bangle and thread for the gold), so a wife's karpu is read off what she has given up. The nurses' இன்னே வருகுவர் is the same promise Mullaippattu's old women hear in an omen; here it is only talk, and it fails. The colophon gives no speaker; the nurses' words are the unit's own speech.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 129-144, 145-155 and 156-171: the queen and the nurses' comfort form one sentence that closes with ஒல்லாள் மிகக்கலுழ்ந்து in line 156; line 156 is kept here and the painted canopy begins at line 157.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife waiting through the season for the husband away at war, comforted with the promise of his return

reading: She looks up at the canopy newly painted in wax on cloth over strong round posts, where the ram heads the circle of signs travelling the sky and the moon, the glorious lord, is shown with Rohini who never leaves him; thinking of Rohini she sighs long, gathers with her red finger-tips the tears that fall from the corners of her dark-lidded eyes and flicks a few away, and lies alone with her grief, this woman of shining beauty.
nuance: The poem says only that she thinks of Rohini and sighs; the contrast with the star that stays with her lord is left for the reader. It is not tagged ullurai or iraicchi, since the vehicle is a painted star and not a native thing of the land (porul 1.50). Lines 157 and 158, on how the canopy posts are made, are obscure.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 156-171: the canopy, the sigh and the tears are one clause that ends with புலம்பொடு வதியு நலங்கிளர் அரிவைக்கு, line 166; the poet's prayer for her begins at line 167.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife lies alone in grief waiting for the absent husband

comparisons.tenor: the knobs of the canopy posts

reading: May the war end now with victory, the poet prays, so that this bright woman's hard grief may end; for at the deep midnight the king, not taking to his bed, walks with a few men about the camp that is at war with many, going out to see the bright sword wounds of the warriors who brought down elephants whose long trunks now roll on the ground; the flames of the many lamps lean south as the cold north wind strikes them, a leader shows the wounded one by one with a strong neem-tied spear, harnessed horses shake off the rain in the muddy lane, and with his left hand holding his slipping cloth and his other arm on the shoulder of a sword-bearing youth, he looks at each face kindly while a pearl-strung white umbrella keeps off the falling drops.
nuance: The whole idyll is one sentence that ends on பாசறைத் தொழிலே, and the king is never named: the neem on the spear is the only sign that he is the Pandya, and the poet's wish in lines 167 and 168 is the only bridge between the queen's chamber and the camp, which never meet in the poem.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 156-171 and 172-188: the poet's wish (இன்னே முடிகதில், lines 167, 168) is the main clause on which the closing camp scene depends, so the unit runs from line 167 to the end of the poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's work in the winter camp and the warriors' wounds, framed by the wish that the queen's grief end

title: குறிஞ்சிப்பாட்டு
theme: Kurinjippattu entire: the friend discloses the secret love to the mother (அறத்தொடு நிற்றல்), telling how on the day the mother sent the girls to guard the millet they bathed, gathered the flowers of every land, were met by a hill hunter, were saved by him from a wild elephant, and how he embraced the girl, swore to marry her and has come every night since, through dangers the girl weeps over.
structure_note: One speech to the mother. Lines 1 to 34 give the reason for speaking; lines 35 to 106 the girls' day of play, with the list of flowers (62 to 96); lines 107 to 186 the man's arrival, the elephant and the union; lines 187 to 233 his land, his oath and his promise at sunset; lines 234 to 261 his nightly visits and the dangers of his path. Thirteen of the sixteen units were moved to sense breaks.
source_issues: Line 42 வலத்த: tamilvu reads வலந்த (woven), which fits the cane implements better; our text is kept.
Line 87 யடும்பம ராத்தி is a genuine அடும்பு + அமர் + ஆத்தி, not a lost comitative ending; karu forms are copied as printed.
Line 142 னென்றென: tamilvu reads என்றனன், which the sense needs (he said); our text is kept.
Line 89 prints சிந் துவாரம் with a space inside the one word சிந்துவாரம்.
The text is printed in the old joined style, so a word whose last consonant fuses with the next vowel is given in karu as printed (for example காந்த ளாம்ப in line 62 gives the forms காந்த and ளாம்ப).

reading: The friend tells the mother that the girl's wasting sickness, which has loosened her bright ornaments and which the mother has tried to cure by asking diviners, praising, worshipping, strewing flowers and offering incense to gods of many forms, is a grief the girl hid until the friend forced her to speak; and since jewels of pearl, gem and gold can be mended when broken but lost worth and fame cannot be washed clean even by sages, she asks whether it is wrong to let the mother know that, passing their father's strict guard, the two chose this marriage themselves.
nuance: The friend's argument for speaking rests on irreparability: a broken ornament can be rejoined, but lost good name cannot be washed back even by the wisest, so silence now would cost what cannot be repaired. The mother's rites are not mocked, only shown to miss the cause. இருவேம் in line 21 most naturally means the lovers; it could also take in the friend, who calls the act hers too in line 32.

thinai_evidence.note: a love chosen in secret past the father's guard, to be disclosed: kalavu, kurinji's punarthal

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the text addresses அன்னாய் (line 1); whether the foster mother or the mother is meant is not said

comparisons.vehicle: முத்தினு மணியினும் பொன்னினு மத்துணை நேர்வருங் குரைய கலங்கெடிற் புணருஞ்
comparisons.tenor: worth, wonder and nature, which once lowered cannot be restored

reading: Saying that even if the union does not come by the proper path it will be theirs in the other world, the girl, her deer-like gaze troubled, wilts helpless; the friend, holding two great fears like the worthy who stand between two great kings driven to war, cannot bear it either, and asks the mother to hear without anger how the protecting deed the two of them dared alone, without weighing lineage, rank, looks or support, came about.
nuance: The simile of the go-between standing between two kings bent on war brings puram diplomacy into akam: the friend's two fears are that the father will be shamed and that the girl will die, and like an envoy she can serve one side only by speaking to the other. Lines 30 to 32 admit the act was undertaken without the weighing of family and fortune that a marriage arranged by kin would have made.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl's resolve to keep the secret union even beyond this life: kalavu

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the text addresses அன்னாய் (line 1); whether the foster mother or the mother is meant is not said

comparisons.vehicle: கன்மீக் கடவு மிருபெரு வேந்தர் வினையிடை நின்ற சான்றோர் போல
comparisons.tenor: the friend caught between fear of the family and fear for the girl

reading: The friend recounts the day: the mother sent them to drive birds from the small millet, whose great ripe heads bent like the drooping trunk of a pearl-tusked elephant that has fed on bamboo, and to come home at sunset; they climbed the tiger-safe platform the hill watchman had built in a tree, took up in turn the cane sling, clapper and rattle, and in the heat of the day, as birds made for their roosts, clouds drew up the sea, mingled with the wind, thundered like a drum and poured on the hill with lightning like the bright spear Murugan raises against his foes.
nuance: The mother herself sent the girls to the field (நீ விடுத்தலின், line 39), so the friend's story makes the mother's own errand the occasion of the meeting. Murugan enters only as the vehicle of a simile for lightning, the same god the mother's rites in lines 5 and 6 had been addressing.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 35-50 and 51-66: the sentence of the storm runs on past line 50 and closes at பொழிந்தென in line 53; line 54 turns to the waterfall where the girls bathe.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field, the parrot-scaring and the watch platform are kurinji's native things

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the text addresses அன்னாய் (line 1); whether the foster mother or the mother is meant is not said

comparisons.tenor: the bent heads of ripe millet

reading: From the great peak the clear water came down in a white waterfall like shining cloth; with desire that would not stop they bathed in it, plunged into the spreading pool like poured crystal, sang on the echoing slope, wrung and dried their dark braided hair hanging down their backs, and their eyes reddened inside from the water.
nuance: The reddened eyes (உள்ளகம் சிவந்த கண்ணேம்) are the effect of long play in the water, the first sign in the story of the girls' freedom on the hill before the man appears.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 51-66: the bathing begins at line 54 and closes with கண்ணேம் in line 61; the catalogue of flowers starts at the end of line 61, where வள்ளிதழ் qualifies the காந்தள் of line 62, so the next unit begins at line 62.

thinai_evidence.note: waterfall, mountain pool and echoing slope

reading: The friend begins the list of the flowers they gathered: bright red kaanthal with large petals, aambal, anichcham, kuvalai of the cool pond, kurinji, vetchi, red-stemmed veri, sweet mango, manichchigai, unthoozh, koovilam, fire-like erutham, sulli, kooviram, vadavanam, vaagai, kudasam, eruvai, seruvilai, karuvilai, payini, vaani, kuravam, pasumpidi, vakulam, kaayaa, aavirai, veral, sooral, poolai, kurunarungkanni, marutham, kongam, pongam, thilakam, paathiri, serunthi, athiral, sanbagam, karanthai, kulavi, mango, thillai, paalai, mullai, kullai, pidavam, sirumaaradam, vaazhai, valli, neythal, thaazhai, thalavam, thaamarai, gnaazhal, mauval, kogudi, sedal, semmal and kurali.
nuance: The list (it runs to line 96) is the girls' play turned into an inventory of every landscape's flowers, sea-shore thaazhai and gnaazhal and field lotus and marutham beside hill kaanthal: the flowers say nothing about the lovers, but they show the girls free and at play just before the man comes. Many of the names cannot now be matched to a plant with certainty; the senses given are only for the common ones.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 51-66 and 67-82: the list of flowers that the girls gathered starts in line 62 (after the bathing, which closes in line 61) and is divided at line 82, where the core unit also ends.

thinai_evidence.note: the girls gather on the hill; kurinji and kaanthal lead the list, with flowers of every land among them

reading: The list goes on: kodal, kaithai, honey-rich vazhai, kaanji, neythal with clustered buds smelling of toddy, paangar, maraam, thanakkam, eengai, ilavam, hanging konrai, adumbu, aathi, long-stemmed avarai, pakanrai, palaasam, pindi, vanji, piththigam, sinthuvaaram, thumbai, thuzhaay, bright thonri, nanthi, naravam, punnaagam, paaram, peeram, kurukkaththi, aaram, kaazhvai, punnai, narantham, naagam, the flower that smells at midnight, kurunthu, vengai and others, with large puzhagu red as spread lac; roaming the rich forest they gathered them all and heaped them on the wide rock the rain had washed.
nuance: The heap of flowers on the rain-washed rock (வான்கண் கழீஇய அகலறைக் குவைஇ) ends the list and gives it a place: the flowers of every land are gathered onto one hill rock, as the whole idyll gathers its world into one day's story. Several names in this half of the list (பாரம், பீரம், நந்தி, காழ்வை) cannot be identified with confidence.

thinai_evidence.note: the heap is made on the wide hill rock, and vengai closes the list

reading: On the slope of the cross-lying hill, where the birds' noise sounds like instruments, the girls now and then sent out clear strong-breathed calls to drive off the parrots, tied leaf skirts of plucked petals and leaves about their waists, bound garlands of many kinds on their soft dark hair, and sat in the cool shade of the asoka, whose tender shoots shine like fire and drop pollen.
nuance: The leaf skirt (தழை) is the dress the hero of kurinji often brings as a love gift; here the girls make their own, so they are still unclaimed when he arrives in the next lines.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 99-113: the girls' play closes with இருந்தனமாக in line 106; line 107 begins the long description of the man who came.

thinai_evidence.note: parrot-scaring and the asoka of the hill slope

reading: Then a man appeared: his dark sapphire-coloured hair washed with butter-smoothed fragrant tagaram, dried with the fingers, scented with agil smoke, and loud with striped bees humming like a lute; on his head, to inspire awe, a cool garland of chosen flowers of every colour from hill, field, branch and pool, with a chaplet of white palm strips; a pitthigam garland curved behind, red asoka shoots tucked in and tender leaves swaying on his strong shoulders; sandal on his broad chest, an old fragrant garland shining with his ornaments; a painted banded bow in his large hand, arrows chosen, a finely worked belt tied tight, and bright warrior's anklets rubbing his fine feet as he walked.
nuance: Line 113 has his garland gathered from hill, field, branch and pool, the same reach across lands as the girls' list of flowers: he comes dressed in what they had just gathered. The warrior's anklet (கழல்) and the painted bow make him a hunter-chief rather than a plain hunter.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 99-113 and 114-129: the description of the man's dress and weapons runs from line 107 and closes at கலாவ in line 127; lines 128 and 129 belong with the hounds of line 131, which they describe.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill hunter with bow and arrows, wearing flowers of the hill

reading: His hounds, with teeth like sharp sprouts and strong claws, fierce like his many-speared young warriors who have seen the backs of enemies and laid waste the frontier, angry at every approach, came round the girls with unblinking eyes; the girls rose trembling, their feet faltering, bewildered and distressed; he came, handsome as a bull among cows that has fought off and driven away a rival, and fearing they would take fright, spoke soft sweet words, praised their hair and their looks and said that he had lost a beast that came this way; when they gave no answer he was troubled and asked whether even speaking with him was a blame, if they would not tell him of the beast.
nuance: The question about a lost beast (கெடுதி) is a pretext and the girls' silence is a rule of modesty, not rudeness: the man's reply, that speaking with him is no blame, names exactly the fear of blame that keeps them silent. Lines 128 and 129 can also be taken as describing his companions, who come with him; the reading here takes இளைஞரின் as the comparison for the hounds.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 114-129 and 130-145: lines 128 and 129 (the young warriors) are the vehicle of a simile for the hounds of line 131, so the unit begins at 128; it ends at the core boundary, line 145, where the man's question closes.

thinai_evidence.note: the hunter's hounds and the hunter asking after his lost game

comparisons.vehicle: மாறுபொரு தோட்டிய புகல்வின் வேறுபுலத் தாகாண் விடையி
comparisons.tenor: the man coming, proud and handsome

reading: He broke a flowering branch where bees settled humming like the strings a master of the paalai mode plucks, swung it proudly as one swings at an elephant that defies the goad, silenced the loud cries of his band and stood waiting for their word; just then, in a short-posted hut thatched with millet stalks, the field watchman, served honey-pressed toddy by his doe-eyed wife, drank and grew merry, and when the watch slackened an elephant broke into the great field; the watchman, unable to bear the loss, strung his snake-like bow, the whistling men shot arrows and raised a din that rang through the forest, and the maddened elephant, trumpeting like thunder of the rains, striking the ground with its trunk, in fierce musth and breaking trees, came at the girls like Death.
nuance: The watchman's drinking is what lets the elephant in, so the poem makes a small domestic lapse the cause of the meeting that the friend calls களிறுதரு புணர்ச்சி in line 212. மடங்கல் in line 165 may be the lion or Death; either way it is the vehicle of the simile. Lines 151 and 152 can also be read as the girls silencing their own loud companions; the reading here gives the act to the man.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 146-169: the elephant's charge closes with எதிர்தர in line 165; line 166 begins the girls' flight to the man.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet watchman's hut and the wild elephant raiding the field

comparisons.tenor: the man swinging the flowered branch

reading: Not knowing where to escape, the girls, bangles jangling, forgetting shame, ran and clung to him trembling like peacocks seized by a spirit; he drew a long feathered arrow and drove it with great force into the noble elephant's face, so that blood gushed down over it and its spotted brow was torn, and it gave way and turned its back; the girls, still holding hands as tightly as the circle of women possessed by Murugan dancing round the thick trunk of the kadamba, trembled like a plantain on a bank beaten by a foaming flood; the noble man told the girl not to fear, that he would enjoy her beauty, stroked her bright brow, thought long, looked at the friend's face and smiled, and though shame and awe made her pull away at once, he would not let her go but drew her close and embraced her.
nuance: Kapilar sets the love union inside the moment of terror: the girls' clinging to the man for safety becomes the embrace. That he looks at the friend's face and smiles (என்முகம் நோக்கி நக்கனன், line 183) makes the friend a witness, which is why she can now speak to the mother. The comparison to Murugan's possessed women, seized by the god, echoes the rites of lines 5 and 6, where the mother thinks a god has seized the girl.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 146-169, 170-185 and 186-201: the flight and rescue begin at உய்விடம் in line 166 and the sentence closes with the embrace, முயங்கலின், in line 186; அவ்வழி in the same line opens the description of the man's hill.

thinai_evidence.note: the first union of the lovers: punarthal

comparisons.tenor: the girls trembling as they cling to him
the girls holding hands in a ring
the girls' clasped hands that do not part

reading: There, in the long rock pool into which ripe pepper had fallen and sweet mangoes dropped, mixed with honey the birds had scattered, the fragrant jackfruit that burst and fell had ripened into toddy, and a peacock drank it thinking it water and staggered like a rope-dancer at a big town's festival keeping time to a well-matched band, drooping like the goddesses of the hill: such is the slope of the lord of the hill country, whose peaks touching the sky are spread with kaanthal flowers like a field spread with new cloth.
nuance: A peacock drunk on toddy that fruit has made by itself in a rock pool is Kapilar's image of the hill's unasked plenty (Akananuru 2 uses the same rock pool and the same toddy for a monkey). Read as iraicchi it would point to the girl who took joy unplanned, but the peacock does nothing a person of the situation does, so it is scene; the description praises the land of the man the girl has chosen.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 186-201: the description of the man's hill begins after முயங்கலின் in line 186 (அவ்வழி) and closes with its subject குன்றுகெழு நாடன் in line 199; his words begin in line 200.

thinai_evidence.note: the rock pool, kaanthal, jackfruit and peacock of the hill

reading: Understanding the girl's heart, the man of great strength whom they desired assured her, making virtue the raft: 'In a rich house that does not stint those who come, with pots of rice as for a festival and doors opened wide, where many eat rice rich with ghee and fresh fat, it will be fitting for me to eat with you, noble one, what is left after we feed guests with our blameless kin'; then, praising the god on the high peak with joined hands, he swore a binding oath in truth and drank the sweet clear water, and their hearts were at rest; so they spent that day of the union the elephant brought, in the hard cleft, in a flowered grove that even the dwellers of heaven would desire.
nuance: The oath is sworn to the hill god and sealed by drinking water, and its content is a household: he promises a house of open doors and guests, not a feeling. The word for the oath, வஞ்சினம், is the one puram uses for a warrior's vow before battle. களிறுதரு புணர்ச்சி (line 212) names the convention, the union an elephant brings about.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 186-201, 202-213 and 214-233: the man's words begin with உள்ளினன் கொண்டு in line 200, and the day of union closes with அப்பகல் கழிப்பி in line 214; line 215 turns to sunset.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover's oath after the union: kurinji's punarthal and its pledge

comparisons.tenor: the pots of rice in his house
his assurance, on which she could cross her fear

reading: As the day went, the many-rayed sun bowed and hid behind the hill; deer crowded at the foot of trees, cows calling their calves filled the common, the curve-beaked anril cried with a horn's moan in the fronds of the tall palmyra, snakes spat out their gems, cowherds in many places played clear notes on ambal flutes, water lilies opened, women in rich houses lit lamps, brahmins did the evening rite, forest men lit torches on their sky-high watch platforms, the sky darkened round the great hill, the forest roared and flocks of birds cried; seeing the evening hasten on like the battle of an angry king, the man took the girl's forearm and said, 'When your people give her, we will hold a good wedding the whole land will know; for these few days, bright-jewelled ones, do not be troubled.'
nuance: The sunset is drawn with mullai's hour and things, cows to their calves and the cowherd's flute, alongside kurinji's forest men and their torches; the evening is the hour when the lovers must part, and the man answers it with a promise of public marriage (நாடறி நன்மணம்), the first word of வரைவு in the poem. The simile of a king's army advancing is the second puram image the friend uses, after the two kings of line 27.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 214-233: line 214 (அப்பகல் கழிப்பி) closes the day of union and goes with the previous unit; the sunset begins with எல்லை செல்ல in line 215 and the unit still ends at the man's promise in line 233.

thinai_evidence.note: forest men's watch platforms round the great hill; the evening's mullai things are borrowed

reading: Having spoken kind good words in full, he came with them like a bull with its mate, brought them to the drinking ford at the gate of the old town where the drums never sleep, and left; since then, with the same desire as that day, he has made night-coming his habit, and every time he comes, if the guards hurry about, if the fierce dog barks, if you wake, if the moon comes out, never getting sweet sleep on her soft bamboo-like shoulders, he goes back without ever being angry; he has not strayed in youth, nor left his station through wealth; and the girl, thinking of the nature of his secret coming in that dreaded town, consoles herself.
nuance: The friend gives the mother a character witness: the man keeps coming, is turned back by every hindrance and is never angry, and has not lapsed through youth or wealth (lines 243 to 245). The list of hindrances is told to the girl's mother, who is herself one of them (நீ துயில் எழினும).
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 234-249: the account of the man's nightly visits closes with தேற்றி in line 246; line 247 turns to the girl's tears, which the next unit carries to the end of the poem.

reading: Her large bold cloud-dark eyes, drooping like flowers beaten by water, weep and their tears drip on her breast; every day her beauty wastes like a peacock caught in a net, and she weeps whenever she thinks that at night his clustered hill's clefts hold inescapable sorrows: the cave-dwelling tiger, the yali and the bear, the hollow-horned wild cattle and the elephant, the cruel fierce thunder and the spirits, the prey-seeking snake, the crooked-legged crocodile, idangar and karaam that move in the deep whirlpools, the slippery places, the narrow broken paths, the ghouls, the pythons and the rest.
nuance: The poem ends not on the union but on the danger of the night path, which is the friend's strongest argument: the mother cannot keep the girl from the man, only from a marriage, and every night without one sends him through the beasts of lines 252 to 259. The netted peacock of line 250 answers the peacock of line 169: the girl who clung to him for safety is now caught.

title: பட்டினப்பாலை
theme: Pattinappalai is one long sentence: 217 lines on Puhar and the Chola land (the unfailing Kaveri, the port, its trade, its festivals, the virtues of its ploughmen and merchants), the hero's three-line refusal to leave her even for that city, and eighty lines on Karikalan's youth, wars, ruin of enemy lands and founding works, all set up for the closing comparison: the forest is hotter than his spear, her shoulders cooler than his sceptre.
structure_note: The core units were cut mechanically and nearly all break inside the poem's single sentence; all seventeen units here are adjusted to sense breaks (see each unit_note). The colophon's thurai, செலவழுங்குதல், is an akam situation, so the puram units have an empty puram_thurai; only the two units with the hero's own words (218-228 and 292-301) are mixed, with the hero speaking to his heart.
source_issues: Line 175 மிசைச்கூம்பி னசைச்கொடியும்: ச்கூ and ச்கொ are impossible clusters; read மிசைக் கூம்பின் நசைக் கொடியும் (flags on the mast tops). Not changed.
Line 190 பயுனும் is probably a misprint for பயனும் (the produce of the Kaveri). Not changed.
Line 30 வல்லாய்ப் (our text) against tvu வல்வாய்ப்: the sense (strong boats) is the same either way.

Lines 235, 245, 256, 258 and 259 show the comitative -ஒடு printed or joined as -அடு/-ஓ (பூளைய டுழிஞை, அறுகோட் டிரலையொடு, நெருஞ்சியோ டறுகை, கூகையோ டாண்டலை); karu forms are copied as printed, so some carry the joined consonant (டுழிஞை, டிரலையொடு, டறுகை, டாண்டலை).
Line 285 துறந்தை is உறந்தை (Uraiyur) with the preceding consonant joined (மாடத் துறந்தை); the entity name is copied as written.

reading: Even if the bright white star of spotless fame strays from its course and goes south, and the sky fails, withholding rain until the bird that sings for raindrops pines, the Kaveri that comes from the hills does not fail: its flood spreads gold over wide fields that never stop yielding, where the fires of the fragrant cane-presses wither the long neythal of the wet plots, the buffalo calf that ate the ripe paddy sleeps in the joined shade of coconut, plantain, areca, turmeric, mango, palmyra, taro and ginger, and in the wide courtyards women throw their heavy earrings at the fowl pecking the drying grain and so block the path of the boys' little three-wheeled carts; these are the many small towns of the long Chola land, which know no quarrel but that obstruction.
nuance: The praise rests on a guarantee: the river does not fail even when the sky does (வான்பொய்ப்பினும் தான்பொய்யா), though line 6 admits the river comes from the hills. The villages' only 'enmity' is a pun: விலங்கு is the earring obstructing a toy cart, set against கலங்கு பகை, the hostility that troubles a people.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 1-15 and 16-31: the buffalo calf of line 15 sleeps in the shade of the trees listed in lines 16 to 19, and the description of the villages closes with நெடுஞ்சோணாட்டு, line 28.

thinai_evidence.note: the unit praises the Chola land that the Kaveri keeps fertile; no love situation is stated

reading: Boats that sold white salt and came back with paddy are tied at their posts like horses in a stall; groves and cool gardens ring the backwaters; near the high temple of fearsome power lie twin lakes bright with flowers, like the moon joined with a white star in a rainless sky; the gates bear the tiger emblem and a strong guard where fortune sleeps; and in the wide alms-kitchen where fame is fixed and dharma is kept, the rich rice-water poured off the cooked rice flows like a river, is churned to mud by fighting bulls and dried to dust by running chariots, so that it soils the white painted temple like an elephant that has rolled in dust.
nuance: The charity is measured by its dirt: the alms-house's surplus rice-water becomes the mud and dust that soil the temples. Lines 34 to 39 are hard to construe; the moon-and-star image may describe the lakes or the temple tank, so the comparison is offered as one reading.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 16-31, 32-48 and 49-64: the boats of lines 29 to 31 begin a new scene after the villages end at line 28, and the simile of line 48 (நீறாடிய களிறுபோல) is completed by the soiled white temple of line 50.

thinai_evidence.note: the unit praises the port's trade, gardens and charity; no love situation is stated

reading: Beyond courtyards with cool wells and many halls, in the low groves of the hermitages where sages with shining matted hair tend the sacred fire, the cuckoo, shunning the fragrant smoke of the oblations, flies off with its dark mate and goes to roost with the pebble-eating doves in the eaves of the hard-to-enter guarded shrine that spirits watch over.
nuance: The birds keep the city's order too: the cuckoo driven off by the sacrificial smoke does not leave the city but lodges with the doves in the spirit-guarded shrine. பகட்டெருத்தின் பலசாலை (line 52) is unclear: halls for bulls, or halls of the bull-necked.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 49-64: lines 51 to 58 are one scene of the halls and hermitages, closed by the cuckoo that lodges with the doves (சேக்கும், line 58); line 59 begins the fishermen's ground.

thinai_evidence.note: a description of the city's halls and hermitages inside the praise

reading: On the sandy mounds of the wrestling ground under old trees, the fishermen of rough work and many kin eat roasted prawns and boiled field tortoise, wear the flowers of the dry-sand adumbu creeper and the water lily, gather in the open common like planets moving among the stars of the dark-blue sky, and grapple with hands and with weapons, the strong ones of fierce fight never turning their backs in their great anger.
nuance: The fight is play, but the poet gives it the war-ethic of never turning the back (புறக்கொடாஅது), the phrase the poem gives Karikalan's warriors in line 290.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 49-64 and 65-79: the fishermen's ground begins at line 59 after the cuckoo scene closes at line 58; the unit ends at line 72 with the fighters who never turn back, before the sling stones and the outer quarter that begin in line 73.

thinai_evidence.note: the fishermen's feasting and play-fighting, described as part of the city

reading: Where birds scatter in fear of the stones flung from slings, by the spotted palmyras, in the outer quarter of ring wells with piglets and fowl, rams play with quails; among the short-roofed homes the long fishing rods stand ranged like the shields and planted spears that fence a hero-stone, and the nets dry on the sandy yards like darkness lodged in moonlight; women wearing cool garlands of white koothaalam from under the hanging thazhai honour the strong goddess they have set in the house by planting a pregnant shark's horn, and on the full-moon day the fishermen, with their women in green leaf skirts, wear thazhai flowers, drink pressed palm toddy and do not go hunting on the wide cold sea, but rest, eat and play.
nuance: The hero-stone, the memorial of a fallen warrior with its shield and spear, appears here only as a picture of stacked fishing gear; that the tenor is the rods of line 80 is my construal of a sentence that runs across the line.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 65-79 and 80-95: the hero-stone simile of line 79 (நடுகல்லின் அரண்போல) has its tenor in the fishing rods of lines 80 and 81, so the fishermen's quarter is kept whole from the sling stones of line 73 to the full-moon holiday that ends at உண்டாடியும், line 93.

reading: On the flowered shore whose sand smells of fish, at the loud meeting of the tides where the river joins the clear sea as a cloud rests on a great hill and as a child clasps its mother's breast, people bathe in the sea to put away sin and in the river to wash off dirt, chase crabs, tread the strong waves, play around sand dolls and marvel at many sights, playing all day in unwavering love; at the great flowered ford of unfailing custom, which is like the ancient heaven hard to reach, young women with their partners put off silk for cotton and wine for mead, the women wear the men's chaplets and the men the women's garlands.
nuance: Lovers appear here only as part of the city's festival, with no speaker or situation; yet the exchange of garlands and the comparison of the ford to heaven prepare the hero's choice in line 218, where even such a city weighs less than her.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 80-95 and 96-110: the shore scene begins at புலவுமணற் பூங்கானல் (line 94), whose two similes in lines 95 and 96 describe the river meeting the sea, and the day's play ends with the exchange of garlands in line 110.

reading: At night they watch the bright fires on the tall-pillared mansions while fishermen in their curved boats count the coloured lights, listen to songs, enjoy plays and take the pleasure of the white moonlight, and at the end of the night, when eyes close, they sleep on the clean sand dunes where the great Kaveri mingles with the sea.
nuance: The fishermen count the mansion lamps from the sea (குரூஉச்சுடர் எண்ணவும்): the city's lights serve as their landmark.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 111-126: lines 111 to 117 are the night's pleasures, ending with sleep on the sand dunes (துயில் மடிந்து, line 117); line 118 turns to the customs officers of the sea street.

reading: In the wide street by the sea lined with white-clustered thazhai, the customs men of ancient fame who guard the good king's revenue work every day without tiring, like the horses yoked to the chariot of the hot-rayed sun, and levy duty without shortfall; as in the rainy season, when water the sky has drawn up pours on the hills and the hills pour it to the sea, goods are landed from the sea and shipped from the land; countless goods without limit pile up, the strong officer of the hard guard stamps them with the tiger and sends them out, and on the heaps of bales the sharp-clawed male dog leaps with the ram in the yards like mountain goats skipping on the cloud-washed slopes of a great hill.
nuance: The water-cycle simile makes trade a natural circulation: goods go from sea to land and land to sea as rain goes from sky to hill to sea. The tiger stamp (புலிபொறித்து) is the Chola seal on dutiable goods.

reading: Past the yards stand houses with short-runged tall ladders, curved verandas, many-doored rooms, small gates and passages, and mansions so high they touch the clouds; there women with red feet, close thighs, green jewels, broad hips, silk at the waist, coral-red bodies, the gait of peacocks, the looks of deer, the prattle of parrots and gentle softness stand at the windows where the wind enters and join in worship of red Murugan their bangled forearms, which are like the bent clusters of kaanthal on a high hillside where fine pollen settles, and crowd close with the women who dance the veri, while the flute calls, the lute hums, the drum throbs and the great drum booms in the wide bazaar that never lacks a festival.
nuance: The kaanthal, a kurinji flower, and the veri rite of the hills are brought into the port: the women of the mansions worship the hill god in the city's bazaar.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 140-153 and 154-168: the houses and their women (lines 142 to 155) are one description with the women's worship and the festival bazaar, which closes at விழவறா வியலாவணத்து, line 158; the catalogue of flags begins in line 159.

reading: Over the city fly flags of many kinds: at the flower-decked doorway of the shrine where the flawless god is installed, worshipped by many; over the shops with granaries of grain and locked stores of cool goods, where white rice is strewn as offering on floors fresh-smeared with syrup, cloth flags on poles above bent screens, bright as the flower of the fearsome reed on a forest stream's white sand; the flags raised in challenge by good teachers of ancient authority who have mastered many branches of learning; the swaying flags on the masts of the ships crowded at the wave-washed ford of sweet Puhar, which rock like an elephant shaking its tethering post; the flags of the toddy sellers, in yards loud with frying fish and flesh, where sand is heaped and flowers strewn at the offering doors of houses that many enter; and so many other banners of every shape mingle that in their shade the sun's rays cannot enter the rich city, guarded by gods of undying fame.
nuance: The flags sort the city by its institutions: shrine, trade, learning in debate (உறழ்குறித் தெடுத்த, flags raised as a challenge), the port and the toddy shop. Line 175 is corrupt in our text.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 154-168 and 169-185: the catalogue of flags runs from the temple flag of line 160 (begun by தெய்வஞ் சேர்த்திய, line 159) to the banner shade the sun cannot enter (lines 182 to 184); line 185 begins the list of imports.

reading: Horses of lofty gait brought by sea, sacks of black pepper brought by land, gems and gold born in the northern mountain, sandal and agil born in the western mountain, pearls of the southern sea and coral of the eastern sea, the yield of the Ganges and the produce of the Kaveri, food from Eelam and goods from Kalakam: rare things and great things crowd together in the wide streets where riches lie heaped and mingled.
nuance: The list is built by the four directions (north, west, south, east), then two rivers, then two overseas lands, so the city is shown as the point where the whole known world's goods meet. காலின் வந்த (line 186) may mean 'by land' or 'by the wind', that is by sailing ship.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 169-185 and 186-201: the list of goods from every quarter runs from the horses of line 185 to the crowded streets of line 193 (நனந்தலை மறுகின்); line 194 begins the safety of creatures on water and land.

reading: In water and on land creatures sleep safe and content, their kin thriving, heedless of enemies, so that fish leap in the fishermen's yards and beasts crowd at the meat-sellers' huts; for the ploughmen of the bent plough, whose cool-shaded life never lacks merit, have banned killing and put away theft, tend the gods and feed the sacrificial fire, keep good cows and oxen, spread the fame of the four-Veda brahmins, give cooked food and fresh provisions; and the merchants, fair-minded like the pin at the middle of those ploughmen's long yoke, fearing blame speak the truth, weigh their own goods and others' alike, take no more than is due and give no less, and sell many goods in the crowded mart of ancient riches; there, as kin of wise speech from many towns each raised in its own way gather at an old town holding its festival, people come from other lands, speaking many tongues, live mingled happily in this blameless country.
nuance: The safety of fish at the fishermen's door and beasts at the meat-sellers' hut is the measure of the ban on killing, though the same city fries fish and flesh in lines 176 and 177. I take lines 199 to 204 as the ploughmen's virtues and lines 207 to 212 as the merchants', with the ploughman's yoke-pin as the simile between them; the sentence can also be read as one class throughout.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 186-201 and 202-217: lines 194 to 217 are one sentence, from the creatures sleeping safe because killing is banned (lines 194 to 199), through the ploughmen's merit and the merchants' fair trade, to the foreigners who live in the city (line 217), the last line of the city's description before பட்டினம் in line 218.

comparisons.tenor: the foreigners living mingled in the city

reading: Even if I were given this city of unfailing glory, I will not come away leaving her of the long dark hair and bright jewels, my heart, long may you live; and the praise of the king begins: like a fierce-striped, sharp-clawed tiger cub growing up in a cage, he grew to full strength while held in others' bonds, and as a great-handed elephant whose tusks have grown breaks the hard bank of the pit, destroys the pit and goes to its cow, he planned with subtle care, climbed his foes' strong guarded wall, drew his sword and in due course gained his fearsome inheritance, yet did not rest content with what he had gained.
nuance: This is the poem's only statement of the love situation, and it comes after 217 lines of the city: the weight of 'even if I got Puhar' is built before it is spoken. The caged tiger cub and the elephant breaking its pit picture the king's own captivity and escape, which the poem states only through images (பிறர் பிணியகத் திருந்து).
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 218-233: the hero's refusal (lines 218 to 220) opens the praise of Karikalan, and the account of his youth, escape and accession ends with பெற்றவை மகிழ்தல் செய்யான் in line 228; the war that follows (செற்றோர் கடியரண் தொலைத்த, lines 228 and 229) begins the next unit.
