reading: His tall elephants, whose tusks broke the doors of his enemies' guarded forts, whose forefeet roll crowned dark heads and whose feet bear claws, fall with horses of polished bells and with warriors, and kites wheel in the great sky; eager for war, his men wear uzhinai mixed with many kinds of poolai, like a boulder overgrown with bush; with the drum of fearsome roar, its eyes like a demon's, booming on its wide face, he goes and wrecks the enemy front, crushes the vanguard, presses deep and lays waste the cool fields: white-flowered reeds grow tall with the paddy, kuvalai with dark petals tangles with neythal in the wide pond full of crocodiles, cherunthi grows tall at the sluices, fields and pools merge dry and the stag with fine horns frolics with its doe; and in the public hall with its sacred post, where captive women once bathed at the drinking ford and climbed to the flower-decked floor lit at dusk with unfailing lamps and worshipped by many, where travellers lodged, the great elephant lives with its cow, rubbing the thick tall pillar until it sways.
nuance: The pairs that akam poems use for tender implication, the stag with its doe and the elephant with its cow, here only show that the enemy's fields and halls have gone wild. The hall's post (கந்து) and worship (பலர்தொழ) mark it as a shrine, now a stable for wild elephants.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 218-233 and 234-251: the war begins with the enemies' forts in lines 228 and 229 (செற்றோர் கடியரண் தொலைத்த) and runs through the march to the wasted fields, which close with the elephant and its cow in the deserted hall, line 251; the boulder simile of line 234 belongs with the warriors of lines 232 and 233.

thinai_evidence.note: the march into enemy land and the wasting of its fields; the uzhinai worn for the siege is part of the same campaign

comparisons.tenor: the warriors decked with uzhinai and poolai
the faces of the war drum

reading: In the common where costly fragrant flowers were once strewn and old bards of wise speech listened with their drums to the sweet strings of the twisted lute, now that the great festivals are over and fear has grown, small-flowered nerunji and arukai grass spread, the fire-mouthed jackal howls fearfully, the owl of weeping cry and the aandalai call, and corpse-eating demon women crowd with hosts of goblins, loosing their hair; in the rich houses with bright walls and high seats where green parrots prattled, where guests crowded the long gates of curved-pillared mansions to eat from kitchens whose great rice never ran out, the hook-beaked owl hoots at broad noon from inside the empty granary that bow-bent hunters, gathered to the beat of the thudi, have looted; so he undoes the beauty of hard-guarded towns, and is not satisfied even with making a great waste.
nuance: The ruined common is the reverse of the festival commons of Puhar earlier in the poem (lines 69 and 158), with the same lute, drum, flowers and feasting named as gone; the owl hooting at broad noon is the sign that the order of day and night has failed.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 252-271: the ruined commons and houses end with பெரும்பாழ் செய்தும் அமையான் in line 270; the hyperbole that follows (மலையகழ்க் குவனே... வளிமாற் றுவனென, lines 271 and 272) belongs with the next unit.

thinai_evidence.note: the ruin of the enemy's towns, told as the king's deed

reading: He would dig out the hills, fill up the sea, bring down the sky and turn back the wind, they say, as he goes the way he has resolved: the Oliyar bow and shrink, the ancient Aruvalar heed his command, the northerners wilt, the westerners droop, the Pandya's strength is broken by his anger; with strong legs that seize the forts of kings, great might and martial power, glaring with red eyes he ends the line of the petty herdsmen and brings down Irungovel's house, clears forests and makes them country, digs tanks and increases wealth, extends Uraiyur of towering mansions, settles people with temples, builds gates and posterns, sets cover on every battlement, and holds the great fortress where fortune dwells, its men having given their names saying 'we will fight' and never turning back saying 'we are only one'.
nuance: The king is praised as destroyer and founder in one sentence: the same man who wastes the enemy's land clears forest into country and digs tanks. போக்கி (line 285) may mean that he extended Uraiyur or that he left it; ஞாயிறொறும் (line 288) is read as ஞாயில் தொறும், 'at every battlement'.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 252-271, 272-287 and 288-301: the hyperbole of lines 271 and 272 is completed by எனத் in line 272 and introduces the conquests, so this unit starts at 271; the conquests and founding works end with the great fortress, திருநிலைஇய பெருமன் னெயில், line 291, before the court scene of line 292.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's victories over many peoples and his founding works

reading: Where kings, their own lustre dimmed as his flashes like lightning, bow until the fresh gems of their crowns rub the anklets on his strong thick legs, where sons with golden bracelets run and play and women in full jewels press their budding breasts against his chest, whose bright ornaments lie on red sandal paste smeared and spoiled, Thirumavalavan of fearsome strength like a lion: the forest is hotter than the spear he raised against his foes, and her broad soft shoulders are cooler than his sceptre.
nuance: The whole eighty-line praise of Karikalan has been the first half of a double comparison: his spear (to enemies) and his sceptre (to his people) become the measures of the forest's heat and of her coolness, so the puram matter ends as the lover's reason for staying. The king is named only here, in line 299.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 288-301: the founding works end with the fortress in line 291; lines 292 to 301 are the court scene and the closing comparison, which ends the poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the hot forest of the journey is weighed against her cool shoulders, the separation given up

title: மலைபடுகடாம் (1/2)
theme: The first half of Malaipadukadam: a bard who has been rewarded by Nannan addresses another troupe through its drums, pipes and great lute, praises Nannan son of Nannan and promises to tell of his land, lists the out-of-season harvest of his hills, promises the hunters' feasts and welcome, and then guides the troupe stage by stage along the dangerous hill road, with rules for sacred places, rivers, forests and night, until it rests and hears the many sounds of the hill.
structure_note: Seventeen of the eighteen core units were cut mid-sentence or mid-description and are adjusted to the poem's sense breaks (address 1-50, praise 51-94, harvest 95-144, feasts 145-188, road 189-291, sounds from 287); 95-113 and 189-199 are kept as cut. The last unit runs past the chapter's end at line 307 into the next chapter's catalogue.
source_issues: Line 68 சுரக்குஅவ நாடுபடு and line 72 சுரக்கும்அவ நீகை have faulty word division (சுரக்கும் அவன் நாடுபடு, சுரக்கும் அவன் ஈகை), as flagged; line 76 சுரக்குமவ நாள்மகி ழிருக்கையும் has the same fault (சுரக்கும் அவன் நாள்மகிழ் இருக்கையும?) and is not flagged.
Line 83 காரிஉண்டிக் கட வுள தியற்கையும் has a stray space inside கடவுள்; the karu form is taken from the unbroken word காரிஉண்டிக்.
Line 267 குறியறிக் தவையவை looks like a misprint for குறியறிந்து அவையவை.
Line 306 மலைமா ரிடூஉம் is hard to construe and may be corrupt.
Core unit boundaries at lines 18, 32, 53, 69, 127, 156, 172, 215, 233, 254, 275 and 291 fall mid-sentence; seventeen units are adjusted (see structure_note).

reading: The poem opens by addressing a bard through the gear his troupe carries, a drum tuned to the thunder of a dark rain-filled sky, a small drum, bright cymbals, a horn dressed with peacock feather, pipes that cry like an elephant, a sweet flute, a clapper and drums of many beats, packed in bags that hang like clusters of jackfruit, as the troupe climbs a rocky hill by a path as steep as a raised wall, where forest bowmen walking with their mates guide travellers without harm, and goes on over the high ridge heedless of its dangers.
nuance: The bard is named by his equipment, not his person, so the troupe's craft is what qualifies it for the road and the gift; the bowmen of lines 17 and 18, who guide travellers without harm, are the first of the poem's hill folk, and they help rather than threaten.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 1-18 and 19-32: the climb that begins at line 14 runs to line 20 (இயவுக்கொண் டொழுகி), and line 21 begins the description of the great lute.

thinai_evidence.note: the speaker addresses a travelling troupe by its instruments; no love situation

comparisons.tenor: the tuned sound of the drum
the flat rocks of the slope

reading: The troupe's great lute is described part by part: frets bound like twisted bangles, strings tuned by ear and rubbed clean, sound-holes as fine as an ear of millet, a bowl fitted with paste and pegs, a new white handle and a fresh cover that gleams like gold and lies like the line of soft hair on the lovely belly of a bride whose hair still smells of the wedding, its body dark as the kalam fruit and its neck curving up.
nuance: The bride of lines 30 to 32 exists only to give the look of the lute's leather; Porunaratruppadai covers its lute with the same picture of a hair-line on a woman's belly, so the image reads as the bards' set way of describing their own instrument.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 19-32 and 33-53: the lute is one noun phrase from line 21 to its head word பேரியாழ் in line 37.

thinai_evidence.note: a description of the bard's instrument inside the address

comparisons.vehicle: மடந்தை மாண்ட நுடங்கெழில் ஆகத்து அடங்குமயிர் ஒழுகிய அவ்வாய்
comparisons.tenor: the seam of the lute's cover

reading: Tuned in its proper mode and fit for the assembly of famous kings, the lute goes with bards who have mastered many forms, and around the leader stand the bright-bangled women dancers, their small feet worn on the hill's rocks till they are as red as the tongue of a spent hunting dog, resting with their hair let down like a flock of peacocks in a shade as cool as stepping into a pond, on a stretch of sand the stream has washed: so the speaker names the leader of the kin of performers who are given vessels as gifts.
nuance: The vessels in line 50 (கலம்பெறு) are the troupe's title: they are named by what patrons give them, so the address already assumes the gift the poem will promise.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 33-53: line 38 begins the tuning, after the lute's description closes at line 37; the address ends at line 50 with தலைவ, and lines 51 to 53 open the sentence completed in the next unit.

thinai_evidence.note: the address to the leader of a troupe that seeks gifts

reading: As a good river with flower-heaped banks runs down to the sea, the speaker says, so we come from him, and you too, if you go with your mind on Nannan son of Nannan like a flock of birds flying fast to feed with their kin in a forest dropping fruit, go to a garlanded, bee-haunted chest, the husband of women with flower-like eyes, whose strength lays waste the enemy's front, who comes like a new flood to the farmers who sow the seed of praise, whose counsel never errs and whose great arm is skilled with the bow, and then you are birds that have met the right hour.
nuance: Lines 60 and 61 make the poets farmers who sow praise and the patron the flood that fills their fields, so the gift is pictured as the harvest of the poet's own work rather than as charity; and in lines 65 and 66 the seekers' mere intention makes them birds of good omen.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 33-53 and 54-69: the sentence that begins with the river simile at line 51 runs to the omen of lines 65 and 66 (புள்ளினிர் மன்ற); line 67 begins the list of what the speaker will tell.

thinai_evidence.note: the speaker directs the troupe to the patron and praises him

comparisons.tenor: the troupe's coming from the patron

comparisons.vehicle: கனிபொழி கானம் கிளையொ டுணீஇய துனைபறை நிவக்கும் புள்ளின

comparisons.tenor: the poets who live by praise
the seekers as birds of good omen

reading: The speaker announces what the seeker is to hear: the length of the roads, the good places to rest, the foods of the land, its hills, groves and forests full of beasts; then the patron's fame that will stand as long as the world, the treasures he takes from those whose backs he has seen and pours like rain on poets, the strength that binds his scorners and the look that thinks nothing enough though he gave his whole kingdom to those who praise him, his daily court of joy that never fails, like a true sky pouring clean rain, the way his men in the assembly of the learned cover the failings of the unskilled and set them forth well, the nature of the god of the famous Naviram hill who ate the dark poison, his own faultless glory like the sun that rises to make the day, the line of his ancestors who conquered distant enemies and paid the debt of giving to poets, and the old town with a rock-cut moat where crocodiles hunt and walls as high as hills.
nuance: Lines 77 to 80 are the poem's one view of the court from the side of the performer who fails: the patron's men cover for the unskilled and present them well, which tells the seeker the gift does not wait on a flawless performance.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 54-69 and 70-94: lines 67 to 94 are one catalogue of the things to be told, closed by கேளினி ... முன்னிய திசையே in line 94.

thinai_evidence.note: a catalogue of the patron's land, fame, giving, court, god and town

reading: Of the patron's rich land the speaker says a new season has come, and this is its nature: the sky flashed and rained without stint and all that was sown grew as hoped, so that on the wide wet hill fields the musundai creeper opened white like stars across the dark sky, the sown plots were blue as sapphire, the pools brimmed like pots, the sesame pods ran full of oil, the millet heads bent ready to pluck like the curling trunk of an elephant calf, the bean vines hung their cold pods, and the great fields of varagu, among rocks that lie like buffaloes, bowed their forked ears to the iron sickle.
nuance: The harvest is the first proof of the patron's rule: plenty is shown before the gift itself; வாதிகை (line 112) is a rare word and the vehicle of that simile is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the plenty of the patron's land, as a sign of his rule

reading: The list goes on: white hill paddy ripened in the wind, its stalks milky; sugarcane, tossed like a routed band of spearmen, bends and goes sweet to the press; thorai rice ripens in the flowered field after the rains; mustard thrives in the fields where blue lilies spread dark and fragrant; ginger and turmeric grow to their full beauty; and the rich yam vines have sunk into every pit like the knees of a pregnant she-elephant.
nuance: Lines 116 to 118 (the routed spearmen) and 125 to 126 (செய்யாப் பாவை, இஞ்சிமா) can be divided more than one way, so which crop each simile describes is not certain.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 114-127 and 128-144: the simile of line 127 (வயவுப்பிடி முழந்தாள் கடுப்ப) is completed by the yam vines of line 128.

thinai_evidence.note: the crops of the patron's land

reading: The fruit of the hills follows: the plantain round the boulders, its bud thrust out like a spear driven into an elephant's face, ripens in tight bunches; the great bamboo sways on the wide rocks; because the trees give fruit even out of season, black jambu fruit falls in the wind, the uyavai creeper runs with water, arrowroot clusters, sweet mangoes are too many for those who eat, breadfruit sheds its seeds, and on the high slope where the owl calls like a small drum struck with a finger, the jackfruit, rained on above and below, hangs heavy from swaying boughs like the drums of wandering players.
nuance: Line 134 gives the reason for the whole catalogue: the trees here give fruit out of their season, so the land's plenty is more than nature's.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 128-144: the unit now begins at line 129, since line 128 closes the yam simile of the unit before.

thinai_evidence.note: the fruit of the patron's hills

reading: On the great hill slope, where a dull-backed hawk snatched up the new bud of a fire-bright kanthal, taking it for meat, and dropped it when it proved no flesh, where the petals lie strewn like fire on every rock as if it were the ground of the veri rite and the slope smells like a wedding house, the speaker promises that if the troupe reaches the rich small village of the hunters, who carry honey, roots and baskets of meat, drive off the small-eyed boar and carry their loads on poles of tusks from elephants killed in fight, they will get food in plenty with all their kin.
nuance: The hawk that drops the flower once it finds it is not flesh is a comic picture of the hill's plenty, where even the birds are fooled; the veri ground of line 150 brings Murugan's rite into the guide only as an image of colour.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 145-156 and 157-172: the promise closes at line 157 with பெறுகுவிர்.

thinai_evidence.note: the promise of food at the hunters' village on the road

comparisons.tenor: the kanthal bud the hawk takes

reading: Staying there that day and resting the night, the troupe, wearing bright clusters of flowers with their kin, is to go on by the path of the red asoka trees to the hamlet on the slope where swaying bamboo creaks, and if they say they are musicians of the victorious Vel, the people will take them in as if it were their own house, embrace them as kin without asking who they are, speak sweet words to end the loneliness of a far country, and give them thick cuts of meat cooked in ghee and heaps of rice.
nuance: The welcome is opened by a name: the strangers are taken in as kin, unasked, once they say they are the Vel's musicians (lines 163 and 164), so the hill people's hospitality is part of the patron's reach and not only their own custom.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 157-172: line 158 begins the next stage of the road (அன்றவ ணசைஇ), and the welcome closes at line 169 with பெறுகுவிர்.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill people's welcome to the patron's musicians

reading: With the hill's goods that the hunters climb up to fetch, the people will give the troupe honey-wine ripened in bamboo to drink without stint, and at dawn, to clear last night's heaviness, a meal of white grains the waterfall brought, fat cuts of sambar deer, slabs of porcupine fat and meat the hound ran down, cooked with sweet tamarind and buttermilk, bamboo rice stirred until the slope smells of it, and the white rice cooked by the hill woman with flowers in her hair; house after house will press it on them with full-hearted joy, holding them back as kin, so that they may stay long and even forget the gift they set out to ask of the warrior lord, for his hill country is more than this.
nuance: Lines 186 to 188 turn the promise round: the danger here is not hardship but too much welcome, for the seeker may forget the gift; the next unit duly tells him not to stay many days. The closing அனைய தன்று may also be read as 'his hill country is not like that', a warning rather than a boast.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 157-172 and 173-188: the second meal begins at line 170 with the goods the hunters bring and ends at line 188 (மலைமிசை நாடே).

thinai_evidence.note: the feast on the road, so rich it may make the seeker forget the gift

reading: If the troupe so much as touches the fragrant blossom of the tiered kuvalai or sees the haunt of the hill goddesses, they may burn and shiver as if life were leaving, so they are not to stay many days but go on toward the plains; because the ripe fields are being raided, heavy stone traps are set for boars at every gap, so they should stop at midnight and go on at dawn, and if they choose a path few people use, there are pits in the broken gravel where snakes hide.
nuance: The first warnings are about sacred ground, not beasts: the flower and the dwelling belong to the hill's goddesses, and to touch or look brings the fever of possession (பனித்தல், line 191).

thinai_evidence.note: warnings for the road through the patron's hills

reading: At the tree marked as sacred the troupe is to look, knock and, while the dancers fold their hands and praise, circle it on the right without idly leaving the path; and where hill farmers on high platforms clap their hands and sling stones to stop the elephants from lingering by day in the thicket, stones that skip off the great wet bamboo so that the black-fingered monkey flees with its young and that come with the force of Death, they must pass under the cover of the trees.
nuance: The rite of lines 200 to 202 turns on rare forms (மரங் கொட்டி, வலஞ்செயா); வலஞ்செயா is read here as the old participle 'having circled to the right', parallel to மரமறையா in line 210, but it could be a negative, 'without circling'.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 200-215: the sling-stone warning closes at line 210 (மரமறையாக் கழிமின்).

thinai_evidence.note: rules for passing a sacred tree and the farmers' sling stones

reading: Where the forest river runs like a moat through a gorge dark as night, with whirling pools where crocodiles lurk that can hide even a strong elephant, the troupe is to keep from slipping, hold on to the thick creepers that twine the tree trunks and cross one by one, each guarding the other, with their small children whose heads are tufted like a sheep's; and by the deep pools of the slope, where those who fall sink and die and fine moss over the stones makes the foot slide, they must take staves of thin reed and soft cane and go on.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 200-215 and 216-233: the river crossing begins at line 211, and its two warnings close at lines 218 and 224 with கழிமின்.

thinai_evidence.note: rules for crossing the forest river

reading: Where arrows from bows pour like rain over the spotted face of the high rock, where garlanded elephants trained for work stand and the pool of bright flowers is adorned like an elephant's brow, if the troupe sees the god of ancient worship at the old walls by the lone river's course, they are not to pass without bowing to him, and they must not strike their instruments idly, for such is the patron's rich hill, where the rain falls thick.
nuance: The rule of lines 231 and 232 concerns the bards' own craft: before the god they must bow, and they must not sound their instruments idly, so the music that wins the gift is not to be spent carelessly on the road. Lines 225 to 228 are hard to construe; ஓரியாற்று (229) may be 'the lone river' or a river named for Ori.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 216-233: the shrine is one warning from line 225 to the close of line 233 (மல்லல் வெற்பே).

thinai_evidence.note: the rule for passing the hill god's shrine

reading: Even if a peacock with its eyed train falters at its nest, a male monkey leaps on the long bamboo like the children of drum-beating players, or beehives hang like a wheel on the cliff the goddesses love, the troupe is not to gape at them, for walking in a line they will lose the path; and if in the forest they find a boar that a watchman's arrow has killed, black as a cut of darkness, its fat white as ghee, lying across the path with its tusks in the earth, they may roast it in a fire of rubbed dry bamboo and eat, drink at the clear kuvalai pool, pack what is left, and, rather than travel by night with their small children, shelter in a rock cave as if going into a house.
nuance: The things not to gape at are each a wonder of the hill, and the cliff of the beehives is the goddesses' (சூர்புகல்), so the warning is both practical and sacred. அலகை (234) is unclear as the vehicle for the feathers.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 234-254 and 255-275: the forest passage ends with the shelter in the cave at line 255 (வதிமின்).

thinai_evidence.note: rules for the forest stretch of the road

reading: Not wearing themselves out by night, the troupe is to rise at dawn and take the straight forest path, avoiding the python that lies like a sleeping tree with a pond-wide mouth that crushes a raging elephant's strength, and the flowers whose scent carries far, the fruit too sweet for those who eat it to forget, and the clumps of great dark-stemmed trees, which the hill people never approach even when their season is past and their yield falls unused; looking left and right and knowing their signs, they are to pass these by, and move away slowly from the wide land where the birds' voices join like a crowd in a many-branched banyan.
nuance: Lines 262 to 267 warn against things good in themselves, fragrant flowers and unforgettable fruit, that the people of the hill will not touch even when they fall unused: the guide's knowledge is of forbidden plenty, and the rule is to read the signs (குறி) rather than trust appetite. Line 263 (மறந்தமை கல்லா) can also be read of fruit that makes the eater forget.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 255-275: the dawn departure begins at line 256, and the forest warnings close at line 270 (மென்மெல அகன்மின்).

thinai_evidence.note: rules for the dawn stretch of the road

reading: If the troupe comes into the hill where even the hill farmers lose their way, a dark thicket of trees in deep shade that the sun does not burn, where bowmen circle searching for game, they are not to scatter noisily over the wide rocks but gather and sound their instruments, for on the high slopes of the singing waterfalls live hunters who guard the forest, and they, like men running at the cry of people swept from a ford by the flood, will come quickly, show them fruit sweet to eat and flowers good to wear, and lead them ahead along the dangerous way, so that the grief in their hearts ends and they and their kin are glad.
nuance: The instruments the troupe was told not to strike idly at the shrine (line 232) are here its signal for help: on this road the bards' music is how they are found.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 255-275 and 276-291: the danger of losing the way (line 271) is answered by the hunters' rescue, which closes at line 286 (இனியிர் ஆகுவிர்).

thinai_evidence.note: the hunters who rescue lost travellers in the patron's hills

reading: Following the directions the knowing have given and going down the short and tall slopes in turn, on a cliff so steep that strangers shiver to look at it, if the troupe rests in the striped shade where flowers have fallen, it will hear many kinds of sound: in every quarter, where the whole hill smells of great fruit that the stag has touched oozing from their wounds, the sweet sound, like their own instruments, of the celestial women bathing in the falls; the uproar of conch-bangled women when a lone tusker strays from its herd and eats the hunters' platform field; the weeping of hunters who slipped while shooting a porcupine in its far cave; the song that the hill women with sand-dark hair sing as a guard to soothe the long deep wound a tiger tore on their husbands' chests; the protective shout raised at the golden vengai that flowered on the first day; and, as the chapter ends, the young soft-headed she-elephant caught in a pit.
nuance: The catalogue sets the goddesses' bathing beside the hunters' weeping and the wives' song over tiger wounds, all as sound offered to musicians; the wives' song (lines 302 to 304) is called காப்பு, a guarding rite, the same rite of song over a wound that Purananuru 281 performs for a warrior.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 276-291 and 292-307: line 287 begins the rest in the shade that introduces the catalogue of sounds (கேட்குவிர், line 291), which runs from line 292 past the chapter's end at line 307.

thinai_evidence.note: the sounds of the patron's hill heard on the road

title: மலைபடுகடாம் (2/2)
theme: The second half of Malaipadukadam takes the bards from the patron's mountain, whose countless sounds make the 'resonance of the mountain', down its dangerous roads and through the hospitality of herders, bowmen, farmers and fishers to Nannan's town and court, where his welcome, his reflection that only fame outlives death, and his gifts close the poem on his title.
structure_note: The chapter is one continuous instruction: a list of sounds closing on மலைபடு கடாஅம் (348), the road with its hazards and hosts, each stage ending in கழிமின் (go on) or பெறுகுவிர் (you will get), then the town, the court, and the parting. Every core unit except 352-372, 373-389 and 390-402 was moved to a sentence or item break, giving 18 units.
source_issues: Line 407 தலையிரும்பு: tvu reads தலையிறும்பு (into the thicket), which suits the bull's flight better; our reading is kept, as flagged.
Line 481 செருவிற் சாறென follows யாறெனக் கிடந்த, which would more naturally describe தெருவின் (streets); the text may have செரு for தெரு. Marked as read.
Line 540 குன்றா நல்லிசைக் சென்றோர் has க் before ச், an irregular doubling (expected நல்லிசைச் சென்றோர்).
Line 515 prints நுகமரு ணூறை with the word boundary moved by sandhi (நுகமருள் நூறை); the karu form is copied as printed.

reading: The catalogue of the hill's sounds goes on: the thunderous roar that the herd sends echoing along the high slope when a bright, strong tiger springs; the endless wailing of a troop of leaf-eating monkeys crowding round when a black-fingered mother loses her grip and her untaught young falls into a deep cleft; the glee of the forest men who, by a ladder fixed up a cliff no stag can climb, have taken a great haul of honey and, having broken a hard stronghold, say it will serve as guest-tribute for their lord of the shapely spear; and the kuravai the hill men dance with their women on the sky-touching heights after a day of brewing toddy, to the beat of the small deer-skin drum.
nuance: Line 308 closes a clause begun in the previous chapter (a mate who guards, the limit of strength). Every item here is a noun of sound (தழங்குகுரல், பூசல், உவகை's shout, குரவை), all of them subjects waiting for the verb இயம்ப in line 348: the idyll's title, the 'resonance born of the mountain', is this whole inventory. The forest men's honey and fort-spoil are reserved as tribute for the lord before they are enjoyed.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 308-321: line 322 (வான்றோய் மீமிசை அயருங் குரவை) completes the item of the kuravai begun in lines 320 and 321, and line 323 opens the item of the echoing stream.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill's life is described as the wealth and joy of the patron's land, whose people bring him tribute: praise of the patron (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the herd at the tiger's leap

reading: More sounds: the deep echo in the clefts where the rocky stream roars as if a tall fine chariot were coming along the track; the cries of mahouts speaking a mixed tongue to cool the rage of a fierce elephant caught in a deep pool, so as to tie it to a great post; the shouts of girls scaring parrots from every millet plot, beating split-bamboo clappers; the clamour as a fine bull with shaking hump, strayed from its herd, clashes with unfailing strength against the eager bull of the wild cattle come down the hill, while cowherds and hill men cheer together and the kulavi and kurinji are crushed; and the noise of the boys who, brandishing fragrant kaanthal stalks, drive off the calves to get the seeds from the leftovers of the sweet jackfruit segments they have eaten.
nuance: The mahouts' விரவுமொழி, a speech of mixed words, is one of the few signs in the idyll of the many tongues of the hill country. The bull fight brings together the herders of the slopes (கோவலர்) and the hill men (குறவர்) in one cheer: the patron's land is shown as a meeting of peoples.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 322-340: it begins after குரவை (322) and ends at the item of the boys, closed by ஓதை in line 339; line 340 opens the item of the sugar mills.

thinai_evidence.note: the work and play of the patron's hill people, heard as one resonance in his praise

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the rocky stream echoing in the clefts

reading: And the work-song of the sugar cane that suddenly bursts its joints in every mill, the vallai song of the girls pounding millet, the drums and the hill echoes of those who guard the taro and turmeric from boars: all these together, gathered in the hollows and on the heights, past counting, make the resonance of the mountain sound in every direction; his wide hill, where the women wear garlands of coloured flowers and the drum never sleeps in the broad town, is like a festival.
nuance: Line 348 is the line that names the poem: மலைபடு கடாஅம், the resonance born of the mountain, compared by its very word (கடாம், the musth of an elephant) to a living beast. The whole list from the previous chapter to here is the subject of இயம்ப. The vehicle of line 340 is uncertain: the mills may be likened to rain clouds for their noise or for the steam over them.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 341-351: it begins at line 340, the start of the item of the sugar mills (ஆலைதொறு ... ஏத்தமும், 340 to 341).

thinai_evidence.note: the sum of the hill's sounds is named as the glory of the patron's mountain

comparisons.tenor: the sugar mills, roaring as when rain clouds gather

reading: Having looked and listened till your eyes are cooled, and praised the many things sweet to eat, saying 'there is more to come for us', you who keep the old custom should leave behind the great thundering mountain of the lord whose fortunate chest loves battle, let your viraliyar sing kurinji on the fragrant rainy slope, worship it with joined hands and go on; when the flock of rain clouds, so low on the dark hill that a hand could touch it, sprays its fine drizzle, enter clefts like wells so that your kin, who cannot tell the way, keep the instruments they carry from harm; and in the gorge where boulders roll and even to stand and look makes the eyes swim, keep away from the broken cliff, use the head-stick of your earth-smeared drum as a staff, guard against slipping and lean on it as you go, for the dangers are very many.
nuance: Leaving the mountain is itself a rite: the troupe sings the mountain's own mode, kurinji, and bows to it before going. The care in the instructions is for the instruments as much as for the people: the drum's stick becomes a walking staff, so the bard's craft is what carries him through the danger.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide's instructions for the road to the patron: the ஆற்றுப்படை speech itself

comparisons.tenor: the rain clouds lying low on the hill
the fine drizzle the clouds spray
the deep clefts that serve as shelter

reading: Over the path where rocks sharp as heated spearheads are guarded by the sun, travel only when the rays' heat has eased; his land has strongholds that shake kings from their footing, with his retinue that never leaves him, whose fame has spread, and many shields raised high like clouds; at every opening of the thickets tangled like braids, keep from the swift-springing shaft the man ahead has drawn, guard the bowl of your sweet yaazh and the stretched head of your drum, keep your grip, and go slowly; boulders packed together like fighting elephants stand in the dripping forest beyond counting, and at the forks of the path there are countless stones planted with the names of undying fame of the honourable warriors who gave themselves on the good path when the hostile foe was routed with a shout.
nuance: The shaft of line 380 is most naturally the branch the walker in front has bent aside, which springs back like an arrow; the reading is not certain. The hero-stones do not mark danger, as they do on the akam roads: they carry names (பெயரொடு நட்ட), and the guide counts them as part of the land's glory. Hour is a precaution: cross the hot rock only when the sun has weakened.

thinai_evidence.note: the road's hazards and the patron's strongholds and warrior stones, told as his land's might

comparisons.tenor: the sharp rock of the path

reading: As your songs please, keep the ancient custom, lower the neck of your instrument and hurry on; you newcomers who have never known this land should tie knots of grass where the ways cross, so as to know the names of the places you are bound for; there are many forks of the forest path where the god stands high in the kadamba with a fine trunk on which letters have been scratched with stones, and many wastes that the foes who fled without joining battle tremble even to mention; if you say you are going to the generous lord with the honey-dripping garland, whose hand flings away chariots and who does not hoard, his ancient town of old lineage is that way, so it is for people like us.
nuance: The tree with letters scratched on it (கல்லெறிந் தெழுதிய, 395) is a signpost: writing on the road, an early witness to letters used for travellers. Lines 391 (மருப்பிகுத்து) and 401 to 402 are hard: what is lowered may be the horn-neck of the yaazh, and தொஃறிணை and ஆங்கனம் அற்றே are read here as 'of old lineage' and 'it is that way', which I cannot confirm.

thinai_evidence.note: directions to the patron whose generosity is the goal of the road

reading: Rest where you tire and go on without fear: beyond the forest where the stag stands calling, remembering the beloved doe the tiger came for, and past the mullai country of fragrant creepers where the red-eyed bull of the wild cattle, frightened by the sound of bows, rushes into the thicket, the cowherds of the hedged land, whose herds with their bulls have gone to other pastures, will pour out the sweet milk of their white cows to the joy of the bangled women, and the loneliness of leaving home in hope of gain will go far from you, and you will be like new; if you come in at nightfall, where the many flocks of rams, ewes and white goats, mixed like the rows of grain at a barter, bleat like the sea in the noisy waste, you will get milk and porridge without asking.
nuance: The stag calling for the doe the tiger took is an image akam poets use for loss, but here it is only the edge of a forest the troupe passes on its way to milk and porridge; in a puram guide poem it carries no hidden sense. The bards' homesickness (புலம்பு) is cured by food, not by return.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 403-416: the condition of line 416 (எல்லினிர் புகினே) is completed by பெறுகுவிர் in line 417, which ends the sentence.

thinai_evidence.note: the hospitality of the herders in the patron's land, promised to the bard

comparisons.tenor: the mixed flocks of rams, ewes and white goats

reading: Sleep on beds of trampled hide flayed from beasts, soft as a mattress packed with fine hair, with the fire for company, and go on; if you meet a band of curved-bow Kooliyar, whose sharp arrows outrun a shout, and say you are going to the husband of the creeper-slender lady, whose unbowing manhood wore down those who stood against him, they will gather meat and roots and bring them to you: there they are guardians, not attackers; go your way, for that is their nature.
nuance: The patron is named only through his wife (கொடியோள் கணவன்) and his manhood, yet saying it is a safe-conduct: men whose arrows are faster than a call for help become providers. The fear the bowmen would raise is called up only to be cancelled (உடற்றுநர் இல்லை), so no meyppadu is shown.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 417-427: line 417 moved to the previous unit, which it completes; this unit begins at துய்ம்மயிர் (418).

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's name turns the road's bowmen into hosts: praise of his power

reading: Wearing lovely garlands of the soft honey-blooming kadamba clusters and all the bright sprouts the elephant has broken, woven with young leaves and tied with dried fibre, eat, bathe and take what you want on the path through the broken gravel that is cool there, and go on; in every grass-roofed hut built with crowded poles in the wide hollow, so that the toil of your night's labour ends, you will get porridge of bamboo rice red as vengai flowers, and green pulse of avarai with paddy grown on the ridge; and if you rest and stay you will get every day rice fine as beaten gold, cooked in white dense balls with cool fine ghee inside.
nuance: The garland of line 430 is made from what an elephant has left (உம்பல் அகைத்த): the troupe adorns itself with the forest's leftovers. The meals rise in richness as the stay lengthens, from roadside eating to porridge in every hut to ghee-filled rice every day.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 428-444: line 444 opens the simile (விசையங் கொழித்த பூழி யன்ன) that governs the flour of line 445, so it moves to the next unit; this one ends at பெறுகுவிர், 443.

thinai_evidence.note: the food and rest promised in the patron's hill country

reading: Lighting a blaze of light wood, eat the fine millet flour, like dust sifted from sugar, that holds back other eaters, sleep sweetly together far from the cold, and at dawn take the birds' omens and go on; whether you stay many days or rest and go, his cool fertile country has much good, with groves and lodges, varied as the modes changed on a fine yaazh, in every town on the soft low ground beside sluices struck by water where the thin-trunked kaanji grows.
nuance: The simile of line 451 is a musician's: passing from town to town is like a bard changing the mode on his yaazh, so the landscape is heard as a performance. Line 445's உண்ணுநர்த் தடுத்த is read as a flour so filling or so sweet that it stops the eaters; the sense is not certain. The country now leaves the hills for the watered low ground.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 428-444 and 445-460: it begins at line 444, whose simile governs the flour of 445, and ends at நாடே, 453, which closes the sentence on his country; line 454 begins the scene of the fields.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's country is praised for its goodness to travellers

comparisons.tenor: the groves and lodges of every town, each different and pleasing

reading: In the fields fragrant with kanpu reeds, the women of the Pazhaiyar, wearing pakandrai garlands, set on the raised bank of a crab-haunted plot the dark-backed vaalai the net-men bring and the red-eyed varaal, like an elephant cow's trunk, taken on the long lines of men who stand to fish, mixed with cut pieces round as the heads of hand drums; and when the workers who make the land rich have finished threshing the hill-like stacks and give out their food, you will get at every threshing floor, in the young sun of morning, toddy from fresh packets poured out of swaying jars.
nuance: Line 460 is a repaired reading (தராய், a raised bank). The workers' gift is made at the moment of harvest: the bard arrives when the land is richest and is fed from the threshing floor itself.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 445-460 and 461-481: it begins at கண்புமலி (454), where the scene of the fields opens, and ends at பெறுகுவிர், 464.

thinai_evidence.note: the farmers' bounty in the patron's fields, promised to the bard

reading: Eat with your troupe, to the wonder of all who see, white rice cooked with cucumber whose spines are scraped off, food you will say is fit even for Nannan of the strong chariot whose honey-dripping garland is fragrant with bees; then rest, playing marutham on your fine yaazh to the shouts of the field-hands driving their oxen, and go on; watching for the charge of the lone bull buffalo, strayed from its red-eyed herd in fright at the drums of the reapers of white paddy, take the one rich bank of the Seyaru, pleasant to the eye and longed for by those who see it, whose swift head-current roars without pause where bubbles whirl like a potter's wheel, and go on.
nuance: As the troupe played kurinji when leaving the hill (359), here it plays marutham among the fields: the bards change mode with the land. வெள்ளரி may be white grain rather than cucumber; the scraped spines (முள்ளரித்து) favour the cucumber.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 461-481: it begins at முள்ளரித் (465) and ends at கழிமின், 477; line 478 begins the description of the patron's town.

thinai_evidence.note: the food fit for the patron himself is given to the bard: praise of his land's bounty

comparisons.tenor: the bubbles whirling in the river's current

reading: His ancient town of old valour is not far: within its high rising enclosure where wealth lies asleep, old families who never leave their place live together; its great market is too crowded for its wide space, its ways lie spread like a river, its festival is like a battle, its lanes forking so that scorners fear them; with a din like the sea and like thunder, mansions rising like mountains and like clouds, people dwelling sweetly in a love that knows no quarrel, and cool groves loud with bees; enter without doubting the closely guarded gate whose doors bear the black-butted spears leaned there by bright-sworded warriors who cut off the heads of hostile foes so that kites gather.
nuance: The town is built of two opposites held together: a market crowded like a battle and people living in love without quarrel; the gate is armed against foes and open to bards (அயிராது புகுமின்). Line 481's செருவிற் சாறென ('a festival like a battle') is odd after யாறெனக் கிடந்த, which would suit தெருவின் (streets).
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 461-481 and 482-497: it begins at நிதியந் (478), where the town's description opens, and ends at புகுமின், 491.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's town and fortress, which the bard may enter freely

reading: In the common ground the suppliants from far lands staying there, remembering the great valour of the red lord who wins his wars, will say 'surely those who have come deserve pity'; all who see you look on you sweetly and gladly, and each comes to meet you with a guest's welcome, so that the toil the long road has beaten into you may end; and there crowd the gifts of the hill: the calf of the gentle-gaited forest cow caught when its herd fled the kadamba whose flowered boughs seem to spit fire, the curve-pawed cub of the silent bear, the great strong-headed ram of the cliff-dwelling varudai with crooked legs and leaping gait, the small-eyed creature that kills the snakes in their holes, the big-eared calf of the soft-eyed wild cow seized by the tiger that lurks in its den, the crooked-legged male monitor that crawls on gravel by ground red as spread lac, the soft-eyed peacock that goes gracing the hill, the forest cock with its forked call, the great drum-like fruits of the forest jack, and the sweet ripe fruit of the fragrant mango, full of juice.
nuance: The welcome is a look before it is a gift: the whole town 'looks sweetly' (அமர்ந்தினிது நோக்கி) on the newcomers. The gifts are the hill's own wild young, caught alive, and its fruits: the patron gives his land, not only his treasury. சேஎய் (493) calls the patron by Murugan's epithet, the red one. தீர்வை (504) is a creature I cannot identify, and the simile of 512 (இடிக்கலப்பு) is unclear.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 482-497 and 498-513: it begins at மன்றில் (492), where the arrival in the town opens; it ends at line 513 inside the long list of gifts (498 to 531), cut there to keep the units within 30 lines.

thinai_evidence.note: the welcome and gifts awaiting the bard at the patron's town

comparisons.tenor: the flowering boughs of the kadamba

reading: With them the growing creeper whose buds have shot up in the spray, the yam like a yoke carried slung from a pole, the many-faceted fine gems shed from great crystal, the pearl-holding tusks, massive and strong, of an elephant wounded in a fight with a striped tiger, kaanthal with large petals like broken conch bangles, naagam, tilakam and the fragrant heartwood of sandal, green pepper in clusters from the dark pepper vine, well-matured toddy of honey, sweet curd of the forest buffalo poured into bamboo, the ghee-eyed honeycomb that rolls like a wheel down the high slope when the dark-blue ori leaps on it, and wild jack clasped together: all of these, crowding at the long gate of his unbearable war like the broad Kaveri, born on Kudamalai, at the mouth where it plunges into the sea; approach the courtyard thick with the pollen-strewn dung of his elephants, as many as the sky.
nuance: The great simile turns the list into a river: the wealth of the hills flows down to the patron's gate as the Kaveri flows down from Kudamalai to the sea, so the gate is the estuary of the land. What ஓரி (524) names is uncertain.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 514-528 and 529-543: it ends at முன்னி (531), where the list of gifts and the approach to the courtyard close; line 532 begins the music at court.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill's riches crowd the patron's gate as tribute: praise of his wealth

comparisons.tenor: the gifts crowding at the patron's gate
the multitude of the patron's elephants

reading: As the drumheads boom as if answering the rain clouds and the holes of the bamboo pipe hum, the sweet-voiced viraliyar, playing marutham on the black-necked small yaazh with strings in unison that never overstep, knowing what is due and keeping their nature by the old custom, first praise the god of great power, then finish the song of welcome, and with long words hail him: 'Lord, scion of those whose good fame does not fail, you who, now that the great ones who could tell merit have died, have paid the debt of giving so that fame does not leave the world today but stays with it'; praising his victories, his many fames and his strength; but he does not let them even tell of their journey: 'Desire brought you; your coming is enough; your toil was great.'
nuance: Giving is called a debt (கொடைக்கடன்), owed to the world now that the old discerning patrons are gone: the patron inherits the obligation along with the line. His interruption is the best praise in the poem: the suppliants are spared the telling of their hardship.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 529-543 and 544-556: it begins at மழையெதிர் (532), the music in the court, and ends at பெரிதென (546), where the patron's words of welcome close.

thinai_evidence.note: the bards' praise of the patron's giving and fame, and his welcome: paadaan proper

reading: He reflects that those who shone among warriors ready for battle, who, wishing to approach the courtyard of a fortunate city, kept their noisy kin about them on the right, who sat on high thrones among fearless kin with wide inheritance and keen wit, and yet spread their hands saying 'we have nothing', died taking their names with them, and they outnumber the sands of the scarred banks of the Seyaru, whose fierce muddy flood pours down from the high hill's waterfall; 'therefore let our allotted days pass with fame': with that sky-touching heart that gives room to all, gladder than you who came in longing, he looks on you sweetly, wraps your waist with fine cloth whose threads cannot be seen, and feeds you with the fresh fat meat the hounds bring and unfailing rice of long white paddy, welcoming you as on the first day however many days you stay.
nuance: On the reading taken here, இலமென மலர்ந்த கையர் (552) are men who spread empty hands saying 'we have nothing', so their names died with them; read instead as hands that opened when suppliants said 'we have nothing', the lines would say that even great givers died, and fame alone remains. Either way the patron's giving is argued from death. Who speaks lines 547 to 557 is not marked: the patron's thought is given as a quotation closed by என (557).
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 544-556 and 557-572: it begins at பொருமுரண் (547), the reflection on the dead, and ends at பெறுகுவிர் (566), which closes the promise of daily hospitality.

thinai_evidence.note: the unit turns on the thought of death and the fame that outlasts it (perunilai of kaanchi), which becomes the motive for giving

comparisons.tenor: those who died taking their names with them

reading: If you tell him gently, 'we will not stay; we go back to our old village', he will crown the leader among you with a lotus and have the viraliyar wear bright jewels of great worth, and with tall chariots that run in rows like flowing water, hill-like elephants too great to be held, great herds with bulls and ringing bells, cut-maned horses bright in golden trappings and treasure heaped till it wears down the ground, all of it filling the outstretched hands of needy poets, from his great hand with its sliding bracelet that tips as it pours out vessels, never knowing a failure of wealth and rich in kind speech, giving like the rain that suddenly pours on the high peak of Naviram where the bamboo grows, he sends you off with gifts on the first day you ask: he, the lord of the land of hill-ringed dwellings where the mountain waters show like victory flags.
nuance: The whole idyll is one sentence whose subject arrives only in its last word, நாடுகிழவோனே: everything the guide has said waits on the patron's title. The leaving gift is given on the first day it is asked (தலைநாள்), matching the welcome 'as on the first day' (565): neither the welcome nor the farewell wears out.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 557-572 and 573-583: it begins at செல்வேந் (567), the guests' word of leaving, and runs to the end of the poem.
